menus.Name: acne
menus.Text:
# ACNE

Acne is an inflammatory skin condition caused by excess sebum production, gland obstruction and infection with Cutibacterum acnes. Early disease manifests with black heads and white heads and little inflammation. Small papules and pustules are present in mild disease. Severe disease occurs when comedones, papules, pustules and less often cysts are present.

The goal of treatment is prevention and reeducation of new comedones and creating an environment that is inhibitory for C. acnes. General skin care treatment measures include utilizing gentle skin cleansers, avoiding aggressive scrubbing, using non-comedogenic skin products, and avoiding picking of lesions.

Diet's role in therapy remains uncertain.

Non-Antimicrobial therapy includes benzoyl peroxide topical/wash, salicylic acid topical, and tretinoin topical. These agents can be used as monotherapy in early disease and in addition to antimicrobial treatment in mild to severe disease.

---

menus.Name: acute-bact-prostatitis
menus.Text:
# ACUTE BACTERIAL PROSTATITIS

Acute bacterial prostatitis typically presents with fever, dysuria, chills, malaise, myalgia, pelvic or perianal pain. On exam, the prostate gland is tense, boggy, and extremely tender. The urinalysis reveals pyuria, and the urine culture is positive. Men with dysuria and fever but without pyuria and/or bacteriuria should be seen by a urologist. If there is any suspicion of abscess, especially in men older than 40 years, the patient should be seen by a urologist and transurethral prostate resection for drainage should be considered.

Most cases in men aged 35 and older, those with recent urinary tract instrumentation or surgery (e.g., prostate biopsy, vasectomy) are associated with enteric Gram-negative rods. Most cases in men under age 35 and those who are at high risk of sexually transmitted infections are associated with N. gonorrhoeae and C. trachomatis. Resistant organisms are more likely if the patient has been in the hospital for more than 48 hours or received a course of antibiotics. There is increasing resistance in urinary pathogens to ciprofloxacin.

A urine Gram stain and culture should be performed in all patients to guide antimicrobial therapy:
Lab menu

## Duration

There is limited data on duration of antimicrobial treatment for prostatitis. 14 days minimum is required. 4 to 6 weeks may be necessary to completely eradicate bacteria in the prostate to ensure patient does not progress to chronic bacterial prostatitis.

---

---

References:

- Lipsky et al., Clinical Infectious Diseases, 2010, 50(12)1641-1652
- Mandell chapter: Prostatitis, Epididymitis and Orchitis
- Sanford keyword: Prostatitis
- Up-To-Date article: Acute Bacterial Prostatitis

menus.Name: acute-sinusitis
menus.Text:
# ACUTE SINUSITIS

Most cases of acute sinusitis are viral and resolve within 10 days. Symptoms (nasal congestion, purulent nasal discharge, and tooth or facial pain) can be treated with decongestants, analgesics, and nasal saline. Diagnosis of acute sinusitis is based on the presence of at least 2 major or 1 major and at least 2 minor symptoms.

## Major Symptoms

1. Purulent anterior nasal discharge
2. Purulent or discolored posterior nasal discharge
3. Nasal congestion or fullness
4. Facial pain or pressure
5. Hyposmia or anosmia
6. Fever

## Minor Symptoms

1. Headache
2. Ear pain, pressure or fullness
3. Halitosis
4. Dental pain
5. Cough
6. Fatigue

If patient meets criteria above for acute sinusitis, treat with antimicrobials according to the following criteria for mild to moderate or severe bacterial sinusitis.

## Mild to moderate bacterial sinusitis

1. Symptoms persisting beyond 10 days

< OR >

2. Double-sickening - Symptoms typical of viral upper respiratory infection initially improving for 5-6 days then worsening with new development of fever, headache or increased nasal discharge.

## Severe bacterial sinusitis

Severe signs or symptoms of high fever (>/= 102 degrees Fahrenheit, >/= 39 degrees Celsius) and purulent nasal discharge for 3-4 consecutive days or facial pain lasting for at least 3-4 consecutive days at the beginning of illness.

---

menus.Name: antiviral-immunosuppressive-malignancy
menus.Text:
# PREVENTION OF ANTIVIRAL INFECTIONS IN A PATIENT WITH MALIGNANCY

## Severly Immunosuppressive Chemo-immunotherapy

## Purine Analogues

Chemotherapy with purine analogues such as fludarabine, cladribine, or pentostatin results in major cellular-immunodeficiency that may outlast the exposure by months and enhances the risk for viral infections.
Recommend antiviral prophylaxis for patients treated with purine analogues, if at least one of the following risk factors is present:
a) Second-line chemotherapy b) Treatment with corticosteroids c) CD4 cell count <50/ul d) Age >65 years e) Prolonged Mild or Moderate Neutropenia: Mild<1000 Neutrophils / ï¿½L (Grade III neutropenia) OR Moderate: <500 Neutrophils/ï¿½L (Grade IV neutropenia)

## Recommendations:

Duration: Antiviral prophylaxis should be initiated in the first week of therapy and continued until 2 months after completion of therapy.
Acyclovir 800 MG PO q12h ($) [R]

References:

- Taplitz RA Journal of Clinical Oncology 2018, 36:3043
- Mandel Chapter: Prophylaxis and Empirical Therapy of Infection in
- Cancer Patients
- Up-to-Date website
- Sandherr M Annals of Oncology 2006, 17:1051

## Outpatient

Guidance

## Recommendations:

Acyclovir 800 MG PO BID ($0.40/day) [R]
menus.Therapy:
## Alemtuzumab Therapy:

Alemtuzumab is a potent reactivator of latent intracellular pathogens, including CMV. Chemotherapy with alemtuzumab results in major cellular-immunodeficiency that may outlast the exposure by months and enhances the risk for viral infections. The risk of viral disease increases with the intensity and duration of functional T-cell suppression experienced with recipients of alemtuzumab.

## Recommendations:

Duration: Initiate antiviral prophylaxis with alemtuzumab therapy and continue therapy for at least 2 months after last dose or until CD4 counts are greater than or equal to 200 cells/ul, whichever is later.
Acyclovir 800 MG PO q12h ($) [R]

menus.Name: antiviral-infection-malignancy
menus.Text:
# PREVENTION OF VIRAL INFECTIONS IN A PATIENT WITH MALIGNANCY

## Prophylaxis for Herpes Simplex Virus (HSV) or Varicella Zoster Virus (VZV)

[Select for recommendations for antiviral prophylaxis](antiviral-immunosuppressive-malignancy)

## Prophylaxis for Influenza and Other Respiratory Viruses

Yearly influenza vaccination with inactivated vaccine is recommended for all patients receiving chemotherapy for malignancy and all family and household contacts and health care providers.
Optimal timing of vaccination for patients being treated for cancer is not established, but serologic responses may be best between chemotherapy cycles (greater than 7 days after the last treatment) or greater than 2 weeks before chemotherapy starts.
Patients with active malignant disease are at higher risk for upper respiratory infections due to influenza, parainfluenza or respiratory syncytial virus (RSV). Although response to vaccination with the attenuated influenza vaccine in patients on chemotherapy is variable, ranging from 24-75%, immnunoprophylaxis with the influenza vaccine is recommended for patients with active malignant disease or chemotherapy, lymphoproliferative disease, or multiple myeloma. In areas and seasons where influenza is endemic, chemoprophylaxis can be considered in addition to vaccination in exposed patients with a high risk of influenza complications.

## Recommendations:

[Seasonal Influenza Recommendations](influenza-recommendations)

## Prophylaxis for Cytomegalovirus (CMV)

Prophylaxis and monitoring for CMV reactivation is not recommended unless the patient has received an allogeneic HSCT. Usually the recommendations for surveillance and prophylaxis of CMV infections from the institution performing the HSCT will be followed.

## Recommendations:

Consult Infectious Disease

## Prophylaxis for Chronic Hepatitis B

Reactivation of chronic hepatitis B in patients undergoing immunosuppressive or antineoplastic treatment is a severe complication. Patients with positive HBsAg, chronic hepatitis B infection, or a previous episode of HBV reactivation who will receive immunosuppressive therapy should receive prophylaxis.
Recommend routine testing for Hepatitis B prior to initiating Rituximab (Anti-CD20 antibody) therapy in patients.

## Recommendations:

[Hepatitis B Evaluation Anti-CD20 Antibody](hepatitis-b-evaluation-anti-cd20-antibody)
Consult Infectious Disease

## References:

- Mandel Chapter: Prophylaxis and Empirical Therapy of Infection in
- Cancer Patients

- Up-to-Date website
- Sandherr M Annals of Oncology 2006, 17: 1051-1059, 2006

menus.Name: antiviral-treatment
menus.Text:
# INFLUENZA ANTIVIRAL THERAPY RECOMMENDATIONS

## Who to Treat:

The decision to treat should be based on clinical symptoms and/or presence of a high-risk condition and should NOT be delayed until laboratory test results are available.

It is important to use antiviral drugs early to treat influenza in people who are very sick with influenza (for example, hospitalized people) and people who are sick with influenza and have a greater chance of getting severe complications. If a patient is not in a high-risk group or is not hospitalized, healthcare providers should use clinical judgment to guide treatment decisions.

## People who have a greater chance of serious influenza complications include:

\*Adults aged 65 years or older
\*Persons who have chronic pulmonary (including asthma) or cardiovascular (except isolated hypertension), renal, hepatic, hematologic, metabolic disorders (including diabetes mellitus), neurologic and neuro-developmental disorders \*Persons who are immunocompromised due to any cause (including immunosuppression caused by medications or by HIV infection)
\*Pregnant women and women up to 2 weeks after the end of pregnancy \*Persons younger than 19 years of age who are receiving long-term aspirin- or salicylate-containing medications and who might be at risk for experiencing Reye syndrome after influenza virus infection \*Residents of nursing homes and other long-term care facilities \*Non-Hispanic Black persons, Hispanic or Latino persons, and American Indian or Alaska Native persons \*Persons who are extremely obese (BMI greater than or equal to 40)

---

References:

- Centers for Disease Control (CDC) (Accessed 9/20/23) https://www.cdc.gov/flu/professionals/antivirals/summary-clinician
- UpToDate Seasonal influenza in adults: Treatment
menus.Therapy:
## Antiviral Treatment:

If indicated, antivirals should be started as soon as possible. Maximal benefit occurs when treatment is started within 48 hours of symptom onset. However, antivirals should not be withheld if symptoms begin more than 48 hours prior and the patient meets criteria for treatment and remains severely ill.

## Treatment Dosing:

Zanamivir is not recommended for patients with chronic respiratory diseases such as asthma or chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. These patients may have bronchospasm with zanamivir. If zanamivir must be used, and patients are using an inhaled bronchodilator, zanamivir should be taken just after the bronchodilator.

Extending the duration of treatment for oseltamivir or peramivir may be needed for those patients with prolonged illness or who are immunosuppressed.

## Preferred:

Oseltamivir 75 mg po bid [R] for 5 days

## \*\*Below is for information only, quick orders are not available

## Alternative:

Requires Infectious Disease Approval

## Inpatient/Outpatient

Zanamivir 2 inhalations (2 x 5 mg) BID [O] for 5 days
< OR >
Baloxavir 80 mg PO x1 dose patients wt 80 kg or greater, 40 mg PO x 1 dose for patients wt < 80 kg [DI]

## Alternative for patients unable to tolerate or absorb oral oseltamivir:

Peramivir may not be available. Contact Infectious Disease for more information.

Requires Infectious Disease Approval
Hospitalized, high risk:
Peramivir 600 mg IV q24h [R] for 5 days
Acute, uncomplicated:
Peramivir 600 mg IV Once [R]

menus.Name: antiviral-type-of-malignancy
menus.Text:
# PREVENTION OF ANTIVIRAL INFECTIONS IN A PATIENT WITH MALIGNANCY

## **Solid Tumors**

## No Antiviral Prophylaxis Recommended

Solid tumors do not significantly compromise the cellular immune system.
Therefore, patients are at low risk for opportunistic viral infections.
Documented invasive viral infections are very rare. Coincidental mucocutaneous infections by herpes simplex are easily treated and do not result in life-threatening invasive infections. Reactivation of Cytomegalovirus (CMV) or Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) is rarely observed.

## **Acute Leukemia**

## Herpes simplex virus-seronegative patients

No Antiviral Prophylaxis Recommended
In patients with acute leukemia, treatment is highly aggressive and consists of a combination of various cytotoxic agents administered in sequential cycles as induction, consolidation and maintenance therapy. Persistent, i.e.
10 days and profound neutropenia (<500 neutrophils) regularly occurs and correlates with the risk of developing fever and infections. Almost all viral infections during neutropenia constitute reactivations of herpes viruses.
None of the available studies demonstrated an effect of antiviral prophylaxis on the initiation of antibiotic treatment, number of febrile days, duration of antibiotic treatment, and onset of opportunistic infections. Therefore, no recommendation for antiviral prophylaxis in patients with acute leukemia can be given.

## Herpes simplex virus-seropostive patients

Patients undergoing leukemia induction therapy should receive prophylaxis.
Acyclovir 800 MG PO q12h ($) [R]

## **Lymphoma**

## No Antiviral Prophylaxis Recommended

Rituximab is a monoclonal anti-CD-20 antibody used for treatment of lymphomas. It leads to a profound depletion of circulating B-cells. B-cells recover usually within 3-6 months after treatment. Prolonged administration of rituximab (e.g., maintenance treatment >12 months) may result in a significant decrease of levels of immunoglobulin M. Parvovirus B19 and JC-papovavirus infections have been reported with maintenance rituximab therapy, but drugs that would prevent these infections are not available. There is no substantial increase in risk of reactivation of herpes viruses (including HSV, VZV, and CMV).
Recommend routine testing for Hepatitis B virus prior to initiating Rituximab therapy in patients.
[Hepatitis B information page](hepatitis-b)
[Hepatitis B Evaluation Anti-CD20 Antibody](hepatitis-b-evaluation-anti-cd20-antibody)

## References:

- Mandel Chapter: Prophylaxis and Empirical Therapy of Infection in
- Cancer Patients

menus.Text:
# APPENDICITIS WITHOUT PERFORATION

[Oral step-down treatment](step-down-treatment)
Patients with an acutely inflamed appendix and no gangrene or perforation are considered to have uncomplicated appendicitis. Patients with gangrene, perforation, peritonitis, or abscess have complicated appendicitis. Treatment with antibiotics is an option for patients who are unfit for surgery or refuse surgery. Treatment with antibiotics should not be used routinely as an alternative to surgery.

# ASPIRATION PNEUMONIA

When a larger than usual volume of orogastric content is aspirated, mechanical/chemical irritation occurs. Some of these develop into bacterial pneumonia.

It is reasonable to wait before starting antimicrobials to see if respiratory impairment improves or worsens before starting bacterial pneumonia treatment, in hemodynamically stable patients.

Therapy directed towards anaerobic pathogens is usually unnecessary. Antimicrobial treatment is warranted if pneumonia is confirmed.

menus.Name: asymp-bacteriuria
menus.Text:
# ASYMPTOMATIC BACTERIURIA

Asymptomatic bacteriuria is common in women and elderly people, especially in those with chronic medical problems (e.g., diabetes, spinal cord injury, institutionalized patients, catheterized patients). Most patients have no adverse outcomes and receive no benefit from treatment of asymptomatic bacteriuria.

Patients who have no symptoms of cystitis (i.e., no dysuria, pain, urgency) should not be treated. The presence of pyuria (>7 wbc/hpf) or positive leukocyte esterase, urine nitrate, or urine bacteria is not a sufficient indication for antibiotic treatment. Screening and treatment of asymptomatic bacteriuria is indicated for pregnant women and patients who will have urological procedures and may be indicated in patients < 1-month post-renal transplant. If an indwelling catheter is in place and can be removed safely, it should be done as the bacteriuria may clear.

Bacteriuria in pregnant women is associated with pyelonephritis, premature delivery, and lower birth weight. Screening for bacteriuria is recommended at least once early in pregnancy. If bacteriuria is not found upon initial testing, further screening cultures are not needed. If bacteriuria (>10,000 CFU/mL) is present, the patient should be treated. Testing should be repeated throughout the pregnancy to detect recurrences.

# AZITHROMYCIN FOR PREVENTION OF EXACERBATIONS IN ADVANCED COPD

## Eligibility Criteria:

\*Age >40 years
\*Clinical diagnosis of COPD (>= 10 pack-years cigarette smoking, a ratio of postbronchodilator forced expiratory volume in 1 second [FEV1] to forced vital capacity of <70%, and a postbronchodilator FEV1 of <80% of the predicted value), _AND_
\*Were either using continuous supplemental oxygen or had received systemic glucocorticoids within the previous year, _OR_ \*Had gone to an emergency room or had been hospitalized for an acute exacerbation of COPD.

## Exclusion criteria:

\*Asthma
\*People with hearing impairments
\*Congestive heart failure
\*Resting heart rate > 100 beats per minute
\*Use of medications that are associated with torsades de pointes (except for amiodarone)
\*Prolonged QTc interval (>450 msec)
\*Use of medications that prolong the QTc interval

Please Click Here for Resource for Drugs that Cause QTc Prolongation If, after trying all the standard treatments, patients are still having acute exacerbations of COPD, long-term antibiotic treatment with Azithromycin may be considered. Note: Guidelines for COPD can be found on the CPRS Tools Menu.

Inpatient COPD Exacerbation Orders
If the patient meets the criteria and is willing to have audiometric testing and an electrocardiogram, please place a Pulmonary Consult for long-term Azithromycin therapy for the prevention COPD exacerbations.

menus.Text:
# BALANITIS AND BALANOPOSTHITIS

Balanitis is inflammation of the glans penis and is often associated with erythema and pruritis. When the foreskin is also involved, the condition is known as balanoposthitis (also referred to as balanitis in this discussion).

There are a variety of causes of balanitis, but most are due to poor hygiene of the foreskin in uncircumcised men resulting in candida infection. Other, less common causes, include bacterial infection (typically sexually transmitted or anaerobic bacteria), dermatologic conditions, malignancy as well as others. Men with Candidal balanitis often have a white curd-like exudate compared to a thick foul-smelling purulent exudate in menu with anaerobic bacterial balanitis.

Patients at risk of sexually transmitted infections should be assessed for treatment:
[Sexually Transmitted Infections and HIV Exposure](sexually-transmitted-infection)

menus.Text:
# BELL'S PALSY

Herpes simplex and varicella-zoster are possible causes of Bell's palsy. Others include Borrelia burgdorferi or trauma. Some cases are idiopathic. Risk factors for Bell's Palsy include pregnancy, diabetes, obesity, hypertension, and upper respiratory infections. Neurology consult is encouraged.

If Lyme disease is suspected, refer to the Lyme disease treatment page:
[Lyme Disease](lyme-disease)

Treatment with prednisone and an antiviral within 72 hours of symptoms onset improves the chances of a complete recovery.

![Bell's Palsy face](/assets/uploads/001-TestStation/palsyExample.jpg "Bell's Palsy")

# BITE WOUNDS WITH STAPHYLOCOCCUS AUREUS

---

## BITE WOUNDS

Bite wounds are prone to infection because of the pathogenic oral flora carried into tissues by teeth. Clean wounds with soap and water as soon as possible.
Consult Orthopedic surgery for bite wounds involving the hand.

## Antibiotic Prophylaxis Indications:

Severe injury less than 8 hours, Crush injury, Bone or joint penetration, Wound of the face or hands or genitals, Immunocompromised host, Asplenia, Advanced liver disease
*Routine use of prophylactic antibiotics for non-immunocompromised patients with superficial wounds with no puncture that do not involve the face/ genitals/hands is not recommended.

## Antimicrobial Treatment:

Empiric treatment for suspected or established infection following bite wound In these cases, therapy should be directed against pathogen identified by Gram stain and culture whenever possible.

## Rabies Prophylaxis:

Consider rabies post-exposure prophylaxis for all animal bite cases. Contact Infectious diseases for assistance.

## Consider tetanus immunization status:

If immunization is up to date, nothing more needs to be done to prevent tetanus.
If immunization is lacking, and: wound IS NOT tetanus prone, bring immunization up to date with Td wound IS tetanus prone, bring immunization up to date with Td < AND > Human Tetanus Immune Globulin Inject 250 units deeply into muscle (deep IM)

## Select below for Tetanus vaccination information page:

[Tetanus, Diphtheria and Acellular Pertussis Vaccine Information Page](tetanus-diphtheria-and-acellular-pertussis-vaccine-information)

## Prophylaxis:

Duration 3 to 5 days:

# BODY LICE (PEDICULOSIS CORPORIS)

Lice are parasitic insects. Human lice survive by feeding on human blood. Body lice proliferate in places where crowding of persons with poor hygiene is common, especially homeless persons. Infested clothing and bed linen should be heat washed or discarded. Itching is the most common symptom, but some patients present only with excoriations and inflammation on the neck and trunk.

# CANDIDA URINARY TRACT INFECTIONS

A positive urine culture for candida usually reflects colonization. Treat cystitis only if the patient has symptoms of urinary tract infection (e.g. dysuria, frequency, urgency, and/or suprapubic tenderness) or if the patient will undergo invasive urological manipulation.

Asymptomatic candiduria in a patient with a urinary catheter should not be treated without an additional indication. Removal of catheter is strongly recommended. Contact Infectious Diseases for more information.

Neutropenic patients with asymptomatic candiduria should be assessed for candidemia because they are at risk of dissemination. Obtain blood cultures and assess potential sources of candidemia such as central venous catheters. Refer to fungemia page for treatment recommendations.
[Fungemia Associated with Candida spp.](candidemia)

menus.Name: candida-vulvo-vaginitis
menus.Text:
# CANDIDA VULVOVAGINITIS

Candida vulvovaginitis typically presents with valvular irritation, burning or pruritus. Vaginal pH should be measured, and the specimen should be examined under the microscope for clue cells (epithelial cell coated with bacteria) to exclude bacterial vaginosis. In candida vulvovaginitis, the vaginal pH is typically normal (4-4.5) and vaginal discharge is typically thick and curdy with white plaques on vaginal mucosa. Diagnosis is confirmed by identifying fungus or yeast with KOH prep.
Most non-C. albicans species respond to fluconazole treatment except C. krusei and C. glabrata. C. krusei can be treated with topical agents as for complicated candida vulvovaginitis below. C. glabrata treatment is complicated and azole therapy is frequently unsuccessful. Consult Infectious Diseases in patients with C. glabrata vulvovaginitis.
Recurrent candida vulvovaginitis is treated as complicated candida vulvovaginitis for induction treatment, followed by maintenance regimen for 6 months.

---

# NON-SEVERE COMMUNITY-ACQUIRED PNEUMONIA TREATED IN AN INPATIENT SETTING

Common alternative explanations include heart failure, thromboembolic disease, COPD exacerbation, viral pneumonitis, aspiration pneumonitis, or tumor. Most of the latter conditions do NOT benefit from antimicrobials.

## Duration of therapy

Patients with CAP should be treated for a minimum of 5 days, should be afebrile for 48-72 hours, and should have no more than 1 CAP- associated sign of clinical instability before discontinuation of therapy.

Temperature less than/equal to 100 degrees F Heart rate less than/equal to 100 beats/minute Respiratory rate less than/equal to 24 breaths/minute Systolic blood pressure greater than/equal to 90 mm Hg Arterial oxygen saturation greater than/equal to 90% --OR-- PO2 greater than/equal to 60 mm Hg on room air Ability to maintain oral intake Normal mental status

menus.Text:
# SEVERE Community-Acquired Pneumonia (CAP) Treated in Intensive Care Unit (ICU)

## Criteria for Defining SEVERE Community-acquired Pneumonia

Validated definition includes either one major or three or more minor criteria
MAJOR CRITERIA:
Septic shock with need for vasopressors
Respiratory failure requiring mechanical ventilation
MINOR CRITERIA:
Respiratory rate greater than or equal to 30 breaths/minute PaO2/FiO2 ratio less than or equal to 250
Multilobar infiltrates
Confusion/disorientation
Uremia (blood urea nitrogen level greater than 20 mg/dl)
Leukopenia* (WBC less than 4,000 cells/microliter)
*Due to infection alone (i.e., not chemotherapy induced)
Thrombocytopenia (platelet count less than 100,000 microliters)
Hypothermia (core temperature less than 36 degrees C)
Hypotension requiring aggressive fluid resuscitation

## Recommendation for duration of antibiotic therapy for CAP:

Patients with CAP should be treated for a minimum of 5 days, should be afebrile for 48-72 hours, and should have no more than 1 CAP-associated sign of clinical instability before discontinuation of therapy.

## Criteria for clinical stability:

Temperature less than/equal to 100 degrees F
Heart rate less than/equal to 100 beats/minute
Respiratory rate less than/equal to 24 breaths/minute
Systolic blood pressure greater than/equal to 90 mm Hg
Arterial oxygen saturation greater than/equal to 90% --OR-- PO2 greater than/equal to 60 mm Hg on room air
Ability to maintain oral intake
Normal mental status

---

---

menus.Term1: Cervicitis associated with sexually transmitted diseases
menus.Text:
# CERVICITIS ASSOCIATED WITH SEXUALLY TRANSMITTED DISEASES

The main diagnostic signs that characterize cervicitis are 1)women who present with purulent or mucopurulent exudate in the endocervical canal or on an endocervical swab specimen and 2)sustained endocervical bleeding induced by gentle passage of cotton swab through the cervical os. One or both signs may be present.

Neisseria gonorrhoeae and Chlamydia trachomatis are the two most common sexually transmitted cervicitis pathogens. Nucleic acid amplification tests for these pathogens are more sensitive than culture and should be used for patients at risk for sexually transmitted cervicitis.
Chlamydia & GC PCR/LCR test

## For patients who have recently been treated for cervicitis

[Treatment of recurrent or persistent cervicitis](recurrent-persist-urethritis)

When diagnosed with sexually transmitted cervicitis, the patient's sexual partner(s) during the previous 60 days should be evaluated for sexually transmitted infection. If diagnostic tests for the cause of cervicitis are not feasible, therapy for both N. gonorrhoeae and C. trachomatis should be given to partners.

## Initial treatment of patients and sex partners

Patients and partners are often infected with both N. gonorrhoeae and C. trachomatis. Treat for both pathogens unless one is ruled out by lab test.
[Treatment for chlamydial or non-gonococcal cervicitis](chlamydia-urethritis-cervicitis-or-proctitis)

menus.Text:
# CHOLANGITIS

[Oral step-down treatment](step-down-treatment)

Most cases are due to common bile duct obstruction. Obstruction (if present) must be relieved with an endoscopical, transcutaneous, or surgical procedure. The most common pathogens isolated are E. coli, Klebsiella, Enterococcus and Enterobacter. Pseudomonas coverage is recommended in severe (grade 3) cholangitis. Anaerobic coverage is recommended if biliary-enteric abnormality is present. Antimicrobials' role in cholangitis is to allow patients to have elective and not emergently scheduled drainage procedures. Due to increasing resistance, fluoroquinolones are only recommended in cases of severe penicillin and cephalosporin allergy.

---

- Mandell chapter: Infections of the Liver and Biliary System (Liver Abscess, Cholangitis, Cholecystitis)

- Solomkin et al, Clin Infect Dis, 2010, 50:133-64

menus.Name: cholecystitis
menus.Text:
# CHOLECYSTITIS

[Oral step-down treatment](step-down-treatment)

Adequate biliary drainage is the definitive treatment. Antimicrobials should be prescribed only if signs of infection like leukocytosis or fever are present or if the patient is elderly. Surgery and Gastroenterology involvement are essential. For acute cholecystitis in grade 1 disease, antimicrobials are primarily prophylactic. For moderate to severe disease grades 2-3, antimicrobials should be continued for 4-7 days. Most cases are associated with E. coli, Enterococcus, Klebsiella, and Enterobacter. Anaerobic coverage is not indicated unless a biliary-enteric abnormality is present. For community-acquired acute cholecystitis, enterococcal coverage is not required because Enterococcus has not been shown to be pathogenic in these patients Due to increasing resistance, fluoroquinolones are only recommended in cases of severe penicillin and cephalosporin allergy.

References:

- Sanford Guide article: Gallbladder Infections, Acute Cholecystitis
- J Hepatobiliary Pancreat Sci (2018) 25:3-16 "Tokyo Guidelines"

menus.Text:
# CHRONIC BACTERIAL PROSTATITIS

Chronic bacterial prostatitis usually presents as recurrent urinary tract infections with the same bacterial etiology. Pain, tenderness, and fever may accompany intermittent episodes of cystitis, but men are usually asymptomatic between episodes and the prostate examination may be normal. Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) often relieve pain. If the diagnosis is uncertain or if the patient's symptoms do not respond to therapy, consult urology. The presence of hematuria may be a sign of carcinoma, especially in older men, and a urology consult should be requested.

A urine culture should be performed in all patients to guide antimicrobial therapy. [Chronic prostate pain syndrome](chron-pros-pelvic-pain-syn) should be considered in patients who have symptoms of prostatitis but have negative urine cultures. Chronic prostate pain syndrome is discussed elsewhere:
Chronic prostate pain syndrome

## Duration

4 weeks minimum and up to 6 weeks of treatment is required. Durations longer than 6 weeks may be needed in treatment of resistant organisms. Treatment with trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole requires a treatment duration of 1 to 3 months.

---

# CMV COLITIS OR ESOPHAGITIS

Infection in immunocompetent patients is rare and usually associated with minimal or no symptoms. Patients in whom the risk for CMV disease is increased include solid organ and bone marrow transplant recipients, persons receiving prolonged immunosuppressive chemotherapy, and persons with advanced HIV disease indicated by a CD4 count of less than 50 cells/microliter. Treatment is complex and requires Infectious Diseases consultation.

## Duration of therapy

Treat for 3-6 weeks. Patients may be converted to oral therapy after initial intravenous therapy and after clinical improvement of severe disease.

## Treatment of severe disease

Refer to Inpatient Antimicrobial CDSS.

menus.Text:
# CMV RETINITIS AND ACUTE RETINAL NECROSIS

Infection in immunocompetent patients is rare and usually associated with minimal or no symptoms. Patients in whom the risk for CMV disease is increased include solid organ and bone marrow transplant recipients, persons receiving prolonged immunosuppressive chemotherapy, and persons with advanced HIV disease indicated by a CD4 count of less than 50 cells/microliter. Treatment is complex and requires Infectious Diseases consultation.
For sight threatening lesions (lesions within 1500 microns of the fovea) intravitreal infections of ganciclovir or foscarnet are recommended in addition to systemic treatment. Contact Infectious Diseases for more information.

## Duration of antimicrobial therapy

Treat retinitis for 14 to 21 days. Patients may be converted to oral therapy after initial intravenous therapy and after clinical improvement of severe disease. Treat acute retinal necrosis with IV therapy for at least 7 days and until disease stabilizes then oral therapy for a minimum of 6 weeks. Maintenance therapy after completion of treatment is indicated when CD4 count <100.
Discontinue maintenance therapy when CD4 count is >100 for 6 months.

---

menus.Name: colonized-respiratory-tract-ventilator
menus.Term1: Colonized respiratory tract in a patient on a ventilator
menus.Text:
# COLONIZED RESPIRATORY TRACT IN A PATIENT ON A VENTILATOR

The respiratory tracts of persons who are intubated, have a tracheostomy, or have other abnormalities of the larynx or trachea are usually colonized with bacteria and often fungi. The bacteria can be of relatively low virulence (e.g. coagulase negative staphylococci, streptococci, candida) or of potentially greater virulence (Staphylococcus aureus, enterobacteriaceae, pseudomonas). Candida and enterococci are common respiratory tract colonizers and they almost never cause pneumonia. There is no benefit from treatment of patients with systemic antimicrobials simply because the respiratory tract is colonized with a potential pathogen and there is no evidence of an infiltrate. Systemic antimicrobial therapy will select for resistant organisms and may lead to other adverse effects.

## Inpatient

See below for ventilator-associated pneumonia treatment recommendations in patients with a new or progressive infiltrate and at least one of the following:
fever greater than 100.4F, leukocytosis, leukopenia or purulent bronchial secretions.
[Nosocomial Pneumonia](noso-pneumonia-new)

## Outpatient

Refer to Inpatient Antimicrobial CDSS for ventilator-associated pneumonia treatment recommendations in patients with a new or progressive infiltrate and at least one of the following: fever greater than 100.4F, leukocytosis, leukopenia or purulent bronchial secretions.
References

- Kalil et al. Clin Infect Dis, 2016, 63(5): e61-e111.

menus.Name: conjunctivitis
menus.Text:
# CONJUNCTIVITIS

Conjunctivitis is associated with viral or bacterial pathogens. Viral conjunctivitis presents with watery discharge. Bacterial infections are more likely to present with thick exudate and conjunctival injection. Allergic conjunctivitis typically presents with stringy mucus. If there is pus (hypopion), corneal involvement, possible bacterial conjunctivitis, or keratitis, consult ophthalmology.

Viral conjunctivitis is most commonly caused by adenovirus. It is self-limited and antivirals provide no benefit. Symptomatic treatment with ophthalmic antihistamine/decongestants and warm or cool compresses may relieve symptoms.

Bacterial conjunctivitis is most commonly associated with Staphylococcus aureus, Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus spp., Moraxella catarrhalis, Corynebacterium diphtheriae, Neisseria spp. or enteric gram-negative rods. It is generally self-limited, but topical antimicrobials reduce duration of symptoms and limit person-to-person spread of infection. If symptoms do not improve after 2 days of antimicrobial therapy, the patient should be seen by an ophthalmologist.

---

References:

- Azari eta al, JAMA (2013) 1721-1730
- Mandell chapter: Microbial conjunctivitis
- Up-to-Date Article: Conjunctivitis
- Sanford keyword: Conjunctivitis, Bacterial

# CUTANEOUS ABSCESS

menus.Text:
# DEEP OROPHARYNGEAL INFECTIONS

Deep oropharyngeal infections may threaten life and must be treated immediately. Assess the risk of airway compromise and monitor the airway if it is threatened. These infections are more common in people with diabetes mellitus and are caused by mixed organisms including streptococcus sp., Staphylococcus aureus and anaerobes. Perform CT scan to diagnose abscess. ENT and Infectious Diseases consults are essential.

## Duration of therapy

If the patient's condition worsens or does not improve during the first 48 hours of antimicrobial therapy, surgical drainage is indicated. If surgical drainage is done, antimicrobials are usually continued for 48 hours after the procedure. If surgical drainage is not done, 2 weeks of antimicrobial therapy until clinical improvement is observed (e.g. resolution of fever and leukocytosis) is appropriate.

menus.Name: derm-prophylaxis
menus.Text:
# ANTIMICROBIAL PROPHYLAXIS AND DERMATOLOGIC SURGERY

Antibiotics are used to prevent infections in patients undergoing surgery in certain well-defined circumstances. They are used to prevent surgical site infection or to prevent endocarditis in circumstances where the risk of endocarditis is high. For many low-risk surgeries, the risks associated with antibiotic use, which can be severe or cause death, outweigh the benefits. The following recommendations are consistent with guidelines published by the American Heart Association and Infectious Disease Society of America.

In general, antibiotics are used to prevent post-operative wound infection in clean-contaminated surgery. Most dermatological surgery involves clean sites, and the risks of antibiotics outweigh potential benefits. Antibiotics are used to prevent endocarditis and hematogenous joint infection in procedures involving infected skin structures. Antibitic prophylaxis is also recommended to prevent surgical site infections in procedures involving high risk surgical sites and conditions.

When they are used, prophylactic oral antimicrobial agents should be administered 30-60 minutes before the first tissue manipulation or incision.

Intravenous antimicrobials should be administered 60 minutes (120 minutes for vancomycin) prior to procedure.

Antimicrobials should not be used to prevent infections in patients with vascular grafts or orthopedic prostheses because the risk of bacteremia or infection of these devices is tiny and antibiotic risks outweigh any theoretical benefit.

A full course of antibiotics should be used to treat skin infections where infection is already present at the time of surgery.

Suggested antibiotic prophylaxis regimens should be targeted against the typical pathogens likely to be present. A risk-based approach for coverage of MRSA should be taken in patients with specific risk factors for MRSA.

References:

- Bratzler et al, Am J Health-Syst Pharm (2013) 70, 195-283
- Nishimura et al, J Am Coll Cardiol (2014) 63, e57-185

menus.Name: diagnosis-of-endocarditis
menus.Text:
## DIAGNOSIS OF ENDOCARDITIS

Diagnosis and management are complex. Cardiology, Infectious Disease, and Surgery services should all be involved in diagnosis and management of infective endocarditis.
Endocarditis is the result of growth of microorganisms on endothelium of the heart. The integrity of the endothelial surface must be compromised in order to allow microorganisms to attach and proliferate. Often such lesions are caused by abnormal blood flow or thrombi resulting from heart valvular disease, prosthetic heart valves, or from foreign material or microorganisms introduced to the bloodstream as byproducts of illicit intravenous drug use.

Endocarditis should be considered a possible diagnosis in a patient with persistent bacteremia without an identifiable focal infection, especially when the patient has a structural heart abnormality, prosthesis, or has a recent history of intravenous illicit drug use.

Diagnosis of endocarditis can be based on several combinations of signs and symptoms. The Duke criteria help categorize cases as definite or possible endocarditis based on major and minor criteria. The Duke criteria also indicate when a diagnosis of endocarditis can be excluded.

[Modified Duke Diagnostic Criteria](duke-diagnostic-criteria)

**Severity of Disease**
Endocarditis is categorized by time course and severity of symptoms of illness into acute and subacute. These classifications help suggest which pathogens may be more likely associated with symptoms.

**Acute**
Acute endocarditis is a rapidly progressing illness that often causes fever. It can be associated with spread of infection to other parts of the body and can cause death within a matter of weeks. In patient with suspected acute endocarditis, three sets of blood cultures should be obtained with the first and last cultures separated by at least one hour. Empiric antimicrobial therapy should then be initiated as soon as possible.
**Subacute**
Subacute endocarditis follows an indolent course. Generally, patients have had some symptoms for at least 2 weeks. Symptoms are more subtle and spread of infection to other systems is uncommon. In patients with suspected subacute endocarditis, every attempt should be made to identify a pathogen prior to initiating antimicrobial therapy. These patients should be observed carefully for signs of heart failure or embolic complications, and if signs are noted, surgery should be consulted immediately.

---

References:

- Baddour et al., Circulation 2015, 132:1-52
- Mandell chapter: Endocarditis and intravascular infections
- Sanford keyword: Endocarditis
- Up-To-Date article: Overview of management of infective endocarditis in adults
- Wang et al., JAMA 2018, 320.1:72-83

menus.Name: drug-allergies
menus.Text:
# DRUG ALLERGIES

# Importance of history

The nature and circumstances of a possible previous reaction including the timing should be considered. In many cases, previous reactions are clearly not due to drug allergy.

# Types of reactions

*Immediate - within one hour of starting drug administration.

Type I reactions present with urticaria, hypotension, angioedema, bronchospasm, or anaphylaxis and occur within an hour of exposure. These reactions are immunoglobulin E (IgE) and mast cell and/or basophil mediated.

*Delayed - After one hour of starting administration (usually after 6 days)

1) Type II reactions manifest as hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia and neutropenia. They are caused by antibody (usually IgG)- mediated cell destruction.
2) Type III reactions can manifest as serum sickness, vasculitis or Arthus reaction, and are caused by IgG:drug immune complex deposition and complement activation.
3) Type IV reactions typically manifest as contact dermatitis, morbilliform reactions, severe exfoliative dermatoses (Stevens-Johnson syndrome/toxic epidermal necrolysis) and other presentations. They are T-cell mediated.

Repeated exposures lead to reactions that are of the same type.

# Beta-lactam allergies

Approximately 10% of patients report a beta-lactam allergy. Up to 90% of these patients can tolerate penicillin and have been designated penicillin allergic unnecessarily. Patients allergic to cephalosporins will have a cross-reaction to penicillins 3% to 5% of the time. Overall, patients with a history of penicillin allergy can tolerate cephalosporins although there are rare reports to severe, sometimes fatal anaphylactic reactions. Neither penicillin- or cephalosporin-allergic patients will react to aztreonam. The degree of cross-reactivity of penicillins and cephalosporins with carbapenems appears to be low.

# Therapeutic implications

If a patient has had an immediate reaction to a drug in the past, an allergy specialist should evaluate the patient before a drug of the same class is administered to the patient. Patients with delayed onset reactions causing fever, systemic symptoms or mucosal involvement should also be evaluated by an allergy specialist before a drug of the same class is administered.

# Desensitization

A patient with previous Type I reaction to a beta-lactam can be desensitized and then receive therapeutic doses of the same class within a day. Severe reactions during desensitization are uncommon. Pharmacy service must be contacted for assistance and drug preparation. Infectious Disease consultation strongly recommended.

[Link to penicillin desensitization protocol](penicillin-desensitization-protocol)

References

- JAMA 2001, 285: 249
- Joint Task Force on Practice Parameters: Drug Allergy - An Updated Practice Parameter (2010)

# DIARRHEA WITH ESCHERICHIA COLI

## Enteroaggretive E. coli (EAEC), Enteropathogenic E. coli (EPEC), and

## Enterotoxigenic E. coli (ETEC)

Antibiotic therapy is not required for mild to moderate disease caused by these organisms because diarrhea often resolves on its own. Do not use antimotility agents in patients with bloody stool. Antimicrobial treatment in patients with AIDS Treatment is complex, consult Infectious Diseases
Primary treatment: Hydration and electrolyte replacement Antimicrobial treatment of severe diarrhea

## Enterohemorrhagic E. coli (EHEC) and Shiga Toxin-producing E. coli (STEC)

EHEC and STEC disease often presents as bloody diarrhea.
Treatment includes supportive measures such as volume repletion and administering appropriate nutrition. Do not use antimotility or antimicrobial agents as they can increase shiga-toxin release and increase the risk of hemolytic uremia syndrome (HUS).

## Enteroinvasive E. coli (EIEC)

EIEC disease typically presents as watery diarrhea, sometimes progressing to bloody diarrhea. Refer to Shigella/Enteroinvasive E. coli treatment recommendations.
[Shigella/Enteroinvasive E. coli treatment recommendations](shigella-species)

---

## Enterohemorrhagic E. coli (EHEC) and Shiga Toxin-producing E. coli (STEC)

EHEC and STEC disease often presents as bloody diarrhea.
Treatment includes supportive measures such as volume repletion and administering appropriate nutrition. Do not use antimotility or antimicrobial agents as they can increase shiga-toxin release and increase the risk of hemolytic uremia syndrome (HUS).

## Enteroinvasive E. coli (EIEC)

EIEC disease typically presents as watery diarrhea, sometimes progressing to bloody diarrhea. Refer to Shigella/Enteroinvasive E. coli treatment recommendations.
Shigella/Enteroinvasive E. coli treatment recommendations

Native valve endocarditis (NVE):

# ENDOCARDITIS WITH HACEK BACTERIA

Ecthyma gangrenosum lesions commonly begin as painless red macules which rapidly evolve into areas of induration that develop into pustules and-or bullae. Ultimately, these become gangrenous ulcers. Ecthyma lesions typically progress rapidly within 12 to 18 hours. They are often associated with Pseudomonas aeruginosa bacteremia, especially in neutropenic patients.
Recommend blood cultures and culture of skin exudates.
#Inpatient Infectious disease consult is suggested.
Consider combination therapy in patients with severe infections.
Treat for 7 days.

menus.Name: elements-of-cdss-advice-page
menus.Text:
# ELEMENTS OF A CDSS ADVICE MENU

Advice menus are comprised of the following elements:

---

# TYPICALLY present on an advice menu

---

1) Diagnosis or condition label-at the top of each advice menu.
2) Treatment. Empirical treatment as well as treatment for selected pathogens is presented with links to antimicrobial quick orders unless stated otherwise.

In addition to the drug, dose, and route, each quick order text includes the drug's approximate cost per day and coding for important drug properties of note. Drugs clustered together are considered equivalent.

3) Help. At the top of each advice menu. There are links to a variety of resources (susceptibilities, important drug properties, section-specific consults, etc.).
4) References. At the bottom on each advice menu. These are key references for the recommendations on the menu.

---

# DISCRETIONARY advice menu components

---

1) (Treatment) Alternative. Following the (preferred) Treatment section with quick orders for common alternative antimicrobials. Antimicrobial listed under each alternative header are equivalents among those listed. A broader selection of medications can be accessed through the Need an alternative menu within the help section. For some conditions we recommend alternative antimicrobials when recommended drugs are not suitable for an individual patient. Unless otherwise stated drugs clustered together under Alternatives are considered equivalent.

If none of the recommended or alternative drugs is suitable you can find more drugs by clicking on the Need an alternative link at the top of the menu.

2) Consults. At the top of the menu, these are consultation requests pertinent to the clinical problem addressed by the menu. Links to context-specific consults can be found on advice menus, as appropriate. For example, the herpes simplex encephalitis menu contains a link to a request for neurology consult.
3) Resources. Pertinent to the clinical problem and addressed by the menu is provided for example. For some menus, supplemental resources have been identified (e.g., PORT score calculator for Community Acquired Pneumonia, diagnostic tools, Epidemiology, etc.) the information is included on the advice menu.

# ENDOPHTHALMITIS

Endophthalmitis is a medical emergency and presents with eye pain and visual loss. It may be associated with gram positive or gram-negative bacteria, including Staphylococcus aureus and Pseudomonas aeruginosa, or with fungi.

Consult ophthalmology immediately. The ophthalmologist will obtain an aqueous or vitreous fluid sample for gram stain and culture and begin intravitreal antimicrobials.

## Fungal endophthalmitis

Fungal endophthalmitis is rarely diagnosed in temperate climates and treatment is complicated. Ophthalmology and Infectious Diseases involvement is essential.

Refer to the Inpatient Antimicrobial CDSS for parenteral therapy.

menus.Name: epididymitis
menus.Text:
# EPIDIDYMITIS AND EPIDIDYMO-ORCHITIS

Epididymitis is inflammation of the epididymis and when testicles are involved is referred to as epididymo-orchitis. Acute epididymitis is the most common cause of scrotal pain in adults. Other features include scrotal erythema and edema, pyuria, dysuria, thickened epididymis, swollen testis, and is usually unilateral. It is primarily caused by infection but can also result from trauma and autoimmune diseases. Testicular torsion should be ruled out before treatment. Most cases in men aged 35 and older, those with recent urinary tract instrumentation or surgery (e.g., prostate biopsy, vasectomy) are associated with enteric Gram-negative rods. Most cases in men under age 35 are associated with N. gonorrhoeae and C. trachomatis. Resistant organisms are more likely if the patient has been in the hospital for more than 48 hours or received a course of antibiotics. There is increasing resistance in urinary pathogens to ciprofloxacin.

A urine analysis, urine culture and urine nucleic acid amplification test (NAAT) should be performed in all cases of suspected epididymitis before starting treatment to guide therapy:
Lab menu

Patients at risk of sexually transmitted infections should be assessed for treatment. Refer to the Urogenital section of the Antimicrobial CDSS for more information.

Patients with bacterial epididymitis treated with antibiotics should improve within two or three days. If no improvement is noted, other causes of scrotal pain and referral to a urologist should be considered. Management should include bed rest, analgesics, and scrotal elevation. Older men should have their residual urinary volume checked. If the residual volume is elevated, the patient should be seen by a urologist as epididymitis is unlikely to respond if the prostate is blocking the vas deferens.

---

---

- Mandell Chapter: Prostatitis, Epididymitis and Orchitis
- Sanford keyword: Epididymo-orchitis
- Taylor, Stephanie, Clinical Infectious Diseases, 2015, 61(S8)S770-3
- Up-To-Date article: Evaluation of acute scrotal pain in adults
- Workowski et al., MMWR Recomm Rep, 2021, 70(4)1-187

# ERYSIPELAS

In contrast to cellulitis, erysipelas has sharply demarcated borders and a characteristic raised, orange-peel appearance. Most cases are associated with streptococcus. In a minority of cases, especially those involving the face, Staphylococcus aureus is also a potential pathogen. In severe cases, methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) coverage must be provided until microbiology results are available.
Treat for 5 to 10days, longer if patient is bacteremic.

---

## Facial

---

Sudden onset of rapidly spreading red edematous tender plaque-like skin on the face in an otherwise healthy host.

menus.Name: erysipeloid
menus.Text:
# ERYSIPELOID (ERYSIPELOTHRIX RHUSOPATHIAE INFECTION)

Erysipeloid is a localized cutaneous infection with Erysipelothrix rhusopathiae.
It is a zoonotic infection of fisherman, fish handlers, and butchers acquired by direct animal contact, most commonly with fish, but also with other animals (e.g., swine). It usually affects the hand or fingers and is characterized by throbbing pain and a red rash with a purple center and an elevated border.
Localized infections can be treated with oral antimicrobials.
Severe, diffuse cutaneous infections or systemic infections with E.
rhusopathiae occur rarely after ingestion of undercooked pork or contaminated seafood in immunosuppressed individuals. These infections are treated initially with intravenous antimicrobials.

---

---

## Treatment of systemic or severe diffuse cutaneous infection with E. rhusopathiae.

---

## Treatment duration is at least 4 weeks. Infectious Disease Consult recommended.

Penicillin G 4 million units IV q4h ($) [R]

---

## Treatment of systemic or severe diffuse cutaneous infection with E. rhusopathiae

Refer to Inpatient Antimicrobial CDSS.

menus.Name: esophagitis
menus.Text:
# ESOPHAGITIS

Esophagitis is usually associated with non-infectious diseases like gastroesophageal reflux disease, mucositis, and pill-induced esophagitis. Esophageal infection occurs primarily in immunosuppressed individuals (e.g. chemotherapy, transplantation, HIV) and rarely in healthy individuals. Most of the infectious esophagitis is caused by Candida albicans, cytomegalovirus (CMV) and herpes simplex virus. Aphthous ulceration of the esophagus is common in HIV infection. HIV screening is recommended.

## Inpatient/Outpatient

[Candidiasis](fungi-candida-albicans)
[CMV Esophagitis](cmv-colitis-or-esophagitis)
[Herpes Simplex Esophagitis](herpes-simplex-esophagitis)

menus.Text:
# FIRST RECURRENCE OF CLOSTRIDIOIDES DIFFICILE INFECTION (CDI)

Discontinue implicated antibiotic(s). Narrow antibiotic spectrum if antibiotic therapy is still needed. Avoid antiperistaltic agents (narcotics, loperamide, etc.). Avoid antacid therapy without clear indication. If diarrhea has improved or resolved prior to starting C. difficile treatment, consider re-assessing the diagnosis before initiating therapy. C. difficile infection usually responds to antimicrobial therapy. If symptoms do not respond to appropriate antimicrobial therapy, re-consider the diagnosis.

---

- Johnson et al, Clin Inf Dis, 2021, 73(5): e1029-e1044

menus.Name: folliculitis
menus.Text:
# FOLLICULITIS

Folliculitis is an infection of the hair follicle with purulent exudate in the epidermis. It is usually associated with Staphylococcus aureus. In patients exposed to swimming pools or hot tubs, folliculitis may be associated with Pseudomonas aeruginosa. Candida albicans can cause folliculitis in patients receiving antimicrobials and/or corticosteroids.

For folliculitis in patients with severe acne, consult Dermatology. For extensive folliculitis or in patients with HIV, consult Infectious Diseases.

[References](references):
Up-to-Date website
Sanford keyword: Folliculitis
Stevens DL Clin Infect Dis 2014 59: 147
menus.Therapy:
Usually self-limiting. For most cases, treat with daily saline compresses until symptoms resolve.

## For moderate to severe cases associated with Staphylococcus aureus:

Mupirocin ointment to affected area q8h for 7 days ($) [M]

## For cases associated with Candida albicans

Clotrimazole cream q8h for 7 days ($) [M]

## Outpatient

## For moderate to severe cases associated with Staphylococcus aureus:

Mupirocin 2% ointment topical to affected area TID for 7 days ($) [M]
Non-VA order for above

## For cases associated with Candida albicans

Clotrimazole cream to affected area TID for 7 days ($) [M]
Non-VA order for above

menus.Name: foot-ulcer-w-infect
menus.Term1: Foot ulcer with infection of surrounding tissues
menus.Text:
# DIABETES-RELATED FOOT INFECTIONS (DIABETIC FOOT INFECTIONS-DFI)

# Wound Cultures:

If there are no systemic symptoms of infection or at least 2 local symptoms (pain, erythema > 0.5cm, purulent drainage, warmth), do not culture or treat with abx.

Do NOT:

- Culture a wound that appears uninfected (at least 2 of following: local pain, erythema >0.5cm, purulent drainage)
- Swab the wound to obtain a culture
- Culture without first cleaning and debriding a wound DFI Do:
- Obtain culture by deep tissue biopsy after cleaning and debriding the wound

# Imaging:

- An x-ray is recommended for all new foot ulcers in patients with diabetes to evaluate for deformity, bony destruction, soft tissue gas, and/or foreign bodies. Antimicrobials aren't indicated unless local cellulitis or systemic infectious symptoms are present.

[Click here for Osteomyelitis Evaluation](osteomyelitis-evaluation)

# INFECTION SEVERITY (IWGDF/IDSA Classification)

---

# Uninfected DFI (Class 1/Uninfected): Chronic ulceration without s/s infection

- if no pain, erythema > 0.5cm, purulent drainage, do not culture or treat Do not culture wound -Do not treat with antibiotics If osteomyelitis identified arrange for bone biopsy --hold antibiotics

---

# Infected DFI (Class 2/Mild):

At least two of the following are present: -Local swelling or induration

- Erythema >0.5cm but <2cm around wound -Local tenderness or pain -Local increased warmth -Purulent drainage

---

- Senneville E Cin Infect Dis 2023:
- Senneville Diabetes Metab Res Rev. (2024) 40(3):e3687
- Stevens DL Clin Infect Dis 2014, 59:147
- Lipsky BA Clin Infect Dis 2012, 54:e132

# CANDIDA ALBICANS

Oropharyngeal candidal disease may present in different patterns, like white plaques in the oropharyngeal area, erythematous macules (often in patients with dentures), or as pseudomembranes. Thrush infection often recurs, especially in patients with AIDS.

Avoid using fluconazole empirically to treat candidal infections in patients who have received an imidazole in the previous year.

Consult MRTC clinic or Infectious Diseases (MRTC may also be consulted in the MVAHCS) for more information on treatment of recurrent infection.

References:

- Mandell chapter: Candida Species
- Pappas et al. Clinical Infectious Diseases. 2016, 62(4)e1-50
- Sanford keyword: Candidiasis, Candidemia or Disseminated
- Up-to-Date article: Treatment of candidemia and invasive candidiasis in adults

menus.Name: furuncles-and-carbuncles
menus.Text:
# FURUNCLES AND CARBUNCLES

Localized purulent infections include furuncles, carbuncles and cutaneous abscesses. Nearly all are caused by Staphylococcus aureus. A furuncle is an inflamed nodule that usually develops as a complication of folliculitis. A carbuncle is a more extensive lesion that extends further into the subcutaneous tissue. Contact a wound care nurse for more information.
Incision and drainage is the mainstay of therapy for carbuncles, cutaneous abscesses, and large furuncles.
The decision to administer antibiotics directed against S. aureus as an adjunct to incision and drainage should be made based on the presence of systemic inflammatory response syndrome (SIRS) or in patients with markedly impaired host defenses.

## For recurrent skin abscesses in addition to culture and antibiotic therapy recommended consider a decolonization regimen.

[Select here for Staphylococcus aureus Decolonization](decolonization-of-staphylococcus-aureus)

## Mild infection: Purulent infection without systemic signs of infection

Recommend incision and drainage. No antibiotic indicated.

## Moderate Infection: Purulent infection with signs of systemic infection.

Recommend incision and drainage. Culture material and use results to guide therapy.
Treat for 5 days and extend/modify treatment if not improved in this time.

---

References:

- Up-to-Date website
- Sanford keyword: Furuncle, carbuncle
- Stevens DL Clin Infect Dis 2014, 59: 147
- Montravers P Curr Opin Infect Dis 2016, 29:131

menus.Text:
# GENITAL HERPES

---

## Immunocompromised patients

---

Immunocompromised patients in whom genital herpes simplex disease is often severe include: patients with HIV infection, organ transplants, malnourishment, eczema or severe burns, and in patients receiving immunosuppressive chemotherapy.

## Duration of antimicrobial therapy

Treat mild to moderate disease for 10 days. In severe disease, treat with intravenous acyclovir for 2 to 7 days based on clinical response, then treat with an oral antiviral for a total duration of 10 days.

---

References:

- Center for Disease Control and Prevention. MMWR (2021) 70:1-192
- Mandell chapter: Herpes simplex virus
- Sanford keyword: Herpes simplex
menus.Therapy:
## Immunocompetent patients

---

Treatment of the initial episode decreases the duration of pain, lesions, and viral shedding by 1 to 2 days. Treatment of the initial episode does not decrease likelihood of recurrent episodes.

Preferred:
Acyclovir 400 mg PO q8h for 7-10 days ($) [R]

Alternative:
Valacyclovir 1 gm PO q12h for 7-10 days ($) [R]

## Episodic therapy for relapses

Treatment of recurrent episodes must be started within 24 hours of symptom onset. Treatment decreases the duration of pain and lesions, and viral shedding by 1 to 2 days. Consider suppressive treatment for patients with more than 6 episodes per year.

Acyclovir 400 mg PO q8h for 5 days ($) [R]
< OR >
Acyclovir 800 mg PO q8h for 2 days ($) [R]
< OR >
Valacyclovir 500 mg PO q12h for 3 days ($) [R]

## Treatment for mild to moderate disease or after clinical improvement of severe disease

## Inpatient

Preferred:
Acyclovir 400 mg PO q8h ($) [R]
Alternative:
Valacyclovir 1 gm PO q12h ($) [R]

## Treatment for severe disease

Infectious Diseases consult encouraged.
Acyclovir 5 mg/kg IV q8h ($$) [R]

## Chronic suppressive therapy

Suppressive therapy is indicated in patients with more than 6 episodes per year, or in patients with less frequent episodes who are desiring to minimize risk of transmission. Some patients may find episodic treatment more convenient. The frequency of recurrences can decrease after 1 to 5 years, and suppressive therapy may be stopped every few years to see if it is still needed.

Preferred:
Acyclovir 400 mg PO q12h ($) [R]

Alternative:
\*Note: Recommend increasing dose to 1000 mg per day for patients that have breakthrough on the 500 mg dose. See recommendation below.
Valacyclovir 500 mg PO Q24h ($) [R]

# HEAD LICE (PEDICULOSIS CAPITIS)

Lice are parasitic insects. Human lice survive by feeding on human blood. To make a diagnosis, use a nit comb, bright light, or lens to find a louse living on the scalp. Dead nits may remain for months after successful treatment. Dead nits are usually located more than 6 mm from the scalp. Lice are often transmitted by infected clothing and bedclothes but not by ordinary furniture that is not typically in contact with hair or scalp.

Refer to the following for advice on household cleaning for lice infestations: https://www.cdc.gov/lice/treatment/index.html

---

References:

- Sanford keyword: lice
- Up-to-date website
menus.Therapy:

menus.Name: hepatitis-a
menus.Text:
# HEPATITIS A

## Disease Management

Most acute disease is self-limited, and the virus does not cause chronic disease. No specific antiviral therapy is available. Patients who appear to be developing fulminant hepatitis, including those with mental status changes should receive supportive treatment.

References:

- Mandell chapter: Acute viral hepatitis
- Sanford keyword: Hepatitis A, Acute, Treatment
menus.Therapy:
## Inpatient

## Prevention for persons with continuing high risk of disease

[Hepatitis A Vaccine Information Page (outpatient orders only)](hepatitis-a-vaccine-information)

## Prevention for persons with a specific, defined exposure

Post-exposure prophylaxis, including immune globulin and vaccination, should be offered to persons with substantial exposure to hepatitis A. Post-exposure prophylaxis must be given within 2 weeks of exposure. Vaccine can be given at the same time as immune-globulin.

Consult GI for treatment recommendations.

---

## Outpatient

## Prevention for persons with continuing high risk of disease

Vaccine should be offered to persons at high risk of hepatitis A infection: men who have sex with men, travelers to endemic areas likely to be exposed, illegal drug users, persons at occupational risk of disease, persons with chronic liver disease or clotting factor disorders.

Give Hepatitis A vaccine 1 ml IM x 2, separated by 6 to 12 months.

## Prevention for persons with a specific, defined exposure

Post-exposure prophylaxis should be offered to persons with substantial exposure to hepatitis A. Specifically, persons exposed to acute hepatitis through household or sexual contact, persons who attend or work in a day care center with a recent case, or employee or patron of a restaurant with a food handler with hepatitis. Post exposure prophylaxis must be given within 2 weeks of exposure. Vaccine can be given at the same time as immune-globulin.

Immune globulin 0.02 ml/kg IM x 1 <AND>
Give Hepatitis A vaccine 1 ml IM x 2, separated by 6 to 12 months

menus.Name: hepatitis-b
menus.Text:
# HEPATITIS B

## Acute disease management

Most acute hepatitis B disease is mild and self-limited. Patients who appear to be developing fulminant hepatitis, including those with mental status changes should receive supportive treatment.

References:

- Mandell chapter: Acute viral hepatitis
- Mandell chapter: Chronic viral hepatitis
- Up-to-date article: Hepatitis B virus: Overview of management
menus.Therapy:
## Inpatient

Antiviral therapy is not indicated. Consult Gastroenterology and Infectious Diseases.

## Chronic disease management

Antiviral therapy for chronic hepatitis B is a complicated, highly specialized task.
Consult Gastroenterology and Infectious Diseases.

## Prevention

[Hepatitis B Vaccine Information Page](hepb-vaccine-information-page)

## Select below for [Hepatitis B evaluation](hepatitis-b-evaluation-anti-cd20-antibody) for patients receiving Anti-CD20

## Antibody Treatment

[Hepatitis B Evaluation](hepatitis-b-evaluation-anti-cd20-antibody)

---

## Outpatient

Fulminant hepatitis is suggested by increased prothrombin time, cholestasis, ascites, decreased liver size, or decreasing serum albumin. Supportive treatment includes maintenance of fluid and electrolyte balance, monitoring and possible correction of coagulation defects, treatment of hepatic encephalopathy, and good nutrition with a low-protein diet. Antiviral therapy is not indicated. Gastroenterology consult encouraged.

## Chronic disease management

Antiviral therapy for chronic hepatitis B is a complicated, highly specialized task. Consult with gastroenterology and infectious diseases.

## Prevention

Vaccinate persons at high risk of disease including men who have sex with men, illegal drug users, and health care workers with substantial exposure to blood or body fluids.
Give Hepatitis B vaccine 1 dose IM in deltoid at 0, then 1 or 2 months, and again at 4 to 6 months.

## Antibody Treatment

menus.Name: herpes-keratitis
menus.Text:
# HERPES KERATITIS

Ocular herpes infection can be caused by either HSV-1 or HSV-2. The majority of cases are caused by HSV-1. The recurrence rate of ocular herpes is 40% over a 5 year period, less than that of oral or genital herpes. Ocular herpes is a major cause of blindness and typically presents as infection of the epithelium of the cornea but can also rarely involve the stroma and endothelium.
Ophthalmology consultation is recommended.
Involvement of the stroma or endothelium requires treatment with topical steroid and close monitoring. For these cases, start oral antiviral and consult ophthalmology for management.
Antiviral prophylaxis is recommended for patients with multiple recurrences, recurrent episodes with ulceration, recurrent inflammation with scar/vascularization approaching visual axis, patients who have had keratoplasty for HSV-related scarring/astigmatism, and patients who have had HSV keratitis while on immunosuppressive therapy. Post-surgical prophylaxis is not discussed here. Please consult ophthalmology for more information.

References:

- Baratz, Arch Ophthalmology, (2012) 130.1: 108-110
- Guess et al, The Ocular Surface, (2007) 5.3:240-250
- Wilhelmus, Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews, (2015), 1:CD002898

# HERPES SIMPLEX ESOPHAGITIS

HSV infection of the esophagus usually occurs in patients who are immunocompromised, typically solid organ and bone marrow transplant recipients.
In healthy patients HSV esophagitis occurs occasionally, usually in men under the age of 40.
Patients usually present with odynophagia and dysphagia. Fever, epigastric pain, nausea, vomiting, and heartburn are less frequent. Some patients may have coexistent herpes labialis or oropharyngeal ulcers. Diagnosis is usually established with an upper endoscopy. Suggestive findings may also be seen during a barium swallow.

## Immunocompetent patients

Spontaneous resolution usually occurs in immunocompetent patients after one to two weeks. Patients may respond more quickly if treated with a short course of oral acyclovir.

## Duration of therapy

Treat for 7-10 days

## Treatment of severe disease

Refer to Inpatient Antimicrobial CDSS

menus.Name: hidradenitis-suppurativa
menus.Text:
# HIDRADENITIS SUPPURATIVA

A chronic inflammatory condition that typically involves occlusion, rupture, abscess formation and infection of hair follicles as well as secondary infection of apocrine glands/surrounding tissues. Lesions most often occur in the intertriginous areas (axillae, inguinal and anogenital) in is associated with smoking and obesity. There is a 40% genetic predisposition for hidradenitis suppurativa (HS) and is often accompanied by pain, malodor, and drainage. Cultures are negative 50% of the time and often are polymicrobial with S. epidermidis and S. aureus most isolated. The Hurley Staging System is often used to determine severity of HS.

Therapy generally consists of treatment of comorbidities that can exacerbate HS, avoidance of triggers, pain management, wound care, and topical/oral antimicrobials. Hormonal agents, steroids, retinoids, and surgery can also be used to treat certain patients. Biologics may be considered in Stage II-III HS.

## Consult Dermatology in all cases.

## Hurley Staging System:

Stage I: recurrent nodules and abscesses with minimal scarring Stage II: limited number of sinuses and/or scarring within a body region Stage III: multiple or extensive sinuses and/or scarring

## Duration of Therapy:

Treatment is typically for 12 weeks but may require longer durations in certain cases. Metronidazole should only be used for a maximum of 6 weeks to avoid neurologic toxicity.

## Interventions for All Patients:

Smoking cessation, weight loss, avoidance of triggers, and pain management should be part of all treatment plans. Consult Dermatology for use of hormonal agents, steroids, retinoids, and surgery.

---

References:

- Alikhan, Ali, et al. Journal of the American Academy of Dermatology 81.1 (2019): 76-90

- Up-To-Date article: Hidradenitis suppurativa: Management

# HIV

## Inpatient/Outpatient

HIV infection and AIDS are associated with several host defense defects. Cell-mediated immune defects render a patient more susceptible to opportunistic infections with pathogens like Pneumocystis jirovecii (formerly Pneumocystis carinii), Toxoplasma gondii, cytomegalovirus, mycobacterium-avium intracellulare complex, and Candida spp.

Contact ID or HIV service for assistance.

<<ORDER>> HIV CLINIC Outpt Consult

- Roitt l, et al, eds. Immunology

menus.Name: hsv-encephalitis
menus.Text:
# HERPES SIMPLEX ENCEPHALITIS

Herpes simplex virus (HSV) type 1 is the leading cause of sporadic fatal encephalitis worldwide and should be suspected in patients who have symptoms unexplained by other causes. Typical symptoms include acute alteration of consciousness for more than 24 hours, fever, new onset seizures and/or focal neurologic deficits. Patients taking natalizumab are at increased risk of HSV encephalitis. Early diagnosis and treatment are essential to achieve resolution of infection and symptoms. If diagnosis is not certain and there is little likelihood of herniation, obtain cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) sample for HSV polymerase chain reaction (PCR). MRI without contrast nearly always show abnormal signs in patients with HSV encephalitis. Neurology and Infectious Disease consultations are strongly encouraged.

References:

- Rabinstein, Neurol Clin, 2017, 695-705
- Sanford keyword: Encephalitis
- Up-to-Date Article: Herpes simplex virus type 1 encephalitis

# IMMUNOGLOBULIN DEFICIENCY (HUMORAL IMMUNE SYSTEM)

Antibody deficiency typically leads to recurrent, severe respiratory tract infections associated with encapsulated bacteria, especially Streptococcus pneumoniae and Haemophilus influenzae, and to a lesser extent, Staphylococcus aureus. Recurrent otitis media, sinusitis, and pneumonia are common syndromes.
Gastrointestinal disease associated with Salmonella, Shigella, Campylobacter, or rotavirus is also common in some patients.

[References](references)
Rich RR, et al, eds. Clinical Immunology
Roitt I, et al, eds. Immunology

menus.Name: immunocom-altered-micro-flora
menus.Text:
# ALTERED MICROBIAL FLORA

A rich, diverse microbial flora lives on or in skin, mucosal surfaces, and respiratory and gastrointestinal tracts of healthy people. This flora prevents disease by inhibiting the growth of potential pathogens. Disruption of the normal flora, usually by antimicrobial therapy, reduces this barrier and increases the risk of infectious disease. Patients exposed to broad-spectrum antimicrobials are at greater risk for colonization with resistant bacteria, fungal infections, and Clostridium difficile colitis. During hospitalization, many patients become colonized with more resistant organisms like methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus and resistant Gram-negative bacilli.
[References](references)
Rich RR, et al, eds. Clinical Immunology
Roitt I, et al, eds. Immunology

menus.Name: immunocom-comp-deficiency
menus.Text:
# COMPLEMENT DEFICIENCY

Complement deficiency can be inherited or acquired. Acquired defects are usually a consequence of other diseases like systemic lupus erythematosus.
Complement deficiency leads to increased rates of infections, usually of the upper respiratory tract, but also occasionally with bacteremia or meningitis.
Pathogens are usually Streptococcus pneumoniae, Neisseria meningitidis, and Neisseria gonorrhea.
Patients presenting with fever or other symptoms suggesting systemic bacterial infection should be treated immediately with antimicrobials active against these pathogens.

[References](references)
Rich RR et al, eds. Clinical Immunology
Roitt I et al, eds. Immunology
