menus.Name: immunocom-diabetes-mellitus
menus.Text:
# DIABETES MELLITUS
Hyperglycemia increases the risk of infectious diseases in diabetic patients, and increased blood glucose slows infection resolution.  Diabetic patients are prone to a variety of infections including urinary tract infections, cholecystitis, and bacteremia.  Peripheral neuropathy and arterial insufficiency predispose to infections of skin, soft tissue, and bone infection in the lower legs and feet.

[References](references)

Rich RR, et al, eds.  Clinical Immunology
Roitt I, et al, eds.  Immunology
Joshi N  New Eng J Med 1999, 341: 1906

menus.Name: immunocom-malignancy
menus.Text:
# MALIGNANCY

## Inpatient/Outpatient/ER Malignancies affect host defenses in many ways. Hematogenous malignancies can

diminish the effectiveness of neutrophils and other cells involved in host defense. Tumors often disrupt mucous membranes or blood vessels and allow contaminating organisms into hollow cavities or the bloodstream. Chemotherapy used to treat these malignancies often impairs mucus membranes and suppresses neutrophil production and function.
Ordinarily, empirical antimicrobials are not indicated for patients with malignancy and fever unless they have neutropenia or a specific infectious disease.
[Neutropenic fever](immunocom-neut-fever)
[Prevention of bacterial infections in a patient with malignancy](prev-infect-bact-prophyl)
[Prevention of fungal infections in a patient with malignancy](prev-infect-fungal-prophyl)
[Prevention of viral infection in a patient with malignancy](antiviral-prophylaxis-malignancy)
[References](references):
Rich RR, et al, eds. Clinical Immunology
Roitt I, et al, eds. Immunology

menus.Name: immunocom-neurol-dysfunction
menus.Text:
# NEUROLOGICAL DYSFUNCTION

## Inpatient/Outpatient

Several types of neurological dysfunction predispose patients to infectious diseases. Comatose patients are unable to keep weight off dependent tissues, predisposing them to decubitus ulcers and pressure necrosis. Atelectasis is common in obtunded patients who cannot cough or breathe deeply. When patients require artificial ventilation, intubation compounds the risk of respiratory infection.
Neurological dysfunction of the bladder can interfere with normal bladder emptying and predisposes patients to bacteriuria. The risk of bacteruria increases if patients are catheterized. Antimicrobial treatment is not indicated for asymptomatic bacteriuria. It provides no benefit and increases risk of colonization with resistant organisms.
Neurological dysfunction predisposes patients to aspiration of oropharyngeal or gastric contents. Aspiration causes fever, inflammation, and/or pulmonary infiltrate, but does not require antimicrobial treatment. Bacterial pneumonia occurs in a minority of patients who experience significant aspiration, typically about 3 days later. Typically, the patient improves for the first 2 days and then worsens as bacterial pneumonia develops with increased fever, new or progressive infiltrates, leukocytosis, and newly purulent sputum.
[Aspiration pneumonia](aspiration-pneumonia)
[References](references)
Rich RR, et al, eds. Clinical Immunology
Roitt I, et al, eds. Immunology

menus.Name: immunocom-neut-fever
menus.Text:
# NEUTROPENIC FEVER

## Inpatient/Outpatient/ER

The risk of severe, rapidly progressive infections increases when the absolute neutrophil count (ANC, segmented neutrophils plus bands) is less than 500 cells/microliter. The risk increases dramatically when the ANC is <100 cells/microliter. Because of these risks, patients with fever and neutropenia to this degree should receive empirical antimicrobial therapy immediately. Empirical therapy should also be given to patients with fever and ANC 500-1000 cells/microliter when the concentration is expected to be <500 cells/microliter within the next 48 hours. For this purpose, fever is defined as a single temperature greater than 38.3 degrees Celsius.

## Initial therapy

Since infection can be rapidly progressive and severe, broad-spectrum antimicrobials are given urgently to patients with neutropenic fever as defined above. Vancomycin should only be given when there are clear indications for its use.

Candidates for empirical treatment with oral antimicrobials include those who are febrile but who have no evidence of focal infection or signs or symptoms of severe disease, like hypotension. Outpatient antimicrobials for neutropenic fever must be ordered only in consultation with Hematology-Oncology or Infectious Diseases.

# Treatment

[If patient IS a candidate for oral therapy](neut-fever-cand-oral-thera)
[If patient is NOT a candidate for oral therapy](neut-fever-cand-not-oral-thera)
[Link to a scoring tool that identifies low risk patients for oral therapy](febrile-neutropenia-scoring-tool)

## Modifcation to therapy

[Modification to neutropenic fever therapy](modification-of-neutropenic-fever-therapy)

Rolston KVI Clin Infect Dis 2004, 39: S44

menus.Name: impetigo
menus.Text:
Impetigo and Ecthyma

Impetigo is a superficial skin infection that rarely causes systemic symptoms. Ecthyma is a skin infection characterized by crusted sores beneath which ulcers form. It is a deep form of impetigo, as the same bacteria causing the infection are involved. Ecthyma causes deeper erosions of the skin into the dermis.

Gram stain and culture of the pus or exudates from skin lesions of impetigo and ecthyma are recommended to help identify whether Staphylococcus aureus and/or beta-hemolytic Streptococcus is the cause.

Bullous and non-bullous impetigo can be treated with oral or topical antimicrobials, but oral therapy is recommended for patients with numerous lesions or in outbreaks affecting several people to help decrease transmission of infection. Treatment for ecthyma should be an oral antimicrobial.

[References](references):
Mandell chapter: Cellulitis and subcutaneous tissue infections Up-to-Date website
Stevens DL Clin Infect Dis 2014 59: 147
Montravers P Curr Opin Infect Dis 2016, 29:131

# INITIAL EPISODE OF CLOSTRIDIOIDES DIFFICILE INFECTION (CDI)

Discontinue implicated antibiotic(s). Narrow antibiotic spectrum if antibiotic therapy is still needed. Avoid antiperistaltic agents (narcotics, loperamide, etc.). Avoid antacid therapy without clear indication. If diarrhea has improved or resolved prior to starting C. difficile treatment, consider re-assessing the diagnosis before initiating therapy. C. difficile infection usually responds to antimicrobial therapy. If symptoms do not respond to appropriate antimicrobial therapy, re-consider the diagnosis.

menus.Text:
# KERATITIS

Keratitis is an emergency requiring prompt treatment to prevent vision loss. Contact Ophthalmology immediately.

Keratitis is associated with viral or bacterial infection, trauma, foreign bodies, or allergies. About half of cases of infectious keratitis are caused by bacterial pathogens, most commonly Staphylococcus spp., Streptococcus spp., and gram-negative bacilli. Viruses are the second leading cause. Fungi and parasites have also been associated with corneal infection. Obtain corneal scrapings for gram stain and bacterial and viral cultures and start empirical therapy immediately.

[Herpes keratitis](herpes-keratitis)

If bacterial keratitis is likely, contact ophthalmology to obtain a corneal scraping and give empirical antibacterial drops immediately. Modify therapy based on Ophthalmology and/or Infectious Diseases recommendations. Ophthalmic corticosteroids are contraindicated in patients with keratitis.

## Duration of therapy

## Inpatient

Treatment should be continued until ulcer and other signs of infectious keratitis have resolved. A minimum of two weeks and, in rare cases, up to a month of therapy may be required.

---

References:

- Lin et al., Ophthalmology. 2019,126(1):1-55
- Mandell chapter: Microbial keratitis

# LIVER ABSCESS

[Oral step-down treatment](step-down-treatment)

Liver abscess should be suspected in all patients with fever, leukocytosis, and a space-occupying liver lesion. Liver abscesses fall broadly into two categories: pyogenic and amebic. In the United States, pyogenic liver abscess is much more common. Amebic liver abscess occurs almost exclusively in travelers and immigrants.

Infectious Diseases consultation is recommended due to prolonged treatment and need for follow-up.

## Duration of Therapy

A typical course for pyogenic liver abscess is 4 to 6 weeks based on improvement and follow-up imaging.

References:

- Mandell chapter: Infections of the Liver and Biliary System
- Sanford Guide article: Hepatic Abscess

menus.Text:
# ACUTE NEUROLOGICAL DISEASE ASSOCIATED WITH LYME DISEASE

Neurological disease is a common manifestation of Lyme Disease that typically occurs within weeks to months after the tick bite. Unilateral or bilateral facial nerve palsy (Bell's palsy) can be treated with oral antimicrobials. Other neurological manifestations, including meningitis, require treatment with intravenous antimicrobials.

## Consult Infectious Diseases in all cases

## Duration of therapy

Treat for at least 14 days. Longer durations, up to 21 days for facial nerve palsy and 28 days for other neurologic disease, may be required in severe cases.

## Treatment of neurological disease other than facial nerve palsy (Bell's palsy)

Refer to Inpatient Antimicrobial CDSS

menus.Text:
# LYME DISEASE AND OTHER TICK-BORNE ILLNESSES

Inpatient/Outpatient/ER Patients who display signs of illness or fever within 30 days of removing an attached tick should be evaluated for tick-borne illness. In the upper Midwest, these are Lyme, anaplasmosis, babesiosis, ehrlichiosis, and Powassan virus disease. Patients who have been bitten by an Ixodes spp. tick (deer tick) but who do not display signs or symptoms of infection should not be treated with antimicrobials. Refer to recommendations below for pathogen specific recommendations.

[Anaplasmosis](anaplasma-phatocytophilum)
[Ehrlichioisis](ehrlichia-chaffeensis)
[Babesiosis](babesia-infections-general)
Powassan virus disease - contact Infectious Diseases for more Information.

## Lyme Disease

Lyme disease results from the transmission of Borrelia burgdorferi from an Ixodes spp. tick bite. Refer to CDC for map of endemic areas.
CDC Lyme Disease Case Map

Prophylactic antimicrobial treatment may be beneficial in certain patients who have been bitten while in endemic areas.
[Lyme Disease Prophylaxis](lyme-disease-prophylaxis)

Except for erythema migrans, Lyme disease is a complicated, difficult disease to diagnose and treat. Infectious Diseases consultation is strongly encouraged.
Refer to recommendations below for
[Erythema migrans](lyme-erythema-migrans)
[Acute neurological disease](lyme-acute-neuro-disease)
[Arthritis](lyme-arthritis)
[Cardiac disease](lyme-cardiac-disease)

# LYME DISEASE PROPHYLAXIS

## Inpatient/Outpatient/ER Patients who have been bitten while in endemic areas of New England, Mid-

Atlantic States, Minnesota, and Wisconsin where local rate of Ixodes spp. tick infection rate with Borrelia burgdorferi in an endemic area may be treated with prophylactic antibiotics for prevention of Lyme disease. Using a wait and see method by monitoring for signs and symptoms of Lyme disease is also an acceptable approach in patients who have been bitten by an Ixodes spp. tick.

---

## All following criteria must be met to be considered for prophylactic treatment

1. Doxycycline is not contraindicated (i.e. allergy, pregnant, lactating)
2. Attached tick is reliably identified as an adult or nymphal Ixodes spp.

Ixodes spp. identification

3. Tick is attached for greater than or equal to 36 hours based on degree of tick engorgement with blood or likely time of exposure to tick infested area.
4. Prophylaxis must be started within 72 hours after time tick was removed.
5. Bite occurs in a highly endemic area.

CDC Lyme Disease Case Map

## Prophylactic treatment if all of the above criteria are met

Doxycycline PO 200mg once ($) [DI]

menus.Text:
# ERYTHEMA MIGRANS ASSOCIATED WITH LYME DISEASE

Erythema migrans is the first manifestation of Lyme disease in 70-80% of cases.
It is typically an erythematous circular rash, 5cm or larger in diameter, with induration and central clearing (although other patterns occur). It usually develops at the site of the bite and/or in one or more distant locations. The rash occurs 3 to 30 days after the bite. Rashes with onset less than 3 days after a tick bite are not from Lyme disease.
If suspected erythema migrans is atypical, serology testing is recommended with repeat in three weeks if negative.
Lyme Panel, Serum

menus.Text:
# MORE ABOUT PHARYNGITIS/ TONSILLITIS AND THE MODIFIED CENTOR SCORE

## Inpatient/Outpatient

As most cases are of viral origin, antimicrobials are not indicated in these cases. Warm saltwater gargle rinses and throat lozenges provide temporary relief of throat pain. Five to 10% of cases are caused by group A Streptococcus.
Antimicrobial treatment reduces symptoms by one day, prevents suppurative complications and prevents acute rheumatic fever, an uncommon disease in US adults.
Streptococcal pharyngitis or tonsillitis should be suspected when patients have fever and exudate on the pharyngeal wall or tonsils without symptoms like cough, nasal congestion, or runny nose that suggest viral infection or common cold. If streptococcal pharyngitis is suspected in adults, perform PCR testing for group A streptococci and treat only if positive.
Neisseria gonorrhoeae is a rare cause of pharyngitis. N. gonorrhoeae should be considered for patients with risk factors for sexually transmitted diseases. N.
gonorrhoeae infections must be reported to the state health department and this will be done by Infection Control if the culture is positive.

## The Modified Centor score

Used to estimate the likelihood that a patient with sore throat has streptococcal pharyngitis and whether rapid PCR testing should be performed.

1) Absence of cough = 1 point
2) Swollen and tender anterior cervical nodes = 1 point
3) Temperature greater than 100.4 degrees Fahrenheit (38 degrees Centigrade) = 1 point
4) Tonsillar exudates or swelling = 1 point
5) Age: 3-14 years = 1 point

15-44 years = 0 points
45 years and older = -1 point
Patients with a score of 0 or 1 are at very low risk. PCR testing and antibiotic treatment are not indicated. Patients with a score of 2 to 4 are at moderate to high risk. PCR testing should be obtained in these patients to determine if GAS is present. In patients with a score of 4 or greater, consider empiric antibiotic treatment.

---

menus.Name: necrotizing-infections
menus.Text:
# NECROTIZING INFECTIONS

Call Surgery immediately and consult Infectious Diseases in all cases. Necrotizing infections involve tissues skin and/or deeper structures, including fascia and muscle. These infections destroy tissue, often rapidly, and are often fatal if not treated promptly and appropriately. Necrotizing infections usually result from trauma, surgery, and/or ischemia. These infections can be monomicrobial (e.g., with streptococci or clostridia) or polymicrobial (usually with a mixture of aerobes and anaerobes). Fournier gangrene is usually associated with mixed infection. Myonecrosis is most commonly associated with Clostridium species.

Necrotizing infections differ from cellulitis in several ways. Necrotic infections typically have one or more of the following: (1) severe, constant pain, (2) bullae, (3) bruising or necrosis of overlying skin, (4) gas in tissues which can be felt or seen on images, (5) edema that extends beyond areas of erythema, (6) local anesthesia, and (7) signs of systemic toxicity, such as fever, leukocytosis, delirium, or renal failure.

Necrotizing infections must be treated with both antimicrobial therapy and surgical procedures (excision and/or drainage). Call surgery to see the patient immediately in all cases. Obtain tissue and blood cultures and begin empirical antimicrobials. For several necrotic diseases and/or pathogens, a combination of two antimicrobials is recommended including a bactericidal antimicrobial active at the cell wall or membrane (e.g., beta-lactam or glycopeptide) and an antimicrobial that rapidly inhibits protein synthesis and thus inhibits toxin production, typically clindamycin.

Repeat debridement should be performed daily until no further debridement is necessary. Antibiotic therapy should be tailored as soon as culture results become available.

Administer antibiotics until further debridement is no longer necessary, the patient has improved clinically, and fever has been absent for 48-72 hours.

menus.Name: duke-criteria-listing
menus.Text:
# MODIFIED DUKE CRITERIA DIAGNOSTIC LISTING

## Major criteria

## Blood culture positive

*Typical microorganisms consistent with IE from 2 separate blood cultures:
Viridans streptococci, Streptococcus bovis, HACEK group organisms (Haemophilus species, Aggregatibacter species, Cardiobacterium species, Eikenella corrodens, and Kingella species), Staphylococcus aureus, or community-acquired enterococci in the absence of a primary focus, or microorganisms consistent with IE from persistently positive blood cultures defined as follows: at least 2 positive cultures of blood samples drawn >12h apart or all 3 or a majority of >/= 4 separate cultures of blood (with first and last sample drawn at least 1 h apart)
*Single culture positive for Coxiella burnetii or anti-phase 1 IgG antibody titer greater than or equal to 1:800

## Echocardiogram positive for endocarditis

*Echocardiographic evidence for endocarditis, defined as:
An echo dense, intracardiac mass attached to valve or supporting structures, in the path of regurgitant jets, or a mass present on implanted material in the absence of an alternative anatomic explanation
< OR >
Paravalvular abscess
< OR >
New partial dehiscence of prosthetic valve or new valvular regurgitation (worsening or changing or preexisting murmur is not sufficient for a major criterion)
Note: Echocardiography should be performed in all patients suspected of having endocarditis. Transesophageal echocardiograph (TEE) is recommended for patients with prosthetic valves. Transthoracic echocardiograph (TTE) is often adequate for patients suspected of having native valve endocarditis, especially on the aortic valve, but TEE may be needed for these patients as well. Contact infectious diseases or cardiology for more information.

## Minor criteria

## Predisposing heart condition or intravenous drug user

## Fever

Temperature over 38 degrees Celsius (100.4 degrees Fahrenheit)

## Vascular phenomena

Major arterial embolus, septic pulmonary infarcts, mycotic aneurysm, intracranial hemorrhage, conjunctival hemorrhages, or Janeway's lesions

## Immunologic phenomena

Glomerulonephritis, Osler's nodes, Roth's spots, or rheumatoid factor

## Microbiological evidence

A case with a positive blood culture, but with results that don't meet the major criterion blood culture criteria listed above or serological evidence of active infection with organism consistent with endocarditis. Microbiological evidence is not intended to include all positive blood cultures. For example, a single positive culture for coagulase-negative staphylococci or a culture yielding an organism that is not a cause of endocarditis would not support a diagnosis of endocarditis.

---

References:

- Baddour et al., Circulation 2015, 132:1-52
- Mandell chapter: Endocarditis and intravascular infections

menus.Text:
# PERITONITIS ASSOCIATED WITH PERITONEAL DIALYSIS

Peritonitis associated with peritoneal dialysis usually presents with abdominal pain, fever, nausea or vomiting, and cloudy effluent. The leukocyte concentration is greater than 100 cells/microliter of dialysate, with more than 50% neutrophils.
Obtain Gram stain, culture, and cell count with differential of dialysate before antimicrobials are given.
Nephrology consultation is essential. If cultures show Gram-negative or mixed bacterial infection, a gastrointestinal tract infectious source is more likely.
Gram-positive organisms like staphylococci usually result from external contamination. Fungal peritonitis is rare and requires immediate catheter removal.
**Antimicrobial recommendations are for empirical therapy only. Regimens should be tailored according to patient response and microbiology results in consultation with Nephrology and/or Infectious Diseases for more information.
If vancomycin is used, trough serum concentrations should be kept above 15 mcg/ml to ensure adequate intraperitoneal levels. Usually vancomycin must be given every 3 to 7 days. Contact Nephrology and/or Pharmacy for more information.

## Consult Nephrology in all cases.

Peritonitis labs

---

## Antimicrobial therapy

## Duration

Duration of therapy depends on the pathogen identified. Treat staphylococcal and streptococcal infections for 2 weeks and all other gram-positive infections for 3 weeks. In patients who have Staphylococcus isolated and had a previous staphylococcal infection, treat for 3 weeks
All antimicrobials below are administered via 2.5% dextrose 2000 mL peritoneal dialysate bag over 6 hours with heparin 1000 units, unless contraindicated

## Empirical treatment while waiting for results of gram stain

Vancomycin 30 mg/kg PD LD then 15 mg/kg PD every 3 to 7 days ($) [R] <AND> cefepime 1 gm PD q24h ($) [R]

---

## Antifungal prophylaxis:

Antifungal prophylaxis may be used for the duration of antimicrobial therapy to possibly reduce the risk of fungal peritonitis. *Order if previous peritonitis* Fluconazole 200 mg PO every other day ($) [R,DI]
<OR>
Fluconazole 100 mg PO q24h ($) [R,DI]

---

menus.Text:
# SEPSIS WITH SUSPECTED MENINGITIS OR OTHER CNS INFECTION

Consider consulting Infectious Diseases if CNS infection is not strongly suspected as the main source of infection.

Empirical regimens listed below have broad coverage of likely pathogens based on infectious site. Resistant gram-negative rods and MRSA coverage is not necessary in most patients except those with recent isolates of these organisms. Strongly consider rapid de-escalation of therapy in the first 24-48 hours based on MRSA nares, isolated pathogen(s), and patient response to therapy. Refer to pathogen specific sections of the Antimicrobial CDSS for additional treatment recommendations.

---

## Inpatient

### Listeria is NOT suspected

Ceftriaxone 2 gm IV q12h <AND> vancomycin 15mg/kg IV q12h

### Listeria IS a concern (Adults >= 50 Years or With Alcoholism, Debilitating Disease, or Impaired Cellular Immunity)

Ceftriaxone 2 gm IV q12h <AND> vancomycin 15mg/kg IV q12h <AND> ampicillin 2 gm
IV q4h

### Ceftriaxone or penicillin allergy (see below for severe reactions)

Meropenem 2 gm IV q8h <AND> vancomycin 15 mg/kg IV q12h

### Severe Beta-lactam reaction

Moxifloxacin 400 mg IV q24h <AND> trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole 5mg/kg (TMP
component) IV Q6H <AND> vancomycin 15mg/kg IV q12h

## ER/UC

### Listeria is NOT suspected

Ceftriaxone 2 gm IV once STAT <AND> vancomycin 15mg/kg IV once STAT

### Listeria IS a concern (Adults >= 50 Years or With Alcoholism, Debilitating Disease, or Impaired Cellular Immunity)

Ceftriaxone 2 gm IV once STAT <AND> vancomycin 15mg/kg IV once STAT  <AND>
ampicillin 2 gm IV once STAT

### Ceftriaxone or penicillin allergy (see below for severe reactions)

Meropenem 2 gm IV once STAT <AND> vancomycin 15 mg/kg IV once STAT

### Severe Beta-lactam reaction

Moxifloxacin 400 mg IV once STAT <AND> trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole
5mg/kg (TMP component) IV once STAT <AND> vancomycin 15mg/kg IV once STAT

menus.Text:
# Acute Respiratory Infection (ARI) Symptomatic Therapy

Contact the CDSS Team.

## Per CDC: Antibiotics Aren't Always the Answer. Be Antibiotics Aware.

Antibiotics do not work on viruses, such as colds and flu, or runny noses, even if the mucus is thick, yellow or green. Antibiotics also won't help some common bacterial infections including most cases of bronchitis, many sinus infections, and some ear infections. When antibiotics aren't needed, they won't help you, and the side effects could still hurt you. Reactions from antibiotics cause 1 out of 5 medication-related visits to ED.

## Select links below to print educational material for patient:

<Link> CDC Print Pamphlet-Symptomatic RX for Acute Respiratory Infections <Link> CDC Print Pamphlet-Antibiotics aren't always the answer

---

menus.Name: otitis-externa
menus.Text:
# OTITIS EXTERNA

## Acute Localized Disease

Often due to furunculosis and usually associated with Staphylococcus aureus.
Treat mild cases with moist local heat. For cases with cellulitis or deep invasion, incision and drainage as well as systemic antibiotics may be needed.
Refer to the [Furuncles and Carbuncles](furuncles-and-carbuncles) page for antibiotic recommendations.
Furuncles and Carbuncles

---

## Acute diffuse and chronic otitis externa

Most commonly associated with Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Staphylococcus aureus and Staphylococcus epidermidis. Irrigate to remove cerumen, desquamated skin and purulent material which can improve effectiveness of topical antibiotics. Avoid products that contain neomycin if the tympanic membrane is perforated. Treat for 7 to 10 days

---

menus.Name: pancreatitis
menus.Text:
# PANCREATITIS

[Oral step-down treatment](step-down-treatment)

Antimicrobials are not indicated for uncomplicated pancreatitis. In cases of necrotizing pancreatitis without infection, antimicrobial prophylaxis does not improve patient outcomes. Antimicrobials increase the risk of fungal superinfection and should not be used.

Antimicrobials are indicated for cases with pancreatic abscess, infected pancreatic pseudocyst, or infected necrotic pancreas (phlegmon). The diagnosis of infection can be difficult and may require aspiration. Consultation with Gastroenterology and/or Infectious Diseases is encouraged.

---

## Uncomplicated pancreatitis

No antimicrobials are indicated.

---

## Pancreatic abscess, infected pancreatic pseudocyst, or infected necrotic pancreas (phlegmon)

## Duration of antimicrobial therapy

Total duration of antimicrobial therapy is typically 2 to 4 weeks

---

- Mandell chapter: Pancreatic Infection
- Sanford Guide article: Pancreatitis
- Solomkin et al, Clin Infect Dis, 2010, 50:133-64
- Up-to-Date article: Management of acute pancreatitis

menus.Name: parotitis
menus.Text:
# PAROTITIS

Infection of salivary tissue is a relatively common disease. It is usually caused by a stone in the parotid duct, dehydration, or a viral infection. Sialolithiasis in elderly patients often leads to ductal obstruction and secondary infection. Other predisposing factors for ductal occlusion include dehydration, anticholinergic medications such as tricyclics and diphenhydramine, general disability and trauma. Once culture results are available adjust antimicrobial therapy based on specific etiologic organism.

[More information on Parotitis](more-about-parotitis)

## Duration of Therapy

Therapy duration varies based on clinical response to treatment and is typically 10-14 days.

## Viral Parotitis

Suspect mumps parotitis if there is fever, malaise, earache and bilateral tender swelling of the parotid glands. For mumps parotitis, treat with warm compresses, analgesics, and maintain good hydration to prevent secondary bacterial infection. Other viral causes of parotitis include influenza and enteroviruses.

---

menus.Name: peri-assoc-w-peri-dial
menus.Text:
# PERITONITIS ASSOCIATED WITH PERITONEAL DIALYSIS

Peritonitis associated with peritoneal dialysis usually presents with abdominal pain, fever, nausea or vomiting, and cloudy effluent. The leukocyte concentration is greater than 100 cells/microliter of dialysate, with more than 50% neutrophils.

Obtain Gram stain, culture, and cell count with differential of dialysate before antimicrobials are given. Nephrology consultation is essential. If cultures show Gram-negative or mixed bacterial infection, a gastrointestinal tract infectious source is more likely. Gram-positive organisms like staphylococci usually result from external contamination. Fungal peritonitis is rare and requires immediate catheter removal.

\*\*Antimicrobial recommendations are for empirical therapy only. Regimens should be tailored according to patient response and microbiology results in consultation with Nephrology and/or Infectious Diseases for more information.

To prevent catheter occlusion by turbid dialysate, add 1,000 units of heparin per dialysis bag each day until one day after the dialysate is clear. If vancomycin is used, trough serum concentrations should be kept above 15 mcg/ml to ensure adequate intraperitoneal levels. Usually vancomycin must be given every 3 to 7 days. Contact Nephrology and/or Pharmacy for more information.

## Consult Nephrology in all cases.

---

## Antimicrobial therapy

## Duration

Duration of therapy depends on the pathogen identified. Treat staphylococcal and streptococcal infections for 2 weeks and all other gram-positive infections for 3 weeks. In patients who have Staphylococcus isolated and had a previous staphylococcal infection, treat for 3 weeks.

---

# PERIANAL/ANORECTAL ABSCESS

Antibiotics should typically be reserved for patients with an anorectal abscess complicated by cellulitis, systemic signs of infection, underlying immunosuppression, or failure to improve with drainage alone. Cultures of abscess fluid are not routinely recommended. Consider in patients who will be treated with adjunctive antibiotic treatment for systemic signs of infection, recurrent infection or nonhealing wounds, or underlying immunosuppression.

## Primary therapy: abscess drainage

---

## Adjunctive antimicrobial treatment for patients with above complications.

## Duration of treatment

5 days of antibiotics after incision and drainage is recommended. In the absence of source control, recommended duration is 7-14 days, based on severity of infection, underlying immunosuppression, and clinical response.

---

# PERIODONTAL DISEASE

Periodontal disease, including gingivitis and periodontitis, may progress into more severe disease or cause hematogenous spreading of bacteria if left untreated. All patients with periodontal disease should be referred to the dental service for assessment and direction of treatment. In the presence of gingivitis, the most commonly isolated subgingival flora includes Prevotella intermedia, Capnocytophaga spp, Finegoldia magna and Peptostreptococcus. In the presence of periodontitis, flora increases in complexity to most commonly include Porphyromonas gingivalis, P. intermedia, Aggregatibacter actinomycetemcomitans, Tanneralla forsythensis and Treponema denticola.

## Consult Dental Service.

# PELVIC INFLAMMATORY DISEASE (PID)

Pelvic inflammatory disease (PID) refers to bacterial infection of the upper female reproductive tract. Likely bacterial pathogens include Neisseria gonorrhoeae, Chlamydia trachomatis, anaerobes, enteric Gram-negative rods, and Streptococcus agalactiae. PID should be considered in sexually active women with pelvic tenderness and signs of lower genital tract inflammation. Signs and symptoms may be mild or non-specific, and providers should have a low threshold to initiate treatment. All women who are diagnosed with acute PID should be tested for N. gonorrohoeae, C. trachomatis, and HIV. Male sex partners of patients with PID should be examined and treated (see below) if they had sexual contact within the 60 days before onset of the patient's symptoms.

Judge severity of infection based on clinical signs and symptoms, including blood pressure, pulse, mental status, and degree of fever.

---

menus.Name: pneumocystis-jirovecii
menus.Text:
# PNEUMOCYSTIS JIROVECII DISEASE

Diagnosis and treatment are complex, consult Infectious Diseases in all cases. Pneumocystis jirovecii (formerly termed Pneumocystis carinii) in an ubiquitious organism that causes disease in people with compromised cell-mediated immunity.

Disease is exceedingly rare in people with intact host defenses. Pneumonia is the usual manifestation but P. jirovecii can infect extrapulmonary sites, especially in patients who have been receiving prophylaxis with aerosolized pentanmidine. P. jirovecii disease occurs most commonly in people with AIDS and fewer than 200 CD4 T lymphocytes/microliter.

The abbreviation PCP is often used for Pneumocystis pneumonia. It was derived from the old species name, Pneumocystis carinii.

Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (TMP-SMZ) is the treatment of choice for P. jirovecii disease, including disease that occurs despite TMP-SMZ prophylaxis.

Corticosteriods should be prescribed for patients with AIDS and P. jirovecii pneumonia and an arterial oxygen tension <70 torr or an alveolar-arterial oxygen gradient of >35 torr.
[Prophylaxis for Pneumocystis Jirovecii](pneumocystis-jirovecii-prophylaxis)

menus.Name: pneumocystis-jirovecii-prophylaxis
menus.Text:
# PNEUMOCYSTIS JIROVECII PROPHYLAXIS (PCP Prophylaxis)

Indications for primary prophylaxis of P. jirovecii include:

1) HIV/AIDS patients with CD4 count <200 cells/microliter
2) Hematopoietic or organ transplantation patients during immunosuppression
3) Patients receiving Alemtuzumab, temozolomide or fludarabine
4) Patients receiving >/= 20mg equivalent of prednisone per day for over 1 month
5) Patients with acute lymphocytic leukemia, rheumatologic disease receiving immunosuppressive therapy and certain primary immunodeficiencies (e.g. severe combined immunodeficiency, idiopathic CD4 T-lymphocytopenia, hyper-IgM syndrome)

Dose and duration of prophylaxis varies with the indication. Please contact Infectious Diseases or Hematology/Oncology for more information.
Prophylaxis should be discontinued when host defenses are restored. In persons with AIDS on highly active antiretroviral therapy, Prophylaxis should be discontinued when the CD4 cell concentrations remain over 200 cells/microliter for 3 to 6 months in patients, except that prophylaxis should be continued for life in those who have had P. jirovecii disease.

References

Inpatient/ Outpatient ## BLOOD CULTURE POSITIVE FOR COAGULASE NEGATIVE STAPHYLOCOCCI (CNS)
CNS are the most common contaminants isolated from blood cultures. When CNS isolated from blood cultures represent true bacteremia, the blood is usually obtained from a patient with plastic or metal in the body. The most common source of coagulase negative staphylococcal bacteremia is an infected intravascular catheter.
When CNS are isolated from blood, the physician should carefully assess the patient to decide whether the isolation represents disease or colonization.
Colonization is more likely if a single bottle is positive or both bottles from a single blood draw are positive. If multiple bottles are positive from separate blood draws, it is more likely that the isolates reflect disease or colonization of an intravascular device. Isolates from contaminated bottles often take several days to become positive. If the patient has risk factors for true coagulase negative staphylococcal bacteremia, catheter-related blood stream infection and/or the patient is severely ill, antimicrobials should be given (see below). If there is a plastic or metal prosthesis in the body, the physician should evaluate the site for possible infection. If the isolates are likely to represent contamination and the patient does not seem ill with CNS, antimicrobial therapy would not be helpful and should not be given.
[Treatment of CNS Bacteremia](coagulase-negative-staphylococci-bacteremia)
[Treatment of CNS Infected Intravascular Catheters](intravas-cath-coag-neg-staph)

# POSTSEPTAL CELLULITIS (ORBITAL CELLULITIS)

Postseptal cellulitis (orbital cellulitis) is often preceded by sinusitis and requires immediate consultation with otolaryngology and ophthalmology. Urgent surgical drainage may be necessary. The most common pathogenic organisms in adults are streptococci, Haemophilus influenzae, anaerobes, and Staphylococcus aureus. Broad-spectrum empirical antimicrobials should be used until a pathogen can be identified from the drainage fluid.

## Duration of treatment

Orbital cellulitis should be treated until all signs of infection have resolved. Uncomplicated orbital cellulitis should be treated for minimum of 2 weeks and complicated orbital cellulitis (severe ethmoid sinusitis and bony destruction of sinus) should be treated for at least 4 weeks.

---

References:

- Carlisle et al., American Family Physician. 2015, 92(2)106-112
- Mandell chapter: Periocular infections
- Up-to-Date article: Orbital Cellulitis
- Sanford keyword: Orbital cellulitis

menus.Text:
# PRESEPTAL CELLULITIS

Preseptal cellulitis involves soft tissues in front of the orbital septum and the eyelids and is often preceded by sinusitis. Infection does not involve the orbital contents. The most common pathogenic organisms in adults are streptococci, Haemophilus influenzae, anaerobes, and Staphylococcus aureus. Treat under the guidance of ophthalmology and/or otolaryngology. Intravenous antimicrobials are indicated initially for treatment of moderate to severe disease. Switch to oral antimicrobials when the patient's symptoms improve and the patient can tolerate oral medications.

## Treatment of severe disease

Refer to the Inpatient Antimicrobial CDSS for parenteral therapy.

---

References:

- Carlisle et al., American Family Physician. 2015, 92(2)106-112
- Mandell chapter: Periocular infections
- Johns Hopkins website
- Up-to-date article: Preseptal cellulitis

# PREVENTION OF BACTERIAL INFECTIONS IN A PATIENT WITH MALIGNANCY

Antimicrobial prophylaxis is often given to patients likely to have profound, prolonged neutropenia. Profound neutropenia is less than 100 neutrophils and bands per microliter, and such neutropenia is considered prolonged when it is expected to last more than 7 days. Most patients who should receive prophylaxis have received stem cell transplants or are undergoing induction chemotherapy for acute leukemia.

## If antibacterial prophylaxis is indicated

Duration of therapy: During period of expected neutropenia Ciprofloxacin 500 mg PO q12h ($) [R,DI] < OR >

menus.Text:
# PREVENTION OF FUNGAL INFECTIONS IN A PATIENT WITH MALIGNANCY

Antifungal chemoprophylaxis is often given to patients undergoing induction chemotherapy for acute leukemia expected to have profound neutropenia (less than 100 neutrophils and bands per milliliter) for more than 10 days and for patients receiving allogeneic stem cell transplantation. For most other patients the expected benefits do not outweigh the risks of adverse effects and selection of resistant fungi.
Antifungal is usually given until the absolute neutrophil concentration increases to more than 500 cells/microliter in patients undergoing induction chemotherapy for leukemia. Duration is 100 days for patients undergoing stem cell transplantation. Some physicians continue prevention after 100 days if corticosteroids are part of the immunosuppressive regimen.
Recommend posaconazole prophylaxis for patients with Acute Myeloid Leukemia.
Contact Hematology Oncology or Infectious Disease for more information.
Patients who have had invasive fungal infection in the recent past and who are about to become neutropenic may require chemoprophylaxis. Contact Hematology- Oncology or Infectious Disease for more information.

References:

- Taplitz RA Journal of Clinical Oncology, 2018, 36:3043
- Mandell chapter: Prophylaxis and empirical therapy for infection in cancer patients
- NCCN Clinical Practice Guidelines, Prevention and Treatment of Cancer-
- Related Infections. Version 1.2019. nccn.org

Guidance

menus.Name: prev-of-bact-endocarditis
menus.Text:
# PREVENTION OF BACTERIAL ENDOCARDITIS

Bacteremia occurs several times a day during daily activities like eating and brushing teeth and rarely results in endocarditis, even in people with abnormal valves. While bacteremia might occur following dental or other procedures, most cases of endocarditis are from the millions more episodes of transient bacteremia a person experiences per year from ordinary daily activities. There is no evidence that antimicrobial prophylaxis prevents endocarditis after procedures. The best available evidence suggests that prophylactic antimicrobials confer more risks than benefits in most situations. A decision about whether to administer antimicrobial prophylaxis should be based on both the risk of endocarditis conferred by the patient's cardiac defect and the risk of bacteremia from a planned dental or surgical procedure.

## Minneapolis VAHCS SOP antimicrobial prophylaxis for dental surgery:

SOP for dental surgery antimicrobial prophylaxis

## Determine the need for prophylaxis through the 2-step process outlined below.

## Step 1. Assess the risk of endocarditis for your patient

Prophylaxis is recommended if a patient has any of the following conditions:
o Prosthetic cardiac valve or material including: Presence of cardiac prosthetic valve, transcatheter implantation of prosthetic valves (e.g. TAVR cardiac valve repair with devices (e.g. annuloplasty, rings, or clips), left ventricular assist devices or implantable heart o A history of infective endocarditis o Certain specific congenital heart conditions - refer to the full SOP (link above) or consult Cardiology for more detailed recommendations o Cardiac transplant that develops a problem in the heart valve

## Step 2. Assess the risk of bacteremia from the planned procedure

Prophylaxis is indicated for these procedures:
o All dental procedures that involve manipulation of gingival tissue or the periapical region of teeth or perforation of the oral mucosa.
o Procedures on the respiratory tract that involve incision or biopsy of the respiratory mucosa, such as tonsillectomy and adenoidectomy. Prophylaxis is recommended for bronchoscopy when procedure involves incision of the respir.
tract mucosa.
o Procedures that involve incision through infected skin, skin structures, or musculoskeletal tissue.
o Dermatologic procedures that breach the oral mucosa.

## Prophylactic Antimicrobials select below:

[Patients undergoing dental or oral mucosa procedures](drug-pt-undergo-dental-proc)
[Patients undergoing procedures on the respiratory tract that involve incision or](head-and-neck-surgery-prophylaxis)
biopsy of the respiratory mucosa
[Patients undergoing procedures for infected skin, skin structures, or infected](proced-for-infected-skin-skin-structures)
musculoskeletal tissues

---

References:

- Up-To-Date Article: Antimicrobial prophylaxis for the prevention of bacterial endocarditis
- Wilson et al., Circulation, 2021, 143(20)e963-e978

menus.Name: prev-of-pertussis
menus.Text:
# PREVENTION OF PERTUSSIS

## Immunization

Give a single dose of tetanus-diphtheria acellular pertussis vaccine (Tdap) in adults regardless of interval between most recent Td vaccine. One dose of Tdap vaccine is given to pregnant women during each pregnancy.

## Postexposure prophylaxis in adults

Household contacts with symptomatic coughing should be treated as if they have pertussis. Consult Infectious Diseases for all suspected cases of pertussis and exposure to pertussis.
CDC recommends postexposure prophylaxis in household contacts within 21 days after exposure to pertussis regardless of immunization history. Non-household contacts who are at high risk of severe illness or who have close contact with high-risk individuals should receive post exposure prophylaxis within 21 days of exposure. Those at high risk of severe illness are infants less than one year of age, women in third trimester of pregnancy and those with preexisting health conditions that may be exacerbated by pertussis (e.g. immunosuppressed and asthmatic individuals).
A single dose of Tdap should be administered in those who are not up to date.

---

References:

- CDC: Pertussis https://www.cdc.gov/pertussis/outbreaks/pep.html
- Kim et al, Annals of internal medicine (2016) 184-194
- Sanford keyword: Pertussis
- Mandell chapter: Bordetella species

## Outpatient

Guidance

# INFECTIONS IN BONE OR JOINT PROSTHESES

## Empirical therapy before a pathogen is identified is not recommended unless patient is clinically unstable.

Some infections may require one or two stage reimplantation. Long-term suppressive antimicrobial therapy or joint removal without replacement may be options depending on patient's condition. Consult Infectious Diseases (inpatient) for more information.

If patient has sepsis or is otherwise unstable, empiric treatment before culture results are obtained may be justified.

menus.Text:
# PUBIC LICE (PEDICULOSIS PUBIS)

Lice are parasitic insects. Human lice survive by feeding on human blood. To make a diagnosis, use a nit comb, bright light, or lens to find a louse living in pubic hair. The presence of nits on a hair shaft, especially when they are located more than 6 mm from the skin, does NOT indicate active infestation. Dead nits may remain present for months after successful treatment.

Household contacts and persons who may have come into contact with personal belongings of an infested individual should be examined for evidence of lice and discarded or cleaned if contaminated.

[References](references)
Sanford keyword: lice
Up-to-date website

menus.Text:
# REACTIVATION OF PRIMARY INFECTION (ZOSTER OR SHINGLES)

Zoster represents reactivation of varicella-zoster virus. After primary infection, virus remains latent in the sensory dorsal root ganglia. Reactivation syndrome is characterized by painful, unilateral, vesicular, dermatomal rash.

## Prevention

Vaccinate all adults greater than or equal to 50 years of age with the recombinant zoster vaccine regardless of past episode or receipt of the live zoster vaccine.

Give recombinant zoster vaccine x2, 2nd dose 2-6 months after the first.

---

References:

- Kim et al. Annals Intern Med. 2018, 168(3):210-220
- Sanford keyword: Varicella-Zoster Virus
- Mandell chapter: Chickenpox and Herpes Zoster (Varicella-Zoster Virus)

## Immunocompetent patients

## Treatment in persons <50 years

Treatment is not beneficial, none is recommended.

## Treatment in persons >=50 years

Treatment with antivirals can shorten duration of pain and rash in patients over 50 years old. Treatment must be started within 72 hours of onset.

Valacyclovir 1000 mg PO q8h for 7 days ($) [R]

There is evidence that addition of corticosteroids to antiviral therapy decreases pain and duration of rash and improves quality of life modestly during the acute shingles episode. Corticosteroids do not decrease the incidence of post-herpetic neuralgia. Some authorities recommend addition of corticosteroid therapy to antiviral therapy for patients over age 50 years.

Corticosteroids are not recommended for patients at greater risk for steroid toxicities (e.g., insulin-dependent diabetes mellitus, hypertension, peptic ulcer disease) or for immunocompromised patients.

Prednisone 60 mg daily for 7 days then 30 mg daily for 7 days, then 15 mg daily for 7 days. ($)

## Treatment in persons >=50 years

## Treatment

Immunocompromised patients at increased risk for complications of VZV disease include: patients with malignancy, current immunosuppressive therapy, or HIV infection. Treatment with antivirals shortens duration of symptoms and reduces incidence of complications. In immunocompromised patients, treatment is recommended to be started at any point during an active infection.

menus.Name: retinitis
menus.Text:
# RETINITIS AND ACUTE RETINAL NECROSIS

Retinitis is a subset of uveitis, is rare in immunocompetent people: in these individuals it is usually caused by varicella-zoster virus (VZV) or herpes simplex virus (HSV). Retinitis is more common in immunocompromised patients and cytomegalovirus being the most common pathogen in these patients. Other retinitis pathogens include Toxoplasma gondii, Bartonella henselae, Histoplasma capsulatum, and Treponema pallidum. In most cases, patients have other neurological symptoms or signs. Patients with candidemia may present with 1-3mm white punctate retinal lesions called cotton-wool spots. These may only be visible on fundus examination. Treatment of candidal retinitis is systemic antifungal therapy. Consult Ophthalmology, Infectious Diseases, or Neurology for help.

VZV and HSV cause nearly all cases of acute retinal necrosis (ARN), with a small number being caused by cytomegalovirus. ARN is a rapidly progressing retinitis that occurs primarily in immunocompetent people and can cause vision loss.

Treatment with intravenous acyclovir or valacyclovir is essential to halt progression of ARN. Ophthalmology and Infectious Diseases consultation is essential.

---

- Mandell chapter: Infectious causes of uveitis

menus.Name: scabies
menus.Text:
# SCABIES

Scabies is an infestation of the skin by the mite Sarcoptes scabiei. It is transmitted by skin to skin contact. Outbreaks occur in nursing homes, day care centers, and residential institutions. Scabies is highly contagious and meticulous infection control is needed. Treatment is a single application of permethrin cream. Some experts recommend a second application 7-10 days after the first application if the patient is still symptomatic or if live mites are found at that time.

Contact Dermatology or Infectious Diseases for more information.

Treat family members and other close contacts to prevent spread and recurrence.

[References](references)
Sanford keyword: Scabies
Up-to-date website

Repeat application 7-10 days after the first application if patient is still experiencing symptoms, or if live mites are found.

# COMPLICATED INTRA-ABDOMINAL INFECTIONS: SECONDARY PERITONITIS, INTRAABDOMINAL ABSCESS, INTRAPERITONEAL ABSCESS

[Oral step-down treatment](step-down-treatment)

Complicated intra-abdominal infections (cIAI) include any infectious process that extends from an intra-abdominal organ into a sterile space and is associated with peritonitis with or without abscess Community-acquired cIAI: patients without recent procedure related to site of perforation or abscess Healthcare-associated cIAI: patients developing a new infection > 48 hours after an incident intra-abdominal procedure

## Primary therapy: abscess drainage

CT or US-guided percutaneous or surgical drainage should be considered in all cases for diagnostic confirmation, microbiologic evaluation, and therapy.

## Duration of antimicrobial therapy

Adequate source control: 4 days after source control
Incomplete source control and no abscess: 5-7 days tailored to improvement.
Re-evaluate need for source control if ongoing signs/symptoms of infection beyond 7 days Abscess: 2-6 weeks depending on resolution on repeat imaging. ID Consult recommended.

---

# SECOND RECURRENCE OF CLOSTRIDIOIDES DIFFICILE INFECTION (CDI)

Discontinue implicated antibiotic(s). Narrow antibiotic spectrum if antibiotic therapy is still needed. Avoid antiperistaltic agents (narcotics, loperamide, etc.). Avoid antacid therapy without clear indication. If diarrhea has improved or resolved prior to starting C. difficile treatment, consider re-assessing the diagnosis before initiating therapy. menus.Name: sepsis-and-shock
menus.Text:
# SEPSIS AND SEPTIC SHOCK

Per the Sepsis-3 task force, sepsis is defined as life-threatening organ dysfunction caused by dysregulated host response to infection. Septic shock is a subset of sepsis in which profound circulatory, cellular, and metabolic abnormalities occur. Septic shock requires vasopressor therapy and is associated with in-hospital mortality greater than 40%.

Early intervention is crucial to prevention of death from sepsis. Antimicrobials active against likely pathogens, based on source infection, and supportive treatment to maintain vascular perfusion should be initiated immediately (within the first hour of patient presentation). Reassess antimicrobial therapy daily to narrow therapeutic spectrum when culture and susceptibility data are available.

## Sepsis/septic shock management bundle (includes empiric antimicrobial treatment)

Emergency department (ED)
Intensive Care Unit (ICU)
Hospital ward

Utilize appropriate management bundle above for treatment in patients. The antimicrobial recommendations below are provided as a reference.

## Initial empiric antibiotic guidelines for sepsis

Empirical antimicrobial choice for sepsis is based on coverage of pathogens that typically cause the source infection. Please choose the suspected source infection below to view recommendations.

menus.Text:
# SEVERE SINUSITIS

Community-acquired bacterial sinusitis is most often due to Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenza or Moraxella catarrhalis. Group A Streptococci, Staphylococcus aureus and anaerobes are isolated less frequently.
For patients who present with severe symptoms (high fever (>/= 102 degrees Fahrenheit, >/= 39 degrees Celsius) and purulent nasal discharge for 3-4 consecutive days or facial pain lasting for at least 3-4 consecutive days at the beginning of illness), initiate empiric antimicrobials and obtain CT of sinuses to determine the extent of infection. If the CT shows extension of sinusitis infection into surrounding structures (i.e. the cranium or orbit) consult ENT immediately. Closely monitor all patients who present with severe signs and symptoms to ensure that signs and symptoms improve within 72 hours.

---

- Chow et al, Clinical Infectious Diseases. 2012, 54(8) e72-e112
- Mandell chapter: Sinusitis

menus.Text:
# Daily Antibiotic Prophylaxis for Asplenia

The need for daily antibiotic prophylaxis and its duration is typically determined individually based on patient age, immune status, history of infection, potential for adverse drug reactions and other factors.

## Consider Prophylaxis:

1) Approximately 1 year prophylaxis for all patients following splenectomy.
2) Lifelong prophylaxis for patients with history of sepsis or other severe infections caused by encapsulated organisms.
3) Prophylaxis for as long as the patient is immunocompromised or for life for patients with concurrent immunocompromising conditions (e.g. hematologic malignancy, hypogammaglobulinemia, solid-organ transplant, advanced liver disease, or HIV infection).

## Alternative for penicillin and beta lactam allergy:

menus.Text:
## Asplenia Functional or Anatomical

Following a splenectomy there is considerably increased risk of developing septicemia from invasive encapsulated organisms, namely Streptococcus pneumonia, Haemophilus inluenza type b, and meningococcus. Key measures to prevent such infections include education, vaccination, prophylactic antimicrobial therapy in selected patients, and early empirical therapy for febrile episodes. It is critically important to educate patients regarding the lifelong risk of postsplenectomy sepsis, the importance of vaccinations, and the need for urgent action in response to a febrile episode.

- Clin Infect Dis 2014, 58:e44-100

menus.Text:
# SPONTANEOUS BACTERIAL PERITONITIS (SBP)

[Oral step-down treatment](step-down-treatment)

SBP is infection of the peritoneal cavity in the absence of apparent trauma or other obvious cause. SBP occurs primarily in people with end-stage liver disease and ascites. The diagnosis is made when a peritoneal fluid sample has >/= 250 polymorphonuclear leukocyte cells per microliter, or when bacterial pathogens are isolated.

Long-term SBP prophylaxis is indicated for patients who experience a first episode of SBP.

# SPOROTRICHOSIS

Sporotrichosis occurs most often in people who have had significant outdoor exposure to soil. In immunocompetent people, disease is usually limited to the skin. In people with decreased host defenses (eg, HIV/AIDS, alcoholism, diabetes mellitus, or chronic obstructive pulmonary disease) sporotrichosis often disseminates to bones, joints, or lungs.

Consult Infectious Diseases or Dermatology.

[References](references):
Kaufman CA Clin Infect Dis 2000, 30: 684
Up-to-date website

# PURULENT SKIN/SOFT TISSUE INFECTIONS

Includes furuncles/boils, carbuncles and cutaneous abscesses with or without surrounding inflammation. The predominant pathogen is Staphylococcus aureus (MSSA or MRSA). Incision and drainage are recommended whenever feasible. Adjunctive antibiotics are typically recommended. Incision and drainage alone are reasonable based on patient preferences when abscess is smaller, limited surrounding inflammation, no systemic signs of infections, and/or limited comorbidities.

---

menus.Text:
# STAPHYLOCOCCAL SCALDED SKIN SYNDROME (RITTER'S DISEASE)

Staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome (SSSS) presents with severe skin blistering and exfoliation resulting from toxins produced by Staphylococcus aureus. SSSS is usually found in children and rarely in older adults. Obtain a skin biopsy to differentiate between SSSS and toxic epidermal necrolysis.
Initiate anti-staphylococcal therapy and obtain cultures and susceptibilities.
Empiric therapy active against both MRSA and MSSA until results available.
If cultures reveal methicillin-susceptible Staphylococcus aureus (MSSA), change to nafcillin or cefazolin for better antimicrobial activity.

[References](references)
Up-to-date website

Mandell chapter: The acutely ill patient with fever and rash Stevens DL Clin Infect Dis 2014, 59: 147

Surgical drainage, scaling and antimicrobial treatment are essential. All patients should be referred to the dental service for assessment and direction of treatment. Empirical coverage for likely pathogens (streptococci, Peptostreptococcus, Finegoldia, Bacteriodes and other oral anaerobes) is required.

## Consult Dental Service.

Surgical drainage, scaling and antimicrobial treatment are essential and tooth extraction is required in most cases. # ENDOSCOPIC RETROGRADE CHOLANGIOPANCREATOGRAPHY (ERCP)

Antimicrobials are not indicated in the absence of obstruction or intervention.

If obstruction is present or intervention is likely antimicrobial prophylaxis is recommended.  Use of gentamicin is optional.  Contact Gastroenterology for more information.  If drainage is incomplete, prophylactic antimicrobials after ERCP may be indicated.

[Antimicrobial prophylaxis after ERCP with incomplete drainage](ercp-with-incomplete-drainage-prophylaxis)

menus.Text:
# PLASTIC SURGERY

Antimicrobial prophylaxis is not recommended for most clean procedures in patients without additional postoperative infection risk factors.
Risk factors that increase the risk of postoperative infectious complications for plastic surgery procedures include implants, skin irradiation before the procedure, and procedures below the waist.
Antimicrobial prophylaxis is recommended for clean-contaminated procedures, breast cancer procedures, and clean procedures with risk factors. A single preoperative dose is recommended.

## If no antimicrobial prophylaxis recommended, select below:

*No antimicrobial prophylaxis recommended

## References

- Bratzler DW, et al. Clinical practice guidelines for antimicrobial prophylaxis in surgery, Am J Health-Syst Pharm. 2013 Vol 70 page 195-283
- Antimicrobial Prophylaxis for Surgery, Treatment Guidelines from The Medical
- Letter 2012 Vol 10 pages 73-77

# RECOMMENDED DOSES AND REDOSING INTERVAL

## Antimicrobial surgical prophylaxis

Existing renal or hepatic dysfunction: for single dose, no modification usually necessary.

| Antimicrobial | Recommended dose | Redosing interval** (from initiation of preop dose) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Ampicillin | 2 grams | 2 hours |
| Ampicillin sulbactam | 3 grams | 2 hours |
| Aztreonam | 2 grams | 4 hours |
| Cefazolin | 2 grams (recommend 3 gm dose in patients >=120 kg) | 4 hours |
| Cefuroxime | 1.5 grams | 4 hours |
| Cefoxitin | 2 grams | 2 hours |
| Cefotetan | 2 grams | 6 hours |
| Ceftriaxone | 2 grams | N/A |
| Ciprofloxacin | 400 mg | Do not redose |
| Clindamycin | 900 mg | 6 hours |
| Gentamicin | 5 mg/kg based on dosing weight* | Do not redose |
| Levofloxacin | 500 mg | Do not redose |
| Metronidazole | 500 mg | 12 hours |
| Piperacillin tazobactam | 3.375 grams | 2 hours |
| Vancomycin | 15 mg/kg based on dosing weight* | 12 hours |

[Select for Gentamicin doses](surg-gentamicin-weight-based-dosing)
[Select for Vancomycin doses](surg-vancomycin-weight-based-dosing)

**For those marked N/A: based on typical case length; for unusually long procedures, redosing may be needed.

*Doses based on Dosing Weight (DW). Calculate Dosing Weight: DW = IBW + 0.4 (ABW - IBW)
IBW = Ideal Body Wt, ABW = Actual Body Wt
Male IBW (kg) = 50 + 2.3 * (Ht - 60 inches)
Female IBW (kg) = 45.5 + 2.3 * (Ht - 60 inches)

---

menus.Name: tinea-capitis-ringworm
menus.Text:
# TINEA CAPITIS (RINGWORM)

Tinea capitis is a common fungal infection of the scalp and hair. It is characterized by itchy, red, raised, scaly patches often sharply defined. Redder margins than centers create impression of ring. Tinea capitis primarily affects prepubescent children but can affect people of any age.

Baseline liver function test monitoring recommended. Repeat LFTs if treating for longer than 6 weeks and there were baseline abnormalities, pre-existing liver disease, or other risks for hepatotoxicity.

---

References:

- Up-to-date website
- Sanford keyword: Tinea Capitis, Ringworm
menus.Therapy:
Treat for 4 weeks.
Terbinafine 250 mg PO QDAY [R,H,DI,O]

menus.Name: tinea-pedis-athlete-s-foot
menus.Term1: Tinea pedis (athlete's foot), tinea corporis, tinea manuum, or tinea cruris
menus.Text:
# TINEA PEDIS (ATHLETE'S FOOT), TINEA CORPORIS, TINEA MANUUM, OR TINEA CRURIS

Dermatophyte fungal infections are common worldwide. Dermatophytes metabolize and subsist upon keratin in the skin, hair, and nails. Most tinea infections can often be cured with topical therapy alone. Systemic therapy is reserved for severe or refractory infection, recurrent infection, or in immunocompromised patients.

Treatment should continue for at least one week after clinical curing of infection.

---

References:

- Up-to-date website
- Sanford keyword: Tinea Corporis, Cruris, Pedis
- Cochrane Database Syst Rev. 2007 Jul 18:2007(3):CD001434
- Am Fam Physician. 2002 May 15:65(10):2095

## Systemic treatment

< OR >
Terbinafine 250 mg PO QDAY x 2 weeks [R,H,DI,O]

menus.Name: tinea-unguium-onychomycosis
menus.Text:
# TINEA UNGUIUM (ONYCHOMYCOSIS)

Obtain a fungal stain of nail sample prior to initiating treatment. Using large nail clippers, remove as much of the unattached dystrophic nail as possible. Place the piece of clipped nail plate in formalin jar and send to pathology for fungal stain (PAS). Treatment should only be initiated if stain is positive for fungal elements. Fungal culture is NOT recommended.

Systemic therapy is most likely to achieve a cure, especially with more nail involvement. If <25% involvement, topical therapy may be considered. If >50-75% involvement, systemic therapy should be considered.

Toenails take 12-18 months to grow out completely, so improvement should not be expected to be observed for at least 6-9 months. Continued improvement can be experienced following treatment completion.

---

References:

- Gupta AK, et al. Br J Dermatol 2020 182(2): 287-299
- Ameen M, et al. Br J Dermatol 2014 171: 937
- Up-to-date website: Onychomycosis Management
- Sanford keyword: Tinea
menus.Therapy:
## Oral Treatment:

Terbinafine works about 70% of the time to cure the fungus, and reinfection is common, so many patients will need to do more than one course of treatment. Fluconazole pulse dosing response rate is approximately 50%. May consider retreatment with oral therapy after one year.

Recommend Dermatology Consult for retreatment after failure of 2 courses of terbinafine or fluconazole.

## Preferred Terbinafine first-line oral:

Toenail infections treat for 12 weeks. Obtain baseline liver enzymes prior to starting. Repeat LFTs if treating for longer than 6 weeks and there were baseline abnormalities, pre-existing liver disease, or other risks for hepatotoxicity.

[Terbinafine 250 mg PO qday for 12 weeks (R,H,DI,O]](psjzid-terbinafine-250mg-po-qday)

Fingernail infections treat for 6 weeks. Obtain baseline liver enzymes prior to starting. Repeat LFTs if treating for longer than 6 weeks and there were baseline abnormalities, pre-existing liver disease, or other risks for hepatotoxicity.

Terbinafine 250 mg PO qday for 6 weeks [R,H,DI,O]

## Alternative oral therapy:

Toenail infections treat for at least 6 months
Fluconazole 300 mg PO q week for total of 6 months [R,DI]

Fingernail infections treat for 3 months
Fluconazole 300 mg PO q week for 3 months [R,DI]

## Topical Treatment:

Ciclopirox is a topical first-line treatment for both fingernails and toenails. Complete resolution occurs in approximately 7 percent of patients treated daily for 48 weeks. Ciclopirox is a well-tolerated treatment. Potential side effects include temporary nail changes and local skin irritation.

Ciclopirox 8% nail lacquer: Apply once daily to affected nail(s)
Remove with rubbing alcohol every 7 days. [M] See accompanying medication pamphlet for specific instructions. Treatment is continued until nail clearance or up to 48 weeks.

# TINEA VERSICOLOR

Topical antifungals can be used for limited disease. For disease that involves nails or does not respond to topical therapy, use oral antifungals. Return of normal skin color often takes several weeks after the treatment course is finished.

---

- AK Gupta AK, J Cutan Med Surg. 2014, 18:79

< OR >
Ketoconazole 2% cream to affected area QDAY for 14 days [M]
< OR >
Terbinafine 1% cream apply to affected area QDAY for 7 days [M]
< OR >
Selenium sulfide lotion 2.5% apply to affected area, leave on for 10 minutes, then rinse/shower thoroughly QDAY for 7 days [M]

## Treatment extensive disease:

Fluconazole 300 MG PO weekly for 2 weeks [R]

menus.Text:
## FULMINANT CLOSTRIDIOIDES DIFFICILE INFECTION (CDI)

## Discontinue any antibiotics if possible.

## Narrow antibiotic spectrum if antibiotic therapy is still needed.

## Discontinue antacid therapy if possible.

## There are no available data supporting the use of fidaxomicin for treatment of fulminant CDI.

## Duration of antimicrobial therapy

Antimicrobial therapy for CDI should be continued for 10 days. In patients being treated with antibiotics for predisposing infections, consider continuing treatment for 7 days after completion of those antibiotics. If patient is being treated for CDI recurrence, pulse taper therapy is indicated after resolution of severe disease. Refer to mild to moderate CDI treatment menu for recommendations.

## _______________________________________________________________________________

Refer to the Inpatient Antimicrobial CDSS

Toxic shock syndrome (TSS) can be associated with either staphylococci or streptococci. Antimicrobial treatment and supportive care is urgent. Click one of the links below for diagnostic criteria.
[Link to Diagnosis of Streptococcal toxic shock syndrome](strep-toxic-shock-syndrome)
[Link to Diagnosis of Staphylococcal toxic shock syndrome](staph-toxic-shock-syndrome)

---

# TRICHOMONAS VAGINITIS AND URETHRITIS

Male sexual partners of women with trichomonas vaginitis will not have symptoms but should be treated to prevent recurrent vaginitis in the female sexual partner.

Recommended to treat all sexual partners exposed during the last 60 days.

## Diagnosis

The discharge is purulent, malodorous, and thin. The vaginal pH is greater than 4.5. Nucleic Acid amplification test (NAAT) for trichomonas has improved sensitivities and specificities compared to wet mount.

---

menus.Name: typhlitis
menus.Text:
# NEUTROPENIC ENTEROCOLITIS (TYPHLITIS)

[Oral step-down treatment](step-down-treatment)

Neutropenic enterocolitis, also known as "typhlitis" or "necrotizing enterocolitis", is a severe intraabdominal infection that occurs in neutropenic patients, especially in those with acute leukemia. Send stool for C. difficile testing to exclude of C. difficile infection.
[Clostridioides difficile infection](clostridiodes-difficile-infection)

Hematology-oncology, Infectious Diseases and general surgery consults are essential. Broad spectrum antimicrobials that include anaerobic coverage should be initiated promptly.

## Duration of antimicrobial therapy

Continue antimicrobial therapy until normalization of body temperature, recovery of neutropenia (unless planning to transition back to antimicrobial prophylaxis), recovery of thrombocytopenia, return of normal gastrointestinal function and resolution of bacteremia if initially present. Infectious Disease consult recommended to guide duration if perforation, abscess, or other complicating feature present.

menus.Text:
# URETHRITIS ASSOCIATED WITH SEXUALLY TRANSMITTED DISEASES

The main differential in a person who presents with dysuria is between cystitis and urethritis. Bacterial urethritis is more likely in people with mild dysuria, onset over a few days, or recent sexual contact.

The two most common sexually transmitted urethritis pathogens are Neisseria gonorrhoeae and Chlamydia trachomatis. Nucleic acid amplification tests for these pathogens are more sensitive than culture and should be used for patients at risk for sexually transmitted urethritis.
Chlamydia & GC PCR/LCR test

## For patients who have recently been treated for urethritis

[Treatment of recurrent or persistent urethritis](recurrent-persist-urethritis)

When dysuria is from a sexually transmitted disease, the patient's sexual partner(s) during the previous 60 days should be evaluated for sexually transmitted infection.

If diagnostic tests for the cause of urethritis are not feasible, therapy for both N. gonorrhoeae and C. trachomatis should be given to partners.

## Initial treatment of patients and sex partners

Patients and partners are often infected with both N. gonorrhoeae and C. trachomatis. Treat for both pathogens unless one is ruled out by lab test.
[Treatment for gonococcal urethritis](gonococcal)
[Treatment for chlamydial or non-gonococcal urethritis](chlamydia-urethritis-cervicitis-or-proctitis)

References:

- St. Cyr S, et al. MMWR Morb Mortal Wkly Rep 2020, 69:1911-1916.

menus.Name: vaginitis
menus.Text:
## BACTERIAL VAGINOSIS

Vaginitis usually presents with discharge, itching, irritation, odor, or pain.
Bacterial vaginosis is the most common form of vaginitis. Normal hydrogen peroxide and lactic acid producing vaginal flora, including Lactobacillus species, is reduced and high concentrations of anaerobic bacterial pathogens are present. Pathogenic bacteria commonly include Gardnerella vaginalis, Mycoplasma hominis, Nobiluncus, Prevotella and other Gram-negative anaerobes.
Vaginal pH should be measured, and the specimen should be examined under the microscope for identification of clue cells (epithelial cell coated with bacteria). In bacterial vaginosis the vaginal pH is high (> 4.5), the discharge is homogenous and gray-white, and the specimen has a positive amine or whiff test characterized by a fishy odor before or after addition of 10% KOH.
Bacterial vaginosis nucleic acid amplification tests are available for common pathogens to aide in identification of pathogen(s).
Bacterial vaginosis may be transmitted sexually. Patients at risk of sexually transmitted infections should be assessed for treatment.
[Sexually Transmitted Infections and HIV Exposure](sexually-transmitted-infection)

References:

- Mandell chapter: Vulvovaginitis and cervicitis
- Sanford keyword: Bacterial Vaginosis
- Up-to-Date article: Bacterial vaginosis: Clinical manifestations and diagnosis

# DISKITIS AND VERTEBRAL OSTEOMYELITIS

When possible, obtain diagnostic cultures before starting empiric therapy.

Obtain blood cultures and image guided aspirates or surgical bone biopsy.

Definitive therapy is based on culture and susceptibility test results.

## Recommended duration of therapy:

Treat for at least 6 weeks of pathogen directed IV/PO therapy for high risk including MRSA infection, ESRD, or undrained abscess or device implantation.

Once culture and susceptibility testing is available switch to pathogen directed therapy.

---

# ANTIMICROBIAL RESTRICTION POLICY

Medication orders placed using the CDSS system will NOT require Infectious Disease approval. Because prescribing advice within the system has been developed with input from a broad, representative group of clinicians and the recommendations that have emerged are based on site-specific susceptibility patterns, clinical evidence, local preferences, and national guidelines, INFECTIOUS DISEASE APPROVAL FOR RESTRICTED ANTIMICROBIALS WILL NOT BE NEEDED at participating VA sites. Clinicians are still encouraged to seek advice from Infectious Diseases whenever it would be helpful.

Restricted antimicrobials ordered outside the CDSS system will continue to need ID approval.

menus.Name: how-to-find-alt
menus.Text:
# HOW TO FIND AN ALTERNATIVE ANTIMICROBIAL WITHIN THE CDSS

The CDSS has been developed locally with input from a broad, representative group of clinicians. All antimicrobial recommendations within the Antimicrobial CDSS are reviewed by a clinical pharmacist and an Infectious Diseases Medical Specialist. Recommendations provided are based on local susceptibility patterns, clinical evidence, local preferences, and national guidelines. In rare cases, the recommended antimicrobials and listed alternatives may not be preferred for the patient you are treating (e.g. isolate resistance, allergies, etc.). In these cases, a broader set of alternative antimicrobials may be ordered through the Antimicrobial CDSS. Like other antimicrobial orders in the CDSS, antimicrobials ordered through the Alternative Antimicrobials menu do on require a prior authorization or ID approval.

To access the Alternative Antimicrobials menu, navigate to the menu containing antimicrobial recommendations for the infectious disease you are treating.

At the top of the menu, select:

#2 Help legend, allergy info, consults, alternative antimicrobials and more Then select- Alternative Antimicrobials to CDSS Recommendations Select the reason an alternative antimicrobial is required then the Alternative Antimicrobial menu will display.

The Alternative Antimicrobial menu contains antimicrobial regimens that have been deemed appropriate for use as alternatives to recommended antimicrobials by the Antimicrobial P&T Subcommittee. If the list does not contain the preferred antimicrobial, contact or consult Infectious Diseases.

The regimens provided in the Alternative Antimicrobial menu are not tailored for a specific infectious disease. The dose, frequency, and duration must be changed based on the infectious disease you are treating as well as for patient specific factors. The usage of alternative antimicrobials are monitored by the Antimicrobial CDSS team for appropriateness and to identify infectious diseases for addition to the system.

menus.Name: beta-lactam-allergy-assessment
menus.Text:
# ASSESSMENT OF BETA-LACTAM REACTION AND ALTERNATIVE TREATMENT

# Streamlined Version (PDF form)

Assessment of Beta-lactam Reaction CLICK HERE

This guide is intended to aid clinicians in assessment of beta-lactam reactions and selection of appropriate alternative therapy. It is not a substitute for clinical judgment and should not be used as a sole resource when selecting antimicrobial therapy.

[Important Beta-Lactam Allergy Facts and Obtaining a Detailed Reaction History](beta-lactam-allergy-facts)

# Reaction Assessment and Selection of an Alternative Beta-lactam

- If the same or a different beta-lactam was subsequently tolerated without reaction, that beta-lactam may be used.
- If reaction was intolerance (e.g. headache, GI symptoms), family history of reaction, or if the patient denies allergy, any beta-lactam may be used.
- See below for treatment based on type of reaction (severe vs non-severe).
- If reaction is unknown and patient denies any severe reactions (see below for list of severe reactions), reaction is considered non-severe.
- If patient is in a suitable care setting, observation during the first 15 minutes to 1 hour after first dose of therapy may be performed to monitor for signs/symptoms of an allergic reaction.

---

# SEVERE REACTION TO BETA-LACTAM:

---

If the patient experienced a known severe reaction (use link below for severe reaction list), AVOID ALL Beta-Lactam Antibiotics. If beta-lactam therapy is ideal, contact Infectious Diseases for desensitization or alternative.

Severe Reaction Examples:

- Anaphylaxis
- Reaction needed medical intervention
- Mucosal, cardiovascular or respiratory system involvement
- Hemolytic anemia
- Immune hepatitis
- Interstitial nephritis
- Acute interstitial nephritis (AIN)
- Skin desquamation
- Drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms (DRESS)
- Stevens-Johnson syndrome (SJS)
- Generalized exanthematous pustulosis
- Toxic epidermal necrolysis (TEN)

---

# NON-SEVERE REACTION TO BETA-LACTAM:

---

Select an alternative non-cross-reactive beta-lactam for therapy based on beta-lactam class patient had a reaction to. Refer to PDF document above for detailed cross-reactivity chart.

# PENICILLIN CLASS REACTION

(e.g. Amoxicillin, ampicillin, cloxacillin, dicloxacillin, nafcillin, oxacillin, penicillin, piperacillin, ticarcillin)

# Use: Cefazolin, cefdinir, cefuroxime, ceftazidime, ceftriaxone, cefepime, ertapenem, imipenem, or meropenem

# 1ST GENERATION CEPHALOSPORIN CLASS REACTION

(e.g. Cefadroxil, cefatrizine, cefazolin, ceftezole, cephalexin, cephalothin, cephapirin)

# Use: Dicloxacillin, nafcillin, cefazolin (unless reaction was to cefazolin) cefdinir, ceftazidime, ceftriaxone, cefuroxime, cefepime, ertapenem, imipenem, or meropenem

# 2ND GENERATION CEPHALOSPORIN CLASS REACTION

(e.g. Cefaclor, cefamandole, cefonicid, cefotetan, cefoxitin, cefprozil, cefuroxime)

# Use: Amoxicillin, ampicillin, dicloxacillin, nafcillin, piperacillin, cefadroxil cefazolin, cefdinir, ceftazidime, ceftriaxone, cephalexin, cefepime, ertapenem imipenem, or meropenem

# 3RD-5TH GENERATION CEPHALOSPORIN CLASS REACTION

(e.g. Cefdinir, cefditoren, cefepime, cefiderocol,cefixime, cefpirome, cefoperazone, cefotaxime, cefpodoxime, ceftaroline, ceftazidime, ceftibuten, ceftizoxime, ceftolozane, ceftriaxone)

# Use: Amoxicillin, ampicillin, dicloxacillin, nafcillin, penicillin, piperacillin, cefadroxil, cefazolin, cephalexin, ertapenem, imipenem, or meropenem

# CARBAPENEM CLASS REACTION

(e.g. Ertapenem, imipenem and meropenem)

# Use: Amoxicillin, ampicillin, dicloxacillin, nafcillin, penicillin, piperacillin, cefadroxil, cefazolin, cephalexin, cefdinir, ceftazidime, ceftriaxone, or cefepime

---

menus.Term1: Information on adding MRSA nares screening with new IV Vancomycin starts: (Navigation)
menus.Text:
# Information on adding MRSA nares screening with new IV Vancomycin starts:

MRSA nares screening will be ordered on all new IV Vancomycin starts.

MRSA nares may be a helpful tool in identifying patients with low risk of MRSA infection in whom empiric vancomycin may not be required.

A negative MRSA nares does not definitively rule out the presence of MRSA elsewhere and is one factor to consider in the de-escalation of vancomycin (and other anti-MRSA antimicrobials).

# References

- Parente DM, Cunha CB, Mylonakis E, Timbrook TT. The Clinical Utility of
