menus.Text:
# Gram-Negative Bacilli Drug Resistance

In some Gram-negative bacilli, potent bacterial enzymes have emerged that inactive many newer broad-spectrum beta lactam drugs. These include extended-spectrum beta-lactamases (ESBLs), serine carbapenemases, metallo-beta-lactamases, AmpC beta-lactamases and oxacillinases. These enzymes are most common in strains of Acinetobacter, Citrobacter, Enterobacter, Escherichia coli, Klebsiella, Proteus, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Salmonella, and Serratia marcescens. The enzymes can be latent under many circumstances. However, in patients receiving beta lactam antibiotics, the enzymes can be expressed and contribute to treatment failure. Because of this, and since the enzymes continue to evolve, they are difficult to detect in clinical microbiology laboratories.

Bacteria carrying these enzymes are often also resistant to many other commonly used antimicrobials, including trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, quinolones, and others, through different mechanisms. Enterobacteriaceae, Pseudomonas and Acinetobacter are increasingly resistant to all antimicrobials.

Clinicians must be aware that these enzymes may not be detected in all strains that carry them. If a Gram-negative infection is not responding to therapy with a beta lactam drug, consider adding or switching to a drug that is not a beta lactam and appears active in the susceptibility report.

If a patient is suspected of having a Gram-negative infection and is likely to be colonized with bacteria carrying these enzymes, empirical therapy with alternative drugs that are not inactivated by them should be considered.

# Risk factors for colonization or infection with resistant gram-negative bacilli

1. Travel to Asia
2. Central venous catheters and other indwelling tube and drains
3. Recent surgical procedures
4. Recent antibiotic therapy
5. Long-term care facility residence
6. Multiple, severe chronic illnesses
7. Ventilator assistance
8. Hemodialysis
9. Long hospital or ICU stay.

# ESBLs alternative antimicrobials

Inactivate most cephalosporins, monobactams, and penicillins. Alternatives include aminoglycosides, carbapenems and colistin.

# Serine carbapenemases, metallo-beta-lactamases and oxacillinases alternative antimicrobials

Confer resistance to all beta-lactams. Most strains are also resistant to most other antibiotic classes. Alternatives include aminoglycosides and colistin.

Infectious Diseases consultation is recommended.

References

- Mandell chapter: Molecular Mechanisms of Antibiotic Resistance in Bacteria
- Up-to-Date article: Extended-spectrum beta-lactamases
- Up-to-Date article: Overview of carbapenemase-producing gram-negative bacilli
- Rodrï¿½guez-Bano et al. Clinical microbiology reviews, 2018, 31(2): e00079-17
- Sanford guide keyword: Gram Negative Bacilli, Drug Resistance, Overview

menus.Therapy:
## AmpC beta-lactamases alternative antimicrobials

Inactivate many cephalosporins, most penicillins, and beta-lactam inhibitor combinations. Alternatives include aminoglycosides, carbapenems, cefepime and colistin.

## Additional alternative antimicrobials

Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole and quinolones are non-beta-lactam alternative antimicrobials, especially useful for IV to PO conversion. Gram negative bacilli co-resistance to these antimicrobials is common however. Tigecycline (restricted to ID) and ceftazidime-avibactam (non-formulary) are also potential options for susceptible isolates. Infectious Diseases consultation is required for their use.

# CONDITIONS NOT BENEFITTED BY ANTIMICROBIAL THERAPY

Several common conditions associated with inflammation or
microorganisms do not benefit from antibiotic therapy in most or all cases.

Yet, antimicrobials are frequently prescribed for these conditions leading to
unnecessary toxicity and costs, rare deaths, and the relentless increase in
antimicrobial resistance. Please review these conditions and do not give
antimicrobials for these conditions unless there are extraordinary
circumstances that make your situation different. If you have any questions,
please contact the infectious disease physician on call.

menus.Name: tpoxx-monkeypox-treatment
menus.Text:
# CDC MPOX TREATMENT WITH TPOXX

# Eligibility:

o Consent: Must have documented consent by patient or legally authorized representative in paper or i-Med consent o Primary/empiric treatment: Confirmed diagnosis or suspected infection based on exposure and/or symptoms while testing is pending.

o Secondary Treatment: Complications from replication competent vaccinia infection from vaccination, secondary transmission, or other exposure. TPOXX may be used after VIGIV treatment or in conjunction with VIGIV and/or with other therapies based on clinical judgement.

o Post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP): May be considered on a case-by-case basis in consultation with the CDC. Eligibility for PEP use depends on high risk exposure confirmed or probable case and alternative or complement to PEP vaccination is needed based on clinical judgment (e.g. vaccine allergy, immunocompromise).

o Dosage and duration: Weight based dosing for 14 days. But it may be longer based on clinical progress but not to exceed 90 days. Oral tecovirimat capsule should be taken by mouth with a full glass of water within 30 minutes after eating a full meal of moderate or high fat (ideally about 600 calories and 25 grams of fat).

o CDC Case Reports Forms:  To be completed and returned to CDC by treating physicians per IND protocol.

CLICK HERE for link to required documents (MPox Taskforce Teams group)

# Exclusions:

o Patient or legally authorized representative unwilling to sign an informed consent and refuse tecovirimat treatment o  Known allergy to tecovirimat and/or excipients of tecovirimat o  Upon negative test results for orthopoxvirus whose treatment was initiated based on clinical manifestations prior to laboratory results.

o For IV tecovirimat only: patients with severe renal impairment (creatinine clearance <30 mL/min)
menus.Inpt: ORZID2 GMENU ABX TPOXX MONKEYPOX TREATMENT
menus.Therapy:
## Oral Treatment:

Patients 40kg to < 120 kg
INV-Tecovirimat 600 mg (3 capsules) orally q12h for 14 days

*Places medication orders for inpatient and outpatient (included in order set)

Patients 120 kg and Above
INV-Tecovirimat 600 mg (3 capsules) orally q8h for 14 days

*Places medication orders for inpatient and outpatient (included in order set)

## Intravenous Treatment:

o Very ill hospitalized patients who are unable to take oral therapy or for whom there is a concern that oral drug absorption may be altered.

o IV tecovirimat should not be administered in patients with severe renal impairment (creatinine clearance <30 mL/min) and should be used with caution in patients with moderate (creatinine clearance 30-49 mL/min) or mild (creatinine clearance 50-80 mL/min) renal impairment.

o IV tecovirimat should be switched to the oral formulation as soon as patients can take oral medications and/or gastrointestinal disfunction impacting absorption has resolved.

Patients 35 kg to < 120 kg
INV-Tecovirimat 200 mg IV q12h over 6 hours for 14 days

*Places medication orders for 2 seperate INV-tecovirimat IV 100mg q12h orders for a total of 400 mg over 24hrs via slow infusion.

Patients 120 kg and Above
INV-Tecovirimat 300 mg IV q12h over 6 hours for 14 days

*Places medication orders for 2 seperate INV-tecovirimat IV 150 mg q12h orders for a total of 600 mg over 24hrs via slow infusion.

menus.Text:
# Guidance on managing Cytokine Release Syndrome (CRS)

# CRS GRADE & DEFINING SYMPTOMS

# GRADE 1 CRS (Floor patients)

# Symptoms require symptomatic treatment only.

# If temperature >/=100.4 F or headache or rigors,

# without hypotension or hypoxia.

# GRADE 2 CRS (Floor patients)

# Symptoms require and respond to moderate intervention.

# -Fever greater than or equal to 100.4F

# -Hypoxia requiring oxygen therapy, AND/OR

# -Hypotension responsive to fluids not requiring

# vasopressors.

# GRADE 3 AND 4 CRS (ICU patients)

# Severe symptoms defined as temperature >/=100.4F with:

# -Hemodynamic instability requiring a vasopressor (with or

# without vasopressin) OR

# -Worsening hypoxia or respiratory distress requiring high-flow

# oxygen.

# Reference:

Lee D., et al. ASTCT Consensus Grading for Cytokine Release Syndrome

and Neurologic Toxicity Associated with Immune Effector Cells

Biology of Blood and Marrow Transplantation (2018) 25:625-638

<!-- COLUMN 2 -->

# MANAGEMENT

# Administer symptomatic treatment:

# Note: Acetaminophen order below placed with Bispecific medication order.

Acetaminophen 650mg PO q6h prn Temp>/=100.4 F or headache or rigors

Give and then NOTIFY Inpatient Medicine Provider.

# In addition to Grade 1 treatment above:

Sodium Chloride 0.9% 1000 ml IV initial bolus over 2 hours for hypotension

Sodium Chloride 0.9% 1000 ml IV bolus over 2 hours (2nd bolus for hypotension)

# If hypotension not responsive to 2 liters NS, administer dexamethasone:

Dexamethasone 8MG IV x1 STAT for CRS Grade 2

# If patient not responding to interventions above, call a rapid response to

# transfer patient to ICU.

# Note: Tocilizumab may be given on 3D if delay in transferring patient to ICU.

# In addition to GRADE 2 treatment above:

Transfer Patient to ICU

Dexamethasone 8mg IV q8h prn up to 3 doses. Notify ICU provider.

# Provider must order EACH dose of Tocilizumab as needed:

May repeat q8h if no improvement, no more than 3 doses/24hours and 4 doses total

Maximum for each dose 800MG

Tocilizumab may be given with corticosteroids.

Tocilizumab 8 MG/KG IV STAT DOSE#1 (Grade 3-4 CRS)

Tocilizumab 8 MG/KG IV STAT DOSE#2 (Grade 3-4 CRS)

Tocilizumab 8 MG/KG IV STAT DOSE#3 (Grade 3-4 CRS)

Tocilizumab 8 MG/KG IV STAT DOSE#4 (Grade 3-4 CRS)

# VASOPRESSORS: use ICU specific orders/order sets

# Guidelines for management of neurologic toxicity, including ICANS (Immune Effector Cell-Associated Neurotoxicity Syndrome)

# ICANS GRADE & DEFINING SYMPTOMS

# MANAGEMENT

# Grade 1

- ICE score 7-9 with no depressed level of consciousness
- Supportive care

# Grade 2

- ICE score 3-6 and/or
- Supportive care
- Mild somnolence awaking to voice

Click here to order Dexamethasone 10mg IV ONCE STAT

Click here to order Dexamethasone 10mg IV q12h

- Monitor neurologic symptoms and consider consultation with neurologist and other specialists for further evaluation and management.

# Grade 3

- ICE score 0-2 and/or
- Recommend intensive monitoring ICU
- Depressed level of consciousness awakening only to tactile stimulus and/or
- Consider mechanical ventilation for airway protection
- Any clinical seizure focal or generalized that resolves rapidly or

Click here to order Dexamethasone 10mg IV q6h

- Nonconvulsive seizures on EEG that resolve with intervention and/or
- Consider repeat neuroimaging (CT or MRI) q 2-3 days if patient has persistent
- Focal or local edema on neuroimaging

Grade >/=3 neurotoxicity

- Consult neurology for seizure control.

# Grade 4

- ICE score 0 (patient is unarousable and unable to perform ICE) and/or
- ICU care
- Stupor or coma and/or
- Consider mechanical ventilation for airway protection
- Life threatening prolonged seizure (>5minutes) or

Click here to order High dose Methylpred 500mg IV q12h x3days THEN taper

- Repetitive clinical or electrical seizures without return to baseline [Taper: 250mg IV q12hx2days, then 125mg IV q12hx2days, then 60mg IV q12hx2days]

in between and/or

- Consider repeat neuroimaging (CT or MRI) every 2-3 days if patient has
- Diffuse cerebral edema on neuroimaging, decerebrate or decorticate posturing persistent Grade >/=3 neurotoxicity or papilledema, cranial nerve VI palsy, or Cushing's triad

menus.Text:
# BACTEREMIA ASSOCIATED WITH ENTEROCOCCI

Enterococcus faecalis is almost always susceptible to penicillins locally, ampicillin is more effective than vancomycin in susceptible isolates.

Enterococcus faecium is typically resistant to some beta-lactams, aminoglycosides, and vancomycin. Consult Infectious Diseases in all cases.

Refer to cardiovascular section for suspected infectious endocarditis.
[Approach to Endocarditis](endocarditis-approach-to)

# Duration of treatment

For uncomplicated infections where blood cultures are sterile after 24 hours of treatment, treat for 7-14 days. A longer duration is needed if infection is complicated or repeat blood cultures are positive.

---

References:

- Sanford keyword: Enterococcus faecium
- Sanford keyword: Enterococcus faecalis
- Up-to-Date article: Detection of bacteremia: Blood cultures and other diagnostic tests
- Up-to-Date article: Treatment of enterococcal infections

## Treatment of resistant enterococcus (Van A/B positive)

menus.Name: streptococci
menus.Text:
# BACTEREMIA ASSOCIATED WITH STREPTOCOCCI

Bacteremia is typically caused by S. pyogenes (Group A), S. agalactiae (Group B) and S. pneumoniae. If other streptococcal species are isolated, contamination is likely. Treat only if greater than one blood culture is positive. Identification and treatment of the source of infection, in addition to antimicrobial therapy, is crucial for resolution of infection.

For patients with toxic shock syndrome refer to those recommendations.
[Toxic Shock Syndrome](toxic-shock-syndrome)

# Duration of treatment

Treatment duration is not well established. Treat for 7 -14 days depending on source control and response to treatment. Consult ID for more information.

---

References:

- Sanford keyword: Streptococcus agalactiae, Group B Strep
- Sanford keyword: Streptococcus pyogenes, Beta hemolytic, Group A, B, C, F, G Strep

Assessment of beta-lactam reaction

menus.Name: empirical-therapy
menus.Text: # NATIVE VALVE ENDOCARDITIS--EMPIRICAL THERAPY
menus.Inpt: ORZID2 GMENU EC NV EMP THERA
menus.Therapy:
## Empirical treatment in a non-intravenous drug user

Wait for identification of pathogen before initiating antimicrobial therapy in most cases. If empiric antimicrobial treatment is necessary, due to hemodynamic instability or other severe disease, use:

Vancomycin 15 mg/kg IV q12h ($) R <AND> ceftriaxone 2 gm IV q24h ($)
< OR >
Vancomycin 15 mg/kg IV q12h ($) R <AND> gentamicin 1 mg/kg IV q8h ($) [R,O]

# Empirical treatment in an intravenous drug user

Staphylococcus aureus is the most likely pathogen, followed by streptococci and enterococci. However, gram negative pathogens are often associated with endocarditis in these patients. Culture results are key for appropriate therapy.

Consult Cardiology and Infectious Diseases for more information.

Vancomycin 15 mg/kg IV q12h ($) R <AND> gentamicin 1 mg/kg IV q8h ($) [R,O]

---

menus.Name: myocarditis
menus.Text:
# MYOCARDITIS

Myocarditis is most commonly associated with enterovirus or coxsackie virus infection. Less common pathogens include pyogenic bacteria, rickettsia, toxoplasmosis, and fungi.

Empirical antimicrobial treatment is not indicated. Supportive care and treatment of CHF are essential. Consult Cardiology and/or Infectious Diseases for more assistance.

Avoid non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDS) and corticosteroids in these patients, as the use of NSAIDs in myocarditis has been associated with worse outcomes.

---

References:

- Mandell chapter: Myocarditis and Pericarditis
- Up-To-Date article: Treatment and prognosis of myocarditis in adults

menus.Name: pericarditis
menus.Text:
# PERICARDITIS

Most cases arise from non-infectious causes or are associated with viruses.

Antimicrobial therapy is not indicated unless pericardial fluid is purulent. If fluid is purulent, pericardial drainage is required in most cases. Modify antimicrobial regimen and narrow coverage based on results of culture and susceptibility tests.

Cardiology consultation is essential for management of therapy. Infectious Diseases consultation is recommended if an infectious origin is suspected.

# Duration of therapy

Duration is based on patient specific factors such as resolution of fever and clinical signs of infection. Generally, duration is 2 to 4 weeks depending on how adequacy of drainage of pericardial fluid and susceptibility of infectious organism.

---

References:

- Adler et al., European Heart Journal 2015, 36.2921-2964
- Mandell chapter: Myocarditis and Pericarditis
- Sanford keyword: Pericarditis
- Up-To-Date article: Purulent pericarditis
menus.Therapy:
## Empirical Treatment

Preferred:

Vancomycin 15 mg/kg IV q12h ($) R <AND> ceftriaxone 2 gm IV q24h ($) R,DI

Alternative:

[Assessment of beta-lactam reaction](beta-lactam-allergy-assessment)

Vancomycin 15 mg/kg IV q12h ($) R <AND> piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 gm

IV q6h ($$) [R]

Influenza Vaccine Outpatient and Inpatient Guidelines

menus.Name: syphilis
menus.Text:
# SYPHILIS

# Consult Infectious Diseases in all cases. Evaluation and management are complex.

Syphilis is a sexually transmitted disease caused by the spirochete Treponema pallidum that can manifest as a variety of signs or symptoms. Primary syphilis typically consists of painless ulcers or chancre at the site of infection with regional adenopathy. Secondary syphilis often includes a skin rash (disseminated and/or including the palms and soles), fever, malaise, mucocutaneous lesions and lymphadenopathy. Tertiary syphilis includes those with cardiovascular or gummatous disease.

Latent syphilis is a period of disease when a patient does not have symptoms but is found to be infected through serologic testing. Early latent syphilis refers to latent syphilis acquired within the preceding year and late latent syphilis refers to all other cases of latent syphilis. Neurosyphilis, Ocular syphilis or Otosyphilis, can occur at any stage of syphilis with early manifestations (e.g. meningitis, stroke, vision or hearing loss) occurring within the first months to years of infection and late manifestations (e.g. dementia, tabes dorsalis) occurring after 10-30 years.

# Diagnosis

A presumptive diagnosis is made through use of a nontreponemal or serologic test (i.e. rapid plasma reagin [RPR]) and a treponemal test (i.e. fluorescent treponemal antibody absorbed [FTA-ABS]). Direct methods through darkfield microscopy and direct fluorescent antibody (DFA) must be used for definitive diagnosis since T. pallidum cannot be cultured.

Syphilis antibody test with reflex to rapid plasma reagin (RPR)

# Management of sex partners

Persons with sexual contact with a person with primary, secondary or early latent syphilis within the last 90 days should be presumptively treated even if serologic test is negative.

# Neurosyphilis, Ocular syphilis or Otosyphilis

Consult Infectious Disease for treatment

---

References:

- CDC STD Treatment Guidelines MMWR (2021) 70.4
- Mandell Chapter: Syphilis (Treponema pallidum)
- Sanford keyword: Syphilis
- Up-To-Date article: Syphilis: Screening and diagnostic testing

## Tertiary and Late Latent Syphilis

menus.Name: mastoiditis
menus.Text:
# MASTOIDITIS

## Acute Mastoiditis

Acute mastoiditis most commonly occurs as a suppurative complication of acute otitis media. Diagnosis is supported by CT or MRI imaging and culture of drainage. Antibiotics and drainage of middle ear are sufficient treatment in most cases. Mastoidectomy is necessary if abscess has formed in the mastoid bone. If complication of first episode of acute otitis media, etiologies typically include Streptococcus pneumonia (most common), Streptococcus pyogenes, or Staphylococcus aureus. If secondary to chronic otitis media, etiologies typically include Staphylococcus aureus or Pseudomonas aeruginosa. Patients usually too ill for outpatient therapy. ENT consultation recommended. Obtain cultures of auditory canal or middle ear fluid (preferred).

## Chronic Mastoiditis

Chronic mastoiditis is usually the result of chronic otitis media with perforation of the tympanic membrane. There is often associated formation of a cholesteatoma (keratoma). Diagnosis is supported by CT or MRI imaging and culture of drainage. Long term treatment with topical antimicrobials is first line therapy. Infection is often polymicrobial, including Staphylococcus aureus, Pseudomonas aeruginosa and anaerobes. Treatment should be managed in collaboration with otolaryngology and includes topical antimicrobials, care of external auditory canal, and is some cases mastoidectomy. If possible, withhold therapy until a pathogen is identified by culture of drainage to direct therapy. Specific drug choice dictated by culture results.

References:

- Mandell chapter: Otitis Externa, Otitis Media, and Mastoiditis
- Loh et. al., The Journal of Laryngology & Otology. 2018, 132(2)96-104.
- Sanford keyword: Mastoiditis
- Up-to-Date article: Chronic otitis media, cholesteatoma, and mastoiditis in adults
menus.Therapy:
Preferred:
Piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 gm IV q6h ($$) R
<AND> vancomycin 15 mg/kg IV q 12 hours ($) [R] for 7 days

Alternative:
[Assessment of Beta-lactam Reaction](beta-lactam-allergy-assessment)
Vancomycin 15 mg/kg IV q 12 hours ($) R < AND > cefepime 2 gm IV q12h ($$) R for 7 days

**Step down treatment after initial intravenous antibiotic treatment in patients who can tolerate oral therapy. Base selection on culture results. Adjust for a total duration of 7 days of antimicrobial therapy.**
Amoxicillin/clavulanate 875-125 mg PO q12h for 7 days ($) R
< OR >
Cefuroxime 500mg PO q12h for 7 days ($) R
< OR >
Doxycycline 100 mg PO q12h for 7 days ($) DI

## Chronic Mastoiditis

Preferred:
Ciprofloxacin-Dexamethasone otic 4 drops in affected ear(s) BID for 4 weeks ($) [M]

Alternative:
Neomycin-polymyxin-hydrocortisone ear drops 4 drops in affected ear(s) QID for 4 weeks ($) [M]

menus.Name: periocular-infections
menus.Text:
# PERIOCULAR INFECTIONS

## Eyelid infections

Patients with moderate or severe eyelid infections should be referred to ophthalmology.

## Blepharitis

Wash margins with baby shampoo daily and use warm compresses daily. Antimicrobials have no benefit.

## Hordeolum (stye)

For external disease (involving the gland of Zeis), daily hot pack massage encourages drainage and relieves symptoms. For internal disease (involving Meibomian glands) ophthalmology consult is encouraged, as the infection seldom drains without intervention.

## Lacrimal infections

Refer cases of lacrimal infection to ophthalmology, including infections of the lacrimal gland (dacryoadenitis), lacrimal sac (dacrocystitis), or tear ducts (canaliculitis).

References:

- Carlisle et al., American Family Physician. 2015, 92(2)106-112
- Mandell chapter: Periocular infections
- Up-To-Date article: Blepharitis
- Up-To-Date article: Eyelid lesions

menus.Name: uveitis
menus.Text:
# UVEITIS

Most cases are non-infectious. Most infectious cases are associated with a pathogen causing systemic or central nervous system infection. Diagnosis of uveitis usually must be made presumptively due to the technical difficulty of sampling the uvea. Cases have been associated with fungi, bacteria, viruses, and protozoa like Toxoplasma gondii.

# For treatment of posterior uveitis (retinitis) or acute retinal necrosis (ARN) due to Varicella-zoster virus (VZV) or herpes simplex virus (HSV) or Cytomegalovirus (CMV)

[VZV or HSV retinitis and ARN](retinitis)

[CMV retinitis and ARN](cmv-retinitis)

# Treatment of uveitis involves treating the underlying infection and is usually systemic. Refer to specific pathogen recommendations for treatment of underlying infection. Contact Ophthalmology and/or Infectious Diseases for assistance.

---

References:

- Mandell chapter: Infectious causes of uveitis

menus.Name: chronic-sinusitis
menus.Text:
# CHRONIC SINUSITIS

Diagnosis of chronic sinusitis is based on presence of at least 2 of the 4 cardinal signs/symptoms lasting >/= 12 weeks. In addition, diagnosis requires objective evidence of mucosal inflammation using nasal endoscopy and/or CT imaging. The initial therapy for chronic sinusitis is treatment with intranasal corticosteroids and saline. For patients with severe nasal blockage by polyps, treat with a short course of oral glucocorticoids. Reassess patient after 1 to 3 months of intranasal therapy or after completion of glucocorticoid therapy. If signs/symptoms have not improved, consult surgery, ENT and Infectious Diseases as treatment is complex.

Acute exacerbations of chronic sinusitis can be caused by discontinuing medical therapy, viral infections, allergens, noxious inhalants and bacterial or fungal infections. Bacterial infections should be suspected when the patient has increased signs/symptoms persisting for more than 10 days. Refer to Severe Sinusitis recommendations for choice of antimicrobial therapy in these patients.

Repeated use of the same agent should be avoided to prevent promotion of drug resistant bacteria or increased fungal colonization.

[Severe Sinusitis](severe-sinusitis)

# Cardinal Signs/Symptoms of Chronic Sinusitis

1. Anterior and/or posterior nasal mucopurulent drainage
2. Nasal obstruction/nasal blockage/congestion
3. Facial pain, pressure, and/or fullness
4. Reduction or loss of sense of smell

# Objective Evidence mucosal inflammation

1. Purulent (not clear) mucus or edema in the middle meatus or ethmoid regions
2. Polyps in the nasal cavity or the middle meatus
3. Radiographic imaging demonstrating mucosal thickening or partial or complete opacification of the paranasal sinuses

menus.Text:
# BACTEREMIA ASSOCIATED WITH STAPHYLOCOCCUS AUREUS

# Consult Infectious Diseases in all cases.

Transthoracic echocardiography (TTE) should be performed to rule out infectious endocarditis. Consult Cardiology or Infectious Diseases for more information.

Refer to cardiovascular section for suspected infectious endocarditis.

[Approach to Endocarditis](endocarditis-approach-to)

Follow-up blood cultures should be obtained within 24-48 hours after initiating antimicrobial therapy.

# Duration of therapy:

Treatment duration requires assessing complexity of infection. Uncomplicated bacteremia are those who meet the following criteria:

1. Infectious endocarditis has been excluded via TTE
2. Resolution of fever within 3 days of initiating anti-staphylococci antimicrobial therapy
3. The primary focus of infection has been promptly removed
4. Negative blood cultures within 2-3 days of removing focus of infection and initiating anti-staphylococci antimicrobial therapy
5. No hematogenous spread of infection to secondary foci
6. No presence of implanted devices

Treat for 2 weeks after last negative blood culture set in uncomplicated bacteremia. If there is an easily removable or drainable focus (e.g. infected intravenous catheter, minor abscess, urinary cystitis, or mild to moderate pneumonia), and this focus has been treated, give parenteral antimicrobials for 2 weeks. Complicated bacteremia requires 4-6 weeks of treatment.

---

# BACTEREMIA ASSOCIATED WITH COAGULASE-NEGATIVE STAPHYLOCOCCI (CoNS)

CoNS are normal commensal human skin flora and are not typically pathogenic. However, they are the most common cause of health care associated blood stream infections (30%). Unlike other commonly isolated CoNS, S. lugdunensis can cause severe disease like S. aureus.

Refer to Bacteremia Associated S. lugdunensis recommendations for treatment.
[Bacteremia associated with Staphylococcus lugdunensis](staphylococcus-lugdunensis-bacteremia)

Other commonly isolated CoNS are S. epidermidis, S. haemolyticus, and S. saprophyticus. In a patient without signs or symptoms of infection, a single positive blood culture for these CoNS isolates often represents contamination and not infection. CoNS are more likely to be pathogens in patients with a prosthetic device. Contact Infectious Diseases for more information.

Refer to cardiovascular section for suspected infectious endocarditis.
[Approach to Endocarditis](endocarditis-approach-to)

Treatment is indicated when there are more than 1 blood culture bottle is positive for CoNS. Follow-up blood cultures should be obtained within 24-48 hours after initiating antimicrobial therapy. Identification and treatment of the source of infection, in addition to antimicrobial therapy, is crucial for resolution of infection. This may include removal of catheters and draining of abscesses if present.

---

menus.Name: endocarditis-approach-to
menus.Text:
# APPROACH TO ENDOCARDITIS

Infectious Diseases and Cardiology consults are essential for proved cases and encouraged for suspected cases. See diagnosis page for more information.

[Diagnosis with Duke Criteria](duke-diagnostic-criteria)

Attempt to identify the pathogen before starting antimicrobials. At least three sets of blood cultures should be obtained from different venipuncture sites.

These cultures should be drawn at different times with the first and last culture separated by at least one hour.

For a patient who is not clinically stable, or if the progression of the illness is rapid, draw 3 sets of blood cultures and then initiate empirical antimicrobial therapy and/or surgical intervention.

Ascertain whether any antimicrobials were taken during the previous 2 weeks to help interpret culture results.

Penicillin susceptibility data are used to determine appropriate antimicrobial therapy for streptococcal endocarditis. Because bacteria in cardiac vegetations are not actively dividing, and are protected from host defense mechanisms, bactericidal antimicrobial regimens are necessary to treat bacterial endocarditis. The minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) cut-off levels used to select therapy for endocarditis differ from those used to select therapy for other infectious diseases (see below).

# Penicillin allergy

Beta-lactam antibiotics are more effective than vancomycin for treating susceptible gram-positive pathogens. For patients with penicillin allergy that is known or suspected to be class I (anaphylaxis, angioedema, or hives), penicillin desensitization or therapy with a cephalosporin is usually the best approach.

[Penicillin Desensitization protocol](penicillin-desensitization-protocol)

When gentamicin is used for synergy against gram positive bacteria, serum concentrations should be 3-4 mcg/ml peak and < 1 mcg/ml trough. Once daily gentamicin dosing can be used for streptococcal cases but not for staphylococcal or enterococcal cases.

---

# INFECTIONS INVOLVING CARDIOVASCULAR DEVICES (EXCLUDING VALVES)

Most infections are associated with Staphylococcus aureus and coagulase-negative staphylococci.

Many of these staphylococci are resistant to methicillin, so initial empiric therapy with vancomycin is required.

Consultation with Infectious Diseases is encouraged for patients with severe allergies to vancomycin or for those who have vancomycin-resistant infections.

At least 3 blood cultures should be drawn prior to the initiation of empirical antimicrobial. Modify antimicrobial regimen and narrow coverage based on results of culture and susceptibility tests Infectious Disease and Cardiothoracic surgery consultations are encouraged.

Device removal is necessary for cure in most cases. However, it may be difficult depending on the nature of the device and specific clinical circumstances. Device removal should be discussed with Cardiology, Infectious Disease, or Cardiothoracic surgery consultants.

If the device removal is not possible, add rifampin.

# Duration of therapy

Duration of therapy should be determined in concert with Cardiology, Infectious Disease, or Cardiothoracic surgery consultants.

Obtain blood cultures before starting empirical antimicrobials. Peripheral vein suppurative thrombophlebitis may require surgical intervention in addition to antimicrobial therapy. The usual treatment for jugular vein suppurative thrombophlebitis (Lemierre's syndrome) and vena cava suppurative thrombophlebitis is prolonged antimicrobial therapy, with or without radiological or thrombolytic clot removal. Consult Infectious Diseases and Vascular Surgery for more information. Modify antimicrobial regimen and narrow coverage based on results of culture and susceptibility tests.

# Duration of therapy

A minimum of 4 to 6 weeks of antimicrobial therapy is appropriate and may be abbreviated in peripheral vein infections based on patient specific factors. Antimicrobial therapy should be continued until there is definite clinical response and oral antimicrobial therapy may be used after completion of initial course of intravenous therapy.

menus.Name: approach-to-acute-meningitis
menus.Text:
# APPROACH TO ACUTE MENINGITIS

Meningitis is an inflammation of the meninges and tissues surrounding the brain and spinal cord. It is characterized by an abnormal amount of white blood cells in the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) and symptoms include headache, fever, mental status changes, nuchal rigidity, and nausea.

# Acute Meningitis

The sudden onset of meningeal symptoms within hours to days caused by several infectious etiologies, including bacterial, viral, fungal and protozoa, as well as non-infectious etiologies. Bacterial meningitis is the most common type of meningitis, accounting for up to 90% of cases where a CSF culture was obtained prior to starting antimicrobials. Non-bacterial meningitis is commonly referred to as aseptic meningitis (refer to "Negative CSF culture" below for recommendations).

Patients with acute bacterial meningitis often have severe symptoms and present soon after onset of infection. The relationship between predisposing factors and common bacterial pathogen are listed below.

# Predisposing Factors and Common Bacterial Pathogens

\*Age 2-50 years - [S. pneumoniae](meningitis-with-streptococcus-pneumoniae), [N. meningitidis](meningitis-with-neisseria-meningitidis)

\*Age > 50 years - S. pneumoniae, N. meningitidis, [L. monocytogenes](listeria-monocytogenes-meningitis), aerobic gram-negative bacilli \*Immunocompromised state - S. pneumoniae, N. meningitidis, L. monocytogenes, aerobic gram-negative bacilli (including Pseudomonas aeruginosa)

\*Basilar skull fracture - S. pneumoniae: H. influenzae, group A and beta-hemolytic streptococci \*Head trauma: after neurosurgery - Staphylococcus aureus, coagulase-negative staphylococci (especially Staphylococcus epidermidis), aerobic gram-negative bacilli (including P. aeruginosa)

# Initial Management of Suspected Acute Bacterial Meningitis

Once a diagnosis of acute bacterial meningitis is considered likely, antimicrobials should be initiated as soon as possible. Two blood cultures should be drawn. Lumbar puncture (LP) should be performed in nearly all patients to obtain CSF for establishing diagnosis and determining infectious organism/susceptibility. Computed tomography (CT) should be performed prior to LP in some patients (see list below). If CT must be obtained prior to LP or there is another delay in performing LP, empiric antimicrobials should not be delayed and initiated immediately after obtaining blood cultures only.

Relative LP contraindications (no absolute contraindications exist):
Anticoagulation therapy or bleeding disorder, spinal epidural abscess, raised intracranial pressure.

Computed tomography scan should be performed prior to lumbar puncture in cases with the following:
Immunocompromise, history of CNS disease, new onset seizure, papilledema, abnormal level of consciousness, focal neurologic deficit.

# LP and CSF Analysis

LP opening pressure is often elevated in bacterial meningitis. CSF findings characteristic of bacterial meningitis include CSF glucose <40mg/dL, CSF to serum glucose ratio </=0.4, CSF protein concentration >/=200 mg/dL and CSF WBC >1000 microL.

# Treatment Based on CSF Isolated Organism

When infectious organism is identified, adjust antimicrobials to optimize therapy:
[S. pneumoniae](meningitis-with-streptococcus-pneumoniae)

[N. meningitidis](meningitis-with-neisseria-meningitidis)

[L. monocytogenes](listeria-monocytogenes-meningitis)

[E. Coli, Pseudomonas, or another organism](meningitis-with-e-coli-pseudomonas-or-other-organism)

# Negative CSF Culture

Patients who have a negative CSF culture but have symptoms and CSF findings consistent with bacterial meningitis should be treated based on likely pathogen.

Patients with negative CSF culture, symptoms of acute meningitis but have labs inconsistent with bacterial meningitis should be considered to have aseptic meningitis. Aseptic meningitis is caused by a variety of non-bacterial infectious etiologies and non-infectious etiologies. Consult Infectious Disease for more information.

## Empiric Treatment After Blood Cultures are Drawn, and CSF is Obtained, or if LP Must be Delayed

[Community acquired meningitis](meningitis-without-gram-stain-results)

[Meningitis associated with trauma or nosocomial infection](meningitis-associated-with-trauma-or-nosocomial-infection)

## Empiric Treatment Based on CSF Gram-Stain Results

When gram stain results are available, adjust antimicrobials to optimize therapy:
[Gram-positive diplococci suggesting Streptococcus pneumoniae](gram-positive-diplococci-meningitis)

[Gram-negative diplococci suggesting Neisseria meningitidis](gram-negative-diplococci-meningitis)

[Gram-positive bacilli/coccobacilli suggesting Listeria monocytogenes](meningitis-with-gram-positive-bacilli-coccobacilli)

[Gram negative bacilli](gram-negative-bacilli-meningitis)

menus.Text:
# APPROACH TO BRAIN ABSCESS

Brain abscess is a focal infection of the brain parenchyma. Symptoms often include headache, fever, altered mental status, seizures, and focal neural deficits. Pathogens vary based on primary site of infection and patient's immune status. Bacteria cause most infections in immunocompetent patients whereas a wider array of pathogens, including fungi, cause infection in immunocompromised patients.

Streptococci are the most isolated pathogen, often isolated from mixed infections. Bacteroides are also commonly isolated in mixed cultures. Enteric gram-negative bacilli are typically isolated in patients with otitic foci, bacteremia, or post-neurosurgery. Staphylococcus aureus is commonly isolated in a pure culture and in patients with endocarditis or cranial trauma. Brain abscess caused by Listeria and Nocardia may occur in patients who are immunocompromised.

Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) should be obtained in all patients with suspected brain abscess for diagnosis and determining number of lesions. Prior to beginning antimicrobial therapy, when possible, computed topographic (CT) - guided aspiration or surgery should be performed to obtain abscess material for determination of infectious pathogen.

Solitary brain abscesses usually result from the spread of focal ear, sinus, or dental infection (contiguous source). Cases with multiple abscesses often result from hematogenous spread from infections such as endocarditis, abdominal infection, or lung abscess.

# Consult Neurosurgery, Neurology, and Infectious Disease

## Empiric Treatment After Obtaining Abscess Sample, When Possible

[Brain abscess from contiguous or hematogenous spread of infection](brain-abscess-from-contiguous-or-hematogenous-spread)

[Post-surgical or post-traumatic brain abscess](brain-abscess-post-surgical-or-post-traumatic)

# Treatment Based on Isolated Pathogen

When infectious organism is identified, adjust antimicrobials to optimize therapy:
[Nocardia spp.](brain-abscess-with-nocardia)

[Pseudomonas spp.](brain-abscess-with-pseudomonas)

[Toxoplasma gondii](brain-abscess-with-toxoplasma-gondii)

# BRAIN ABSCESS FROM CONTIGUOUS OR HEMATOGENOUS SPREAD OF INFECTION

Prior to beginning antimicrobial therapy, when possible, computed topographic (CT) - guided aspiration or surgery should be performed to obtain abscess material for determination of infectious pathogen. Adjust antimicrobial regimen to optimize therapy and treatment duration to optimize therapy based on pathogen once isolated.

Broad spectrum empiric antimicrobials are indicated initially for brain abscess. Staphylococcus aureus is a common pathogen. Beta-lactam antibiotics are more effective than vancomycin for susceptible Staphylococci. If Staphylococcus is isolated, once methicillin- resistance is ruled out, switch to an anti-staphylococcal beta-lactam antibiotic. Pseudomonas is a potential pathogen in post-surgical patients, and those who are known to be colonized with Pseudomonas.

# Consult Neurosurgery, Neurology, and Infectious Disease

# Duration of Therapy

Duration is typically 6-8 weeks, with the shorter duration for those with cerebritis only or drained abscess, longer for undrained or encapsulated abscesses, multiple or loculated abscesses, abscess in an immunocompromised host.

# BRAIN ABSCESS WITH NOCARDIA SPP.

Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) should be obtained in all patients with suspected brain abscess for diagnosis and determining number of lesions. Prior to beginning antimicrobial therapy, when possible, computed topographic (CT) - guided aspiration or surgery should be performed to obtain abscess material for determination of infectious pathogen.

Nocardia brain abscesses typically occur in immunocompromised patients and is often concomitant with disseminated or pulmonary infection. May occur with meningitis and/or ventriculitis.

# Consult Neurosurgery, Neurology, and Infectious Disease

# Duration of Therapy

Treat with IV therapy for total duration of 3-6 weeks in immunocompetent and 6 weeks in immunocompromised patients. Switch to oral antimicrobials after completing IV therapy and treat for an additional 3 months or more (longer for meningitis, immunocompromise or extensive disease).

---

- Brouwer et al. N Engl J Med, 2014, 371(5)447-56
- Mandell chapter: Brain Abscess
- Sanford keyword: Brain Abscess
- Up-to-Date article: Treatment of Nocardiosis

# CRANIAL EPIDURAL ABSCESS

Treatment involves source control by drainage procedure and antimicrobial therapy.

Beta-lactam antibiotics are more effective than vancomycin against susceptible Staphylococci. If Staphylococcus is isolated, once methicillin-resistance is ruled out, switch to an anti-staphylococcal beta-lactam antibiotic. Pseudomonas is a potential pathogen in post-surgical patients or patients with known Pseudomonas colonization.

# Consult Neurosurgery, Neurology, and Infectious Disease

# Duration of Therapy

Treat for 6 weeks after surgical drainage. In patients with associated osteomyelitis, patients in whom surgical drainage did not occur, and patients in whom the response to therapy has been slow, treat for 6 to 8 weeks.

---

# Osteomyelitis Evaluation:

- Consider osteomyelitis in any infected, deep, or large foot ulcer, particularly those that are chronic and over bony prominences.
- Plain films along with the probe-to-bone test are reasonable first steps in evaluating for osteomyelitis.
- Patients where the diagnosis remains unclear should undergo MRI.
- Patients with findings suggesitve of osteomyelitis should undergo debridement with bone culture BEFORE antibiotics are started, if possible
- Consult surgery (orthopedics or vascular) for potential surgical intervention. (Vascular preferred for known PVD)
- Consult Infectious Diseases for evaluation and management of long-term antibiotics.

menus.Name: decolonization-of-staphylococcus-aureus
menus.Text:
# STAPHYLOCOCCUS AUREUS DECOLONIZATION

From 10% to 40% of adults are colonized with Staphylococcus aureus, and the anterior nares is the most common site of colonization. A majority of people never have disease with S. aureus, but a tiny fraction of people develop clinical infections with the S. aureus that has colonized their skin or anterior nares. Steps to decolonize the skin and anterior nares can transiently diminish or eradicate S. aureus colonization and can prevent post-operative wound infection in certain high-risk circumstances. For people who have other forms of recurrent S. aureus disease, not associated with an operation, results with decolonization have been disappointing, and decolonization is not routinely recommended. Colonization typically reappears in most patients within a few days or weeks after decolonization has been attempted. Clinicians occasionally wish to attempt decolonization for patients with frequent, troublesome recurrences.

The procedure here is one of several that have been studied, but none have been particularly effective over the long run.

Consultation with Infectious Diseases is recommended.

# Inpatient Decolonization Order Set:

Mupirocin 2% ointment topically q12h M <AND> chlorhexidine 4% liquid
topically q24h nursing text order [M] for 5 days

# Outpatient Decolonization Order Set:

Order if patient is being discharged within 5 days
Mupirocin 2% ointment topically BID M <AND> chlorhexidine 4% liquid
topically qday [M] for 5 days

# Instructions

* Patient must wear clean clothes after bathing to prevent recontamination
* Bedding and linens must be changed/cleaned daily until the end of the decolonization protocol.

---

# References:

- Bradley S Clin Infect Dis 2007, 44: 186
- Lonneke G NEJM 2010, 362: 9
- Schweizer et al, JAMA 2015, 313.212:162-2171
- Up-To-Date article: Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) in adults: Prevention and control

# APPROACH TO URINARY TRACT INFECTION (UTI)

## IDSA 2025 complicated and uncomplicated UTI definition updates:

Uncomplicated UTI is an infection confined to the bladder in afebrile women or men without urinary catheter.

[Uncomplicated urinary tract infection](uncomp-uti)

Complicated UTI is an infection beyond the bladder and accompanied by symptoms including fever/other signs of systemic illness. Complicated UTI includes pyelonephritis, febrile or bacteremic UTI, catheter-associated (CAUTI).

[Complicated UTI without catheter](complicated-uti-no-catheter)
[Complicated UTI catheter associated](complicated-uti-catheter-associated)
[Acute prostatitis](acute-bact-prostatitis)

For patients presenting with septic shock from a suspected urinary tract infection: Refer to Inpatient Antimicrobial CDSS Asymptomatic bacteriuria occurs in patients who have bacteria in the urine but do not have symptoms of a urinary tract infection.

[Asymptomatic bacteriuria](asymp-bacteriuria)

Patients at risk of sexually transmitted infections should be assessed for treatment:

[Sexually Transmitted Infections and HIV Exposure](sexually-transmitted-infection)

Candida urinary tract infections are discussed elsewhere:

[Candida urinary tract infections](candida-uti)

---

Treat for 5 days with fluoroquinolones or 7 days with non-fluoroquinolone antibiotics.

menus.Text:
# COMPLICATED UTI (NO CATHETER)

# Complicated UTI is an infection beyond the bladder accompanied by symptoms including fever/other signs of systemic illness, flank pain, and costovertebral tenderness. This includes pyelonephritis and febrile or bacteremic UTI.

NOT signs or symptoms: abnormal urinalysis alone, pyuria, falls, change in urine odor or color, delirium (acute mental status change, confusion) without systemic signs of infection. These may occur in patients with a UTI but alone are inadequate for diagnosis and empiric treatment.

---

For patients without signs or symptoms of UTI:
[Asymptomatic bacteriuria](asymp-bacteriuria)

For patients presenting with septic shock from a suspected urinary tract infection: Refer to Inpatient Antimicrobial CDSS

---

# Duration

Treat for 5 days with fluoroquinolones or 7 days with non-fluoroquinolone organisms, presence of obstruction, underlying renal disease, immunosuppression, and neurologic or structural abnormality in some cases. Often therapy can be completed with an oral agent pending clinical stability and susceptibility testing.

---

# Staphylococcus aureus

S. aureus is an uncommon urinary tract pathogen and presence in the urine may be due to hematogenous seeding from another site. Blood cultures are indicated to rule out bacteremia in patients who have S. aureus isolated from the urine.

Consult Infectious Diseases for more information.

menus.Text:
# Concurrent Male Partner Treatment for Recurrent, Symptomatic Bacterial Vaginosis

In monogamous relationships where the female partner has confirmed symptomatic, recurrent bacterial vaginosis (defined as three or more episodes within a 12-month period), concurrent treatment of the male partner is recommended to to reduce the risk of recurrence. Concurrent treatment should be considered when the male partner is willing to complete a full 7-day treatment course.

Couples should agree to sexual abstinence or consistent condom use until both partners have completed therapy. Additionally, continued condom use for at least three months following treatment is advised to further minimize the risk of reinfection.

menus.Name: more-about-nosocomial-pneumonia
menus.Text:
# MORE ABOUT NOSOCOMIAL PNEUMONIA

# Types of nosocomial pneumonia

Hospital acquired pneumonia (HAP): Development of pneumonia 48 hours or more after hospital admission.

Ventilator-associated pneumonia (VAP): Pneumonia occurring 48 hours or more after endotracheal intubation.

# Criteria for diagnosis of pneumonia

1.  Presence of new or progressive infiltrate <AND>
2.  At least two of the following:

Fever greater than 38 C (100.4 F)

Leukocytosis or leukopenia

Purulent bronchial secretions

# HAP OR VAP suspected:

Gram stain and culture of lower respiratory tract secretions and blood cultures are important for guiding therapy.

[Re-evaluate Nosocomial pneumonia at 72 hours](nosocomial-pneumonia-re-evaluation-at-72-hours)

# Duration of therapy

Treatment for 7 days is generally sufficient if the initial empiric therapy covered the pathogen and the patient is clinically responding. Narrow therapy to treat specific pathogen(s) based on results of culture and susceptibility tests.

Longer duration of therapy is recommended for more resistant organisms (e.g.

Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Acinetobacter baumanni, and Legionella pneumophila).

---

menus.Text:
# SUBOPTIMAL VANCOMYCIN RESPONSE AT 72 HOURS

If the patient has not improved, consider the following:

1. The patient has pneumonia with a pathogen resistant to empirical antimicrobials (e.g., resistant bacteria, fungi, mycobacteria)
2. The patient does not have bacterial pneumonia.  Consider alternative diagnoses including pulmonary edema, atelectasis, pulmonary embolus, ARDS, pulmonary hemorrhage, underlying disease, and neoplasm.
3. The patient has infectious disease outside the lungs.
4. The patient has one or more complications of pneumonia (e.g., empyema, lung abscess, mediastinitis, or pericarditis)
5. The patient has an adverse drug event

Infectious Disease or Pulmonary consultation is strongly encouraged for patients who do not respond to initial therapy.

menus.Text:
# Functional or Anatomical Asplenia Vaccine & Antibiotic Prophylaxis Guideline

Following a splenectomy there is considerably increased risk of developing septicemia from invasive encapsulated organisms, namely Streptococcus pneumonia, Haemophilus inluenza type b and meningococcus. Key measures to prevent such infections include education, vaccination, prophylactic antimicrobial therapy in selected patients, and early empirical therapy for febrile epsisodes. It is critically important to educate patients regarding the lifelong risk of postsplenectomy sepsis, the importance of vaccinations, and the need for urgent action in response to a febrile episode.

# Management of an Episode of Fever in an Asplenic Patient

*See Inpatient CDSS*

# Initiation of vaccine regimen:

Routine vaccines should be up to date.

See CDSS Immunization section to order, if needed.

click here Vaccinations for Adults without a Spleen

Ideally splenectomy vaccinations should be given 10 to 12 weeks before elective splenectomy.  Where this is not possible they can be given up to two weeks before or at least two weeks post-splenectomy.

[click here Place order for specific vaccines for asplenia](splenectomy-chart)

# Use of Antibiotic Prophylaxis for Asplenia:

Use of antibiotic prophylaxis, in addition to vaccination, further reduces the risk of infection and poor outcomes.

# [Daily Antibiotic Prophylaxis](splenectomy-daily-antibiotic): (in addition to emergency supply)

[Daily Antibiotic Prophylaxis](splenectomy-daily-antibiotic)

# Emergency Supply Empiric Abx for Fever or Other Signs of Systemic Infection:

[Self-medicate Empiric Antibiotics](splenectomy-empiric)

menus.Name: fever-in-asplenic-patient
menus.Text:
# FEVER IN AN ASPLENIC PATIENT

Patients with impaired splenic function are at risk for severe and overwhelming infection with encapsulated bacteria. Streptococcus pneumoniae is the most common cause of fulminant sepsis in patients with impaired splenic function, followed by Haemophilus influenzae and Neisseria meningitidis. Infection with Capnocytophaga species is possible in asplenic patients with anteceding scratches and animal bites, especially dog bites. Babesiosis is also more likely in asplenic patients exposed to tick bites.

If fever develops in an asplenic patient, immediate administration of an antimicrobial agent is indicated, because fever can be the initial manifestation of a fulminant infection and prompt administration of an antimicrobial agent may prevent the development of clinical sepsis.

Administration of antibiotics should not be delayed for performing diagnostic studies, including lumbar puncture.

# Streptococcus pneumoniae meningitis suspected

[Bacterial meningitis with S. pneumoniae](meningitis-with-streptococcus-pneumoniae)

# Anteceding animal bite or scratch

Consult Infectious Diseases
For tick bites consider treatment for Babesia species
[Babesia Species](babesia-infections-general)

Other animal bites or scratches
Piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 gm IV q6h ($$) R

# Daily Antibiotic Prophylaxis for Asplenia

The need for daily antibiotic prophylaxis and its duration is typically determined individually based on patient age, immune status, history of infection, potential for adverse drug reactions and other factors.

# Consider Prophylaxis:

1) Approximately 1 year prophylaxis for all patients following splenectomy.
2) Lifelong prophylaxis for patients with history of sepsis or other severe infections caused by encapsulated organisms.
3) Prophylaxis for as long as the patient is immunocompromised or for life for patients with concurrent immunocompromising conditions (e.g. hematologic malignancy, hypogammaglobulinemia, solid-organ transplant, advanced liver disease, or HIV infection).

# Daily antibiotic prophylaxis is in addition to the emergency supply.

# Recommended:

Amoxicillin 500MG PO bid for daily prophylaxis for asplenic patient ($) R

< OR >
Cephalexin 250MG PO bid for daily propylaxis for asplenic patient ($) R

menus.Name: rosacea
menus.Text:
# ROSACEA

Rosacea is an inflammatory skin condition resulting in erythema and telangiectasia of nose, cheeks, eyelids, and forehead. It typically occurs in mid-life and the etiology is unknown. Erythematous rosacea is the early stage of the disease and usually manifests with flushing reactions and persistently erythematous skin. Late-stage disease is known as papulopustular rosace.

Symptoms include papular, pustular, cysts and nodules. Severe disease results in tissue atrophy and rhinophyma (bulbus nose).

The goal of treatment is control of symptoms, not cure. General treatment measures include avoiding triggers (e.g. spicy food, alcohol), skin care (e.g. moisturizing, gentle cleansing, avoiding topical irritants) and using sun screen. Medical treatment includes topical agents as first line therapy and oral treatment for refractory disease.

---

**FOR DERMATOLOGY USE ONLY, REQUIRES DERMATOLOGY CONSULT PRIOR TO TREATMENT**
[Recalcitrant Rosacea](recalcitrant-acne-and-rosacea)

---

menus.Name: post-operative-wound-infection
menus.Text:
POST-OPERATIVE WOUND INFECTION
Surgical site infections are categorized by the extent of tissues involved.

Superficial incisional infections involve only the subcutaneous space and occur within 30 days of operation.  Deep incisional infections involve deep layers of soft tissue, such as fascia and muscle, and occur within 30 days of operation, or within 1 year of operation if prosthetic material was inserted.  Organ/space infections involve anatomical areas other than the incisional wound that were opened or manipulated during operation.  Organ/space infections should be treated as infections of the relevant area of the anatomy.  Return to the main page and choose the pertinent organ system for advice on management of these infections.

Post-operative wound infections usually occur between 2 and 30 days after the operation.  Infections within 48 hours of the surgery are uncommon, but are serious when they do occur.  Symptoms commonly begin to appear no sooner than 5 days after the operation and may take up to 2 weeks to appear.

[Patients with signs of infection WITHIN 48 HOURS of procedure](surg-w-i-48hrs-procedure)

[Patients with signs of infection 48 HOURS OR MORE after procedure](surg-48hrs-after-proc)

1.)  Isolation of Group A Streptococcus from a normally sterile site (eg, blood cerebrospinal, pleural, or peritoneal fluid, tissue biopsy, or surgical wound)

< AND >
2.)  Hypotension (systolic blood pressure 90 mm Hg in adults
< AND >

# Renal impairment

(creatinine in adults, 2 mg/dL, in children, two-times upper limit of normal for age, in patients with pre-existing renal disease two-fold elevation over baseline)

# Coagulopathy

(eg, thrombocytopenia, disseminated intravascular coagulation)

# Liver involvement

(eg, two-times upper limit of normal for age of transaminases or bilirubin, in patients with pre-existing liver disease two-fold elevation over baseline)

# Adult respiratory distress syndrome

# Erythematous macular rash

may desquamate
Soft tissue necrosis (eg, necrotizing fasciitis, myositis, or gangrene)

menus.Name: staph-toxic-shock-syndrome
menus.Text:
CDC CRITERIA FOR DIAGNOSIS OF STAPHYLOCOCCAL TOXIC SHOCK SYNDROME These criteria were developed for epidemiological purposes.  Treat cases when fewer criteria are met if staphylococcal TSS seems likely.

Definite:  All 6 of the following criteria are met.

Probable:  Five of the 6 criteria are met.

# Fever

T >38.9 degree Celsius (102.0 degree Fahrenheit)

# Hypotension

Systolic blood pressure 90 mmHg, orthostatic drop in diastolic 15 mmHg, orthostatic syncope or dizziness

# Rash

Diffuse macular erythroderma

# Desquamation

Occurs 1 to 2 weeks after onset of illness and usually involving palms and soles

# Multisystem involvement (3 or more of the following organ systems)

# GI

Vomiting or diarrhea at onset of illness

# Muscular

Severe myalgia or CPK elevation >2 times the normal upper limit

# Mucous membranes

Vaginal, oropharyngeal, or conjunctival hyperemia

# Renal

BUN or serum creatinine >2 times the normal upper limit, or pyuria (>5 WBC/hpf)

# Hepatic

Bilirubin or transaminases >2 times the normal upper limit

# Hematologic

Platelets <100,000/microLiter

# Central nervous system

Disorientation or alterations in consciousness without focal neurologic signs in the absence of fever and hypotension

# Negative results on the following tests, if obtained

Blood, throat, or cerebrospinal fluid cultures for another pathogen (blood cultures may be positive for S. aureus).

Serologic tests for Rocky Mountain spotted fever, leptospirosis, or measles
[References](references)

MMWR 1990, 39(RR-13):1
DeVries AS PLoS One 2011, 6(8):e22997

menus.Name: cmv-main-page
menus.Text:
# CYTOMEGALOVIRUS (CMV)

---

# Immunocompetent patient

Infection is rare and usually associated with minimal or no symptoms. Mononucleosis can be associated with CMV, but is more commonly associated with Epstein Barr virus. Antiviral treatment is not usually necessary as most patients recover without intervention.

---

# Immunocompromised patient

Patients in whom the risk for CMV disease is increased include solid organ and bone marrow transplant recipients, persons receiving prolonged immunosuppressive chemotherapy, and persons with advanced HIV disease indicated by a CD4 count of less than 50 cells/microliter.

## Antiviral toxicity information

The major toxicities of both ganciclovir and valganciclovir are neutropenia. Nephrotoxicity is the major toxicity associated with foscarnet, which may be reduced by concomitant saline administration (generally 0.5-1L).

# CMV treatment recommendations

# INFECTIOUS DIARRHEA / GASTROENTERITIS

Most episodes of acute diarrhea are self-limited. In most mild to moderate cases, antimicrobial therapy does not provide benefit.

# Bloody diarrhea

Bloody diarrhea can represent hemorrhagic colitis or dysentery. Antimicrobial therapy and antimotility agents are not recommended in most patients with bloody diarrhea due to an increased risk of hemolytic uremic syndrome when using these agents.

## Primary treatment

Hydration and electrolyte replacement

menus.Text:
# HELICOBACTER PYLORI INFECTION

H. pylori infection is associated with peptic ulcers, gastritis, gastric adenocarcinoma, and gastric lymphoma. Antimicrobials should be given to patients with confirmed H. pylori infection. Antisecretory therapy should be given concurrently.

Test of cure should be completed at least 4 weeks after completion of therapy (recommended within 4-8 weeks after completion). Any PPI therapy must be held for 2 weeks prior to testing.

Lab H. Pylori, stool

Note: American College of Gastroenterology (ACG) advises adult household members of individuals who have a positive non-serological test for H. pylori to seek testing trough their provider.

References:

- Chey et al. ACG Clinical Guideline: Treatment of Helicobacter pylori infection. Am J Gastroenterol, 2024, 119(9):1730-1753.
- VA PBM Clinical Recommendations November 2024. Use of newer combination products in the treatment of H. pylori infections.
- Mandell chapter: Helicobacter pylori and Other Gastric Helicobacter Species
- Sanford Guide article: Gastric/Duodenal Ulcer, Helicobacter pylori
- Up-to-Date article: Treatment regimens for Helicobacter pylori
menus.Therapy:
## First line treatment:

Bismuth subsalicylate 524 mg PO q6h <AND> Tetracycline 500 mg q6h DI

<AND> metronidazole 500mg PO q6h [DI] <AND> omeprazole 20mg po q12h.

Take all for 14 days.

Non-VA order for above

## Alternative treatments:

Alternatives may have lower efficacy and higher resistances rates. Test of cure extremely important.

**_Consider referring patients who cannot take first line therapy to GI pharmacist for treatment management and follow-up testing._**
Gastroenterology (OP) Consult - Pharmacists

## Rifabutin triple (Talicia):

Note: place medication order and PADR using order below
Amoxicillin/Omeprazole/Rifabutin (250/10/12.5MG) 4 caps po tid x14days DI,H

Non-VA order for above

< OR >

Note: place medication order and PADR using order below

per package instructions
NonVA order for above

< OR >

## Clarithromycin Quadruple:

Resistance to clarithromycin is increasing. Do not use for patients with prior exposure to macrolides. Consider susceptibility testing prior to use.

Clarithromycin 500 mg PO q12h R,DI <AND> Amoxicillin 1000 mg PO q12h R

<AND> metronidazole 500 mg PO q12h [DI] <AND> omeprazole 20 mg PO q12h.

Take all for 14 days.

menus.Name: idp-ciprofloxacin-po
menus.Text:
---

# Ciprofloxacin PO

---

# Usual dose:

250-500 mg q12h

# Dose adjustments for renal or hepatic insufficiency:

# Creatinine clearance (ml/min) Dose adjustment

< 30250 mg q12h

Hemodialysis  250-500 mg q24h

# Drug Interactions:

Hypoglycemia that can lead to coma especially in diabetics taking oral hypoglycemic medicine or insulin.

Calcium, dairy products, iron, zinc, magnesium, aluminum  inhibit the absorption of oral ciprofloxacin.  Give ciprofloxacin 2 hours before or 6 hours after these drugs.

Increases effects of caffeine and theophylline by inhibiting  metabolism.

Monitor the patient for signs of agitation or anxiety.

Increases the effect of warfarin.  Monitor international normalized ratio (INR) ratio (INR) frequently in patients taking warfarin.

# Adverse Drug Reactions:

# FDA Drug Safety Communication

The U.S. Food and Drug Administration advised that the serious side effects associated with fluoroquinolone antibacterial drugs generally outweigh the benefits for patients with acute sinusitis, acute bronchitis, and uncomplicated urinary tract infections who have other treatment options. For patients with these conditions, fluoroquinolones should be reserved for those who do not have alternative treatment options.

An FDA safety review has shown that fluoroquinolones when used systemically are associated with disabling and potentially permanent serious side effects that can occur together. These side effects can involve the tendons, muscles, joints, nerves, and central nervous system.

FDA identified cases of hypoglycemic coma, resulting in death in some instances. Most pateints had risk factors for hypoglycemia such as older age, diabetes, renal insufficiency, and concomitant use of hypoglycemic drugs, especally sulfonylureas.  FDA also identified reports of additional mental health side effects, and requires that all fluoroquinolones include six psychiatric adverse reactions (disturbance in attention, memory impairment, delirium, nervousness, agitation and disorientation).

# Other adverse reactions:

Nausea/vomiting, diarrhea, dizziness, confusion, CNS stimulation, rare seizures, rare QT interval prolongation, and tendinitis/tendon rupture. Six psychiatric adverse reactions including disturbance in attention, memory impairment, delirium, nervousness, agitation and disorientation.

Hypoglycemia that can lead to coma, occuring more frequently in the elderly and those with diabetes.

# Pregnancy Risk Factor Category: C

menus.Name: sa-decolonization
menus.Text:
# STAPHYLOCOCCUS AUREUS DECOLONIZATION

From 10% to 40% of adults are colonized with Staphylococcus aureus, and the anterior nares is the most common site of colonization. A majority of people never have disease with S. aureus, but a tiny fraction of people develop clinical infections with the S. aureus that has colonized their skin or anterior nares. Steps to decolonize the skin and anterior nares can transiently diminish or eradicate S. aureus colonization and can prevent post-operative wound infection in certain high-risk circumstances. For people who have other forms of recurrent S. aureus disease, not associated with an operation, results with decolonization have been disappointing, and decolonization is not routinely recommended. Colonization typically reappears in most patients within a few days or weeks after decolonization has been attempted. Clinicians occasionally wish to attempt decolonization for patients with frequent, troublesome recurrences.

The procedure here is one of several that have been studied, but none have been particularly effective over the long run.

Consultation with Infectious Diseases is recommended.

# Decolonization Order Set:

Mupirocin 2% ointment topically BID M <AND> chlorhexidine 4% liquid
topically qday [M] for 5 days
Non-VA order for above

# Instructions

* Patient must wear clean clothes after bathing to prevent recontamination
* Bedding and linens must be changed/cleaned daily until the end of the decolonization protocol.

---

# References:

- Bradley S Clin Infect Dis 2007, 44: 186
- Lonneke G NEJM 2010, 362: 9
- Schweizer et al, JAMA 2015, 313.212:162-2171
- Up-To-Date article: Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) in adults: Prevention and control

menus.Term1: Cv surgery (open heart) mvahcs postoperative prophylaxis recommendations
menus.Text:
# CV SURGERY (OPEN HEART) MVAHCS POSTOPERATIVE PROPHYLAXIS RECOMMENDATIONS

Place post-op IV antimicrobial prophylaxis orders after admission to ward.

Duration of antimicrobial prophylaxis should not exceed 24 hours. Durations longer than 24 hours have not been shown effective in preventing cardiothoracic surgical site infections. There is no benefit to continuing antimicrobial prophylaxis until all indwelling drains and intravascular catheters are removed.

For CIED surgery postoperative antimicrobial prophylaxis click link below:

[CIED Surgery Postoperative Prophylaxis](surg-vascular-surg-postop)

# CV Surgery (including CAB and TAVR) Postoperative Prophylaxis

Cefuroxime 1.5 gm IV q8h x 1 dose post-op ($$) R <AND> vancomycin 15 mg/kg

(pharmacy to dose) IV q12h x 1 dose post-op ($) [R]

References:

- Bratzler DW et al, Clinical Practice Guidelines for Antimicrobial Prophylaxis in
- Surgery, Am J Health-Syst Pharm (2013) 70:195-283
menus.Therapy:
Alternative for patient with cephalosporin allergy
Levofloxacin has a duration of action of 24 hours. If patient received a pre-op dose of levofloxacin, a post-op dose is not required.

Vancomycin 15 mg/kg (pharmacy to dose) IV q12h x 1 dose post-op ($) R

menus.Name: surg-vascular-surg-postop
menus.Text:
# Vascular surgery postop antimicrobial prophylaxis:

Prophylactic antibiotics should be discontinued within 24 hours.

Antimicrobial prophylaxis is not recommended for some procedures, including brachiocephalic procedures (e.g., carotid endarterectomy, brachial artery repair) without implantation of prosthetic material.

Antimicrobial prophylaxis is recommended in vascular procedures that involve implantation of prosthetic material and procedures for which there is greater risk of infection, such as aneurysm repair, thromboendarterectomy and vein bypass. Longer duration of antimicrobial prophylaxis therapy is warranted for graft placement.

# Prophylaxis for vascular procedures OTHER THAN graft placement*

**No postop antimicrobial doses recommended for procedures that do not involve graft placement.**

[References](references)

Bratzler DW, et al.  Clinical practice guidelines for antimicrobial prophylaxis in surgery, Am J Health-Syst Pharm. 2013 vol 70 pages 195-283 Antimicrobial Prophylaxis for Surgery, Treatment Guidelines from The Medical Letter 2012 vol 10 pages 73-77

# NATIVE VALVE ENDOCARDITIS WITH STAPHYLOCOCCI

Endocarditis with Staphylococcus aureus and coagulase-negative staphylococci are treated similarly.

Retrospective studies show that patients with native valve staphylococcal endocarditis treated with valve replacement and antimicrobials have a lower mortality rate than those treated with antimicrobials alone. Consult cardiothoracic surgery for all patients with staphylococcal endocarditis.

Most patients need 6 weeks of antimicrobial treatment. For vancomycin-resistant strains Infectious Disease consultation is recommended.

menus.Text:
# APPROACH TO INTRAVASCULAR CATHETER-ASSOCIATED INFECTION

The likelihood of colonization of an intravenous catheter increases with time, increasing noticeably after 3 days. Patients whose catheters become colonized may or may not develop local or systemic signs or symptoms. All types of catheters are associated with risk of local and catheter-associated bacteremia.

Since central catheters are usually used for more days than peripheral catheters, central catheters have a greater risk of catheter-associated bacteremia.

When catheter-related bacteremia is suspected, draw blood cultures from both the catheter and a peripheral vein. Growth rate between the two cultures may be used to determine if the source of bacteremia is likely catheter-associated. If the catheter obtained culture's time to positivity is 2 hours or more before the peripheral vein obtained culture's time to positivity, this suggests catheter-associated infection. Sample any exudate at the catheter site for gram stain and culture.

[Suppurative thrombophlebitis](suppurative-thrombophlebitis) presents with inflammation in and around a vein.

There may be local thrombosis and/or bacteremia. Cases may be life-threatening and can require surgical drainage.

[Suppurative thrombophlebitis](suppurative-thrombophlebitis)

For patients with catheter-associated bacteremia with virulent pathogens like Staphylococcus aureus, gram-negative bacilli, or candida, catheter removal is almost always necessary. For mild or moderate cases with less virulent organisms like coagulase-negative staphylococci, antimicrobial therapy is successful without catheter removal about half of the time. The decision about whether to remove the catheter depends on severity of illness, the need for the catheter, and how difficult catheter replacement would be.

# Antimicrobial lock therapy

For cases in which an infected catheter is not removed, the success rate is improved when the infected catheter is filled with an antimicrobial solution during periods when the catheter is not used. Consult Infectious Diseases or Pharmacy for information.

In Staphylococcus aureus cases, document that bacteremia has cleared during antimicrobial therapy. Infectious Disease consultation is required for all cases of S. aureus bacteremia.

For a patient whose blood cultures remain positive for more than 3 days or with a catheter tunnel abscess or who has a prosthetic device, contact Infectious diseases.

References

- Gaur et al., Clinical infectious diseases 2003, 37.4
- Mandell chapter: Infections Caused by Percutaneous Intravascular Devices
- Mandell chapter Sepsis, Severe Sepsis and Septic Shock
- Mermel et al., Clinical Infectious Diseases 49 (2009)
- Up-to-Date article: Prevention of Intravascular Catheter Associated Infection

menus.Term1: Early treatment of influenza as an alternative to chemoprophylaxis
menus.Text:
# EARLY TREATMENT OF INFLUENZA AS AN ALTERNATIVE TO CHEMOPROPHYLAXIS

In most cases, if a person is suspected of having been exposed to influenza, early treatment, should signs or symptoms develop, is preferred rather than chemoprophylaxis.

The provider should explain the early signs and symptoms of influenza to the patient and advise the patient to immediately contact a health care provider for evaluation and possible early treatment if these symptoms or signs develop.

Influenza-like symptoms or signs include fever, cough, sore throat, runny or stuffy nose, body aches, headache, chills, fatigue, vomiting, and diarrhea.

Influenza can present without fever.

Health care providers should use clinical judgment regarding situations where early recognition of illness and treatment might be an appropriate alternative to chemoprophylaxis.

# Early treatment alternative or chemoprophylaxis may be considered:

\*Persons who are part of a high-risk group and are household or close contacts of someone with influenza-like illness Chemoprophylaxis duration: 7 days after last known exposure

# Chemoprophylaxis recommended:

\*For control of outbreaks in institutional settings (long-term care facilities and hospitals)

Chemoprophylaxis duration: minimum of 2 weeks and continuing up to 1 week after the last known case is identified.

Note: Antiviral chemoprophylaxis is recommended for all residents, including those who have received influenza vaccination.

# Chemoprophylaxis considered:

\*Atypical situations (such as case clusters). Contact the state health department for consultation.

---

References:

- Centers for Disease Control (CDC) (Accessed 9/8/23) https://www.cdc.gov/flu/hcp/antivirals/summary-clinicians.html
- UpToDate Seasonal influenza in adults: Role of antiviral prophylaxis for prevention

menus.Text:
PATIENTS WITH SIGNS OF INFECTION WITHIN 48 HOURS OF PROCEDURE Fever within 48 hours of procedure is usually due to anesthesia or other non-infectious factors but Clostridium species and Streptococcus pyogenes can cause early infections.  Examine the wound of any patient with systemic signs of infection, like fever, within 48 hours of surgery.  If there are signs of infection consider opening the wound.  Obtain a STAT Gram stain and culture of any drainage. If the Gram stain shows evidence of streptococci or clostridia refer to the section on necrotizing infections.  If signs of wound infection are absent seek an alternative source of the fever.

[Necrotizing infections](necrotizing-infections)

[References](references)

menus.Name: surg-48hrs-after-proc
menus.Text:
PATIENTS WITH SIGNS OF INFECTION MORE THAN 48 HOURS AFTER PROCEDURE Most post-operative infections appear at least 4 days after the operation.  If the wound appears normal to examination surgical site infection is unlikely.

Seek other source of fever.  Consider opening wounds that show induration or erythema.  Obtain material for gram stain and culture whenever possible.

Determine whether the patient has signs of invasive or systemic infection like erythema (diameter greater than 5 centimeters), temperature greater than 38.5 degrees Celsius (101.3 degrees Fahrenheit) or heart rate higher than 100 beats per minute.

If there are no signs of invasive or systemic infection systemic antimicrobials are unnecessary.  Dressing changes alone are indicated.

# For wounds that require complicated care

Wound care (ET) nurse consult

If there are signs of invasive or systemic infection obtain blood cultures and wound Gram stain and cultures.  Whenever possible select antimicrobial therapy based on the Gram stain.  When the Gram stain cannot provide guidance give empirical therapy as indicated:

[References](references)

Stevens DL Clin Infect Dis 2014, 59: 147

menus.Text:
# CLOSTRIDIOIDES DIFFICILE INFECTION (CDI)

# Initial CDI diagnosis (all are required)

(1) Unexplained diarrhea (e.g., no laxative or increase in tube feed)
(2) New onset diarrhea (e.g., 3 or more unformed stools in 24 hours)
(3) Laboratory confirmation of CDI

[Information on C. difficile lab testing](c-difficile-2-step-testing)

The Infectious Disease service is available to discuss CDI testing and results.

# Recurrence

Typically defined as symptomatic, laboratory confirmed CDI within 12 weeks after a prior episode. Recurrence rates are up to 25%. Recurrence is usually due to failure of normal colonic flora to re-establish itself, rather than antimicrobial treatment failure.

# Fulminant CDI

Hypotension, shock, ileus, megacolon: General Surgery consult is essential for ileus or megacolon.

# Treatment

[Initial Episode](ini-epi-assoc-colitis)

[First Recurrence](first-recurrence-assoc)

[Second Recurrence](second-recur-assoc-colitis)

# Fulminant CDI: Refer to Inpatient Antimicrobial CDSS

# Third Recurrence: Consult Gastroenterology and/or Infectious Disease

# VIRAL GASTROENTERITIS

Infectious diarrhea caused by viral pathogens such as Adenovirus, Astrovirus, Norovirus, Rotavirus, and Sapovirus is usually self-limited. Treatment includes supportive measures such as oral rehydration and unrestricted nutrition.

Antiviral therapy is not recommended and for most viruses is unavailable.

Antimotility agents may be used for one or two days in patients with mild to moderate volume depletion. Antiemetic agents may be used for one or two days in patients with vomiting.

---
