# ABOUT THE ANTIMICROBIAL COMPUTERIZED DECISION SUPPORT SYSTEM (CDSS)

The Antimicrobial CDSS is a tool within the Computerized Patient Record System that offers antimicrobial prescribing advice to clinicians at the point of order entry. The system is structured as an order menu decision tree that contains quick orders pre-programmed with appropriate antimicrobial regimens for specific infectious diseases.

# Goals

Improve patient outcomes, reduce rates of microbial resistance, prevent adverse patient outcomes, optimize costs and improve providers' lives. In addition to these goals, the program fulfills antimicrobial stewardship quality standards implemented by the Joint Commission.

# Rationale

*Improved patient outcomes
In a 2013 study, Minneapolis Veterans Affairs Medical Center (MVAMC) antimicrobial courses ordered through the Antimicrobial CDSS were significantly more likely to be appropriate from start to completion, (44%) compared to non- CDSS courses (33%, P = 0.013). This is consistent with other studies that have shown significant improvement in appropriate use of antimicrobials when CDSS programs are utilized.

*Restricted formulary
The Minneapolis VAHCS has a restricted antimicrobial formulary. A restricted formulary reduces cost of health care and is an integral part of antimicrobial stewardship. The Antimicrobial CDSS provides a method of formulary restriction that doesn't require a call back from pharmacy or a prior authorization for the antimicrobial to be approved.

[More information on antimicrobial restriction policy](restriction-policy)

*Increased efficiency
Along with being able to order restricted antimicrobials without a prior authorization or call back from pharmacy, the Antimicrobial CDSS provides quick orders pre-programmed with appropriate antimicrobial regimens for specific infectious diseases. Using the system saves time and increases the efficiency of the ordering provider.

# Features

The CDSS has been developed locally with input from a broad, representative group of clinicians. Recommendations have been based on local susceptibility patterns, clinical evidence, local preferences, and national guidelines. The CDSS provides a way for clinicians to select alternative drugs when the recommended drugs are contraindicated.

Detailed instructions can be found in the link below.

[How to use the CDSS](how-to-use-the-cdss)

References

- Dellit et al. Clinical Infectious Diseases 2007, 44:159-7
- Filice et al. Infection Control and Hospital Epidemiology. 2013, 34.6
- Rawson et al. Clinical Microbiology and Infection. 2017, 1e9

# Initial CDI diagnosis (all are required)

(1) Unexplained diarrhea (e.g., no laxative or increase in tube feed)

(3) Laboratory confirmation of CDI

Typically defined as symptomatic, laboratory confirmed CDI within 12 weeks after a prior episode. Recurrence rates are up to 25%. Recurrence is usually due to failure of normal colonic flora to re-establish itself, rather than antimicrobial treatment failure.

menus.Name: bronchitis-not-benefit
menus.Term1: Bronchitis, no benefit from antibacterial therapy
menus.Text:
# BRONCHITIS, NO BENEFIT FROM ANTIBACTERIAL THERAPY

Acute bronchitis is a clinical syndrome with a brief, self-limited pneumonia on chest radiograph. It is accompanied by dry or productive cough lasting up to 3 weeks, is most prevalent in winter, and is primarily caused by viruses. More than 1 in 20 people have acute bronchitis per year, with highest rates during the winter months.  This discussion does not pertain to acute exacerbations of chronic bronchitis, a clinical syndrome also frequently associated with viral infection, but in which bacteria play a more important role.

Narcotic cough suppressants, expectorants, antihistamines, decongestants, and beta 2-agonists have been used to treat patients with acute bronchitis, but controlled trials have not clearly concluded that they are beneficial.

Empirical antibacterial therapy has repeatedly been shown to provide no benefit for most patients.  Acute bronchitis remains one of the five most frequently cited rationales for excessive antibiotic use in outpatients. Acute bronchitis and other acute respiratory syndromes (otitis media, sinusitis, pharyngitis, upper respiratory infections) account for approximately 75% of ambulatory prescriptions in the United States.  Current guidelines, endorsed by several national societies, including the Infectious Diseases Society of America, do not recommend the routine use of antibiotics for uncomplicated acute bronchitis in normal people.

If pertussis is suspected, early therapy with macrolides or tetracyclines is indicated to prevent transmission, although the clinical findings early in pertussis infection are indistinguishable from viral causes of bronchitis, and the incidence of disease is very low.  Treat for pertussis only when a patient has likely been exposed to other cases.

Asthma attacks often have symptoms resembling bronchitis.  Asthma attacks do not benefit from antimicrobial therapy.

# HIGH RISK FOR SURGICAL SITE INFECTIONS ANTIBIOTIC PROPHYLAXIS

Antibiotic prophylaxis is recommended for prevention of infection for the listed high risk conditions:

1. Extensive inflammatory skin disease (e.g. high tension)
2. Groin or Lower Extremities
3. Skin flaps and grafts
4. Wedge excision of lip or ear

Contaminated, dirty or infected wound may warrant antibiotic prophylaxis if patient is not currently on an antimicrobial for treatment of infection at the surgical site. Surgical prophylaxis is covered by antimicrobials for treatment of infection at time of surgery. No additional antimicrobials are necessary.

# DURATION OF ANTIMICROBIAL THERAPY

In general, duration of therapy is based on multiple factors, including infection severity, rapidity of improvement, and pathogen susceptibility. For a few diseases guidelines are established based on available evidence and opinion.

For many more diseases, guidelines have not been established.

For outpatient prescriptions, when a range is recommended by CDSS, the prescription order will default to the lowest dose and day supply. For inpatient orders, durations are listed in the recommendations but are not included in the quick order. The provider must select a duration, if desired, when completing an inpatient quick order.

For all cases clinical judgment is important. More information is given within specific diagnoses or syndromes sections.

menus.Name: how-to-use-the-cdss
menus.Text:
# HOW TO USE THE CDSS

The CDSS has been designed to offer antimicrobial prescribing advice quickly and efficiently. Since inpatient and outpatient drugs are ordered differently, the CDSS has both and inpatient and outpatient versions for prescribing.

The Antimicrobial CDSS is located within CPRS. When CPRS is open, click on the Orders tab at the bottom left hand side of the CPRS window.

# For inpatients

On the left-hand side of the "Orders" tab, click on the "Medicine Inpt Orders."

option.  In the right-hand column of the window that pops up, select "#77 Antimicrobials (CDSS).". The main menu of the Inpatient Antimicrobial CDSS will now be open.

# For outpatients

On the left-hand side of the "Orders" tab, click on the "Medicine Outpt Orders."

option.In the right-hand column of the window that pops up, select "#55 Antimicrobial (CDSS).". The main menu of the Outpatient Antimicrobial CDSS will now be open.

# Navigating Within the CDSS

*Using the decision tree
The main menu of the Antimicrobial CDSS contains links to categories of infectious diseases based on syndrome/organ system (e.g. cardiovascular, genitourinary, etc.), organisms (e.g. gram-positive bacteria, gram-negative bacteria, viruses, etc.) and other special cases. To navigate to specific infectious disease, select the category the infectious disease is associated with. Within the category menu, select the specific infectious disease sub-menu for recommendations, quick orders and pertinent resources (e.g., section-specific consults, important drug properties, CDSS system help resources, etc.).

*Using the Index
The Index is in the main menu at the top of the left-hand column under the header Index of Antimicrobial CDSS content. The Index contains an alphabetized list of Antimicrobial CDSS content. Find the infectious disease, organism or other topic you are looking for by scrolling down the list. When you locate the term you are looking for, click on it to be linked to the menu containing specific recommendations, quick orders and pertinent resources.

# Quick Orders

Quick orders are preprogrammed with the usually recommended antimicrobial dose, frequency and solution for the specific infectious disease.

[More information on duration of antimicrobial therapy](duration-of-antimicrobial-therapy)

Quick orders are not tailored to specific patient factors such as renal insufficiency, comorbidities, contraindications, weight, allergies, etc. The provider must assess every patient closely for these factors and modify recommended antimicrobials if needed. To assist the provider, additional drug information is provided within specific infectious diseases recommendation menus and a link to more in depth information is provided at the top of these menus.

# Elements of a CDSS Advice Page

[Click Here](elements-of-cdss-advice-page)

# If you need to modify existing therapy

[Adjusting existing antimicrobial therapy](adj-exist-therapy)

# If you need an alternative antimicrobial

[How to find an alternative antimicrobial within the CDSS](how-to-find-alt)

menus.Name: beta-lactam-allergy-facts
menus.Text:
# Important Beta-lactam Allergy Facts

1. 10% of patients report an allergy to penicillin.
2. Less than 1% of patients are truly allergic to penicillin.
3. 80% of patients who had an immediate allergic reaction (Type I, Immunoglobulin E (IgE)-mediated) to penicillin lose sensitivity after 10 years.
4. Cross-reactivity between penicillin and cephalosporins occurs in only 2% of patients and most patients do not have clinically significant reactions.

# Obtaining a Detailed Reaction History

- Locate documented reaction information within the Computerized Patient Record System (CPRS)

Reported reactions can be found in the Cover Sheet under Allergies/Adverse Reactions. Double click on the specific reaction for more information, including signs/symptoms and date of reaction.

A reaction report can also be found here: Reports tab -> Clinical Reports - Allergies.

- Determine beta-lactam medication history. A list of all locally prescribed medications can be found here: Reports tab -> Clinical Reports -> Pharmacy -> All Medications.
- Interview the patient or family for details about the reaction. Questions to ask during the interview:

What medication were you taking when the reaction occurred? DO NOT accept Penicillin or Cephalosporin as an allergy, ensure specific offending medication is identified.

How long after taking the medication did the reaction occur? Immediate reactions typically occur within 1 hour and up to 72 hours after administration. Delayed reactions occur after 72 hours.

How long ago did the reaction occur? Did it occur over 10 years ago?

What kind of reaction occurred? Did the reaction require medical attention?

---

menus.Name: non-streptococcal-pharyngitis
menus.Text:
# PHARYNGITIS

Acute pharyngitis is common, accounting for 2 percent of all ambulatory visits in the United States.  The major treatable pathogen, group A streptococcus (GAS), is the cause of pharyngitis in only approximately 10 percent of adults who seek medical care.  The vast majority of patients receive presumptive antibiotic therapy for pharyngitis which in most cases is unnecessary and results in adverse effects including death, increases costs, and adds to pressure on antimicrobial resistance.  Typical causes of pharyngitis include viruses in about ï¿½, beta-hemolytic streptococci other than group A in 18%, Mycoplasma pneumoniae in 10%, Chlamydophila pneumoniae in 8%, Group A streptococci in 5%, and no microbe identified in 1/3.

Rheumatic fever is rare in the United States, especially in adults, so that some authorities recommend no treatment even if GAS is a potential cause of pharyngitis.Others feel it is important to detect GAS  since antibiotic therapy can slightly shorten the acute illness, prevent acute rheumatic fever and possibly prevent suppurative sequelae.  Other potential causes of pharyngitis that should be considered and diagnosed if likely include Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) mononucleosis, primary HIV infection, influenza, gonococcal pharyngitis, diphtheria, and suppurative pharyngeal infections.

The Centor criteria are used to predict whether GAS pharyngitis is present.

*  Tonsillar exudates
*  Tender anterior cervical adenopathy
*  Fever by history
*  Absence of cough

If three or four of these criteria are met, the positive predictive value is 40 to 60 percent.  If fewer than three criteria are present, the likelihood GAS is causing pharyngitis is less than 20 percent.  If 3 or > Centor criteria are met, obtain a throat culture for group A streptococcus.  Treat empirically for GAS if the patient has severe symptoms or treat later for GAS if the throat culture is positive.

[References:](references)

Mandell chapter: Pharyngitis

# PENICILLIN DESENSITIZATION PROTOCOL

Pharmacy Service must be involved. Contact satellite pharmacist at ext. 2040 or menu 648-6746. Infectious Diseases Consult strongly recommended.

When penicillin is the drug of choice for an infectious disease in a patient with Type I penicillin allergy, one option is to desensitize the patient.

Severe reactions cannot be predicted accurately with skin testing in the clinical setting.

# Penicillin Desensitization

Perform in an ICU or similar setting.

Discontinue all beta-adrenergic antagonists.

Have IV line in place and EKG and spirometer ready.

Once desensitization has been accomplished, therapy with this drug must not lapse or the risk of allergic reactions increases.

A history of Stevens Johnson syndrome, exfoliative dermatitis, or erythroderma are nearly absolute contraindications to desensitization.

menus.Name: antiviral-prophylaxis-malignancy
menus.Text:
# PREVENTION OF VIRAL INFECTIONS IN A PATIENT WITH MALIGNANCY

Viral infections reactivate in a small percentage of people with malignancy.

Most viral infections in patients with hematologic malignancies or solid tumors result from reactivation of asymptomatic latent infections, predominantly of herpes viruses, including herpes simplex virus (HSV), varicella zoster virus (VZV) and cytomegalovirus (CMV). Exogenous respiratory tract infections caused by influenza, parainfluenza or respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) are less common.

The main risk factor for clinically relevant reactivation is profound disruption of cellular immune response, usually due to chemotherapy.

The duration and severity of neutropenia are of lesser importance.

The risk of viral disease increases with the intensity and duration of functional T-cell suppression. Patients receiving conventionally dosed chemotherapy regimens for solid tumors experience no major T-cell suppression and do not have a higher incidence of invasive viral infections.

# This section is organized mainly by type of malignancy.

There are separate sections for purine analogues (fludarabine, cladribine, pentostatin), alemtuzumab and rituximab.

Select below for recommended antiviral prophylaxis:

[Solid Tumors, Acute Leukemia, or Lymphoma](antiviral-type-of-malignancy)

menus.Name: cell-mediated-immunity-defects
menus.Text:
CELL-MEDIATED IMMUNITY (CMI) DEFECTS
Patients with reduced CMI include those with HIV/AIDS, hematologic malignancies, cytotoxic chemotherapy, and congenital abnormalities.  Patients with cell-mediated immune defects are more susceptible to infections from ubiquitous microorganisms that do not usually cause infection in healthy patients.  The specific organisms that are more likely to be associated with disease vary depending on the specific type of immune defect present, but include:

Pneumocystis jirovecii (formerly Pneumocystis carinii), Mycobacterium avium, Mycobacterium tuberculosis, Salmonella spp., Candida spp., Aspergillus spp., Toxoplasma gondii, varicella-zoster virus, cytomegalovirus, Epstein-Barr virus, and Cryptosporidium parvum.

These infectious diseases usually have a subacute or chronic presentation.  The best approach in most circumstances is for the clinician to conduct a methodical diagnostic workup to identify the specific pathogen and guide therapy.

Empirical antimicrobials are not indicated for patients with CMI defects who present only with fever.  Contact Infectious Disease for more information.

[References](references)

Rich RR, et al, eds.  Clinical Immunology
Roitt I, et al, eds.  Immunology

menus.Name: immunocompromise-basic-concepts
menus.Text:
BASIC CONCEPTS
Humans are protected by a broad array of host defenses that fall into two major categories: innate and immune host defenses.  Innate defense operate continuously without specific antigenic stimulation and immune defenses are primed by and respond to antigenic stimulation.

Each type of host defense protects against a specific set of organisms.  As a result, infectious diseases more common because of host defense defects in an individual patient are usually predictable from that patient's host defense defects.  For example, antibody or complement deficiencies predispose patients to disease with encapsulated organisms but not fungi.  Defects in cell-mediated immunity predispose patients to infections with mycobacteria or cytomegalovirus but not Escherichia coli or influenza virus.  Suspected cases of infectious disease must be evaluated in the context of the patient's host defects.

Management, including possible antimicrobial therapy, should be initiated on the basis of the most likely offending pathogens.

[References](references)

menus.Name: hypochlorhydria
menus.Text:
HYPOCHLORHYDRIA
Diminished gastric acid allows increased numbers of bacteria in the stomach and predisposes to infection with several potentially pathogenic bacterial species.

These changes increase the risk of nosocomial pneumonia and possibly the risk of community-acquired respiratory infections.  However, interventions to decontaminate the upper gastrointestinal tract do not prevent infectious disease.

[References](references)

Rich RR, et al, eds.  Clinical Immunology
Roitt I, et al, eds.  Immunology

menus.Name: malnutrition
menus.Text:
MALNUTRITION
Adequate nutrition is necessary for optimal host defense function.  A few days of malnutrition can decrease host defenses, mainly cell-mediated immunity. The degree of compromised immunity increases with the duration of malnutrition.

However, nutritional replacement has not been shown to improve outcomes in patients with mild-moderate malnutrition.  Enteral nutritional replacement is far superior to and safer than intravenous hyperalimentation.

# Treatment

Empirical antimicrobials are not indicated for malnourished patients with fever but without evidence of a specific infectious disease.

[References](references)

Rich RR, et al, eds.  Clinical Immunology
Roitt I, et al, eds.  Immunology

menus.Name: neutropenia
menus.Text:
NEUTROPENIA
Patients with neutropenia are at risk of infection from pyogenic organisms including Staphylococcus aureus, streptococci, Gram-negative bacilli, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, candida, and certain filamentous fungi, most notably Aspergillus and the zygomycetes.  The risk is inversely related to the absolute neutrophil count (ANC), the disease or condition associated with neutropenia, duration of neutropenia, and the presence of other host defense defects or underlying diseases.

[References](references)

menus.Name: stress
menus.Text:
STRESS
Acute psychological stress is associated with immune stimulation and increased cellular host defenses.  However, chronic stress decrease humoral and cell-mediated immunity.  Chronic stress has been correlated with increased risk of respiratory tract infection.

Critically ill patients are usually profoundly stressed.  The risk of infection is subtle and the defects are non-specific.

[References](references)

Rich RR, et al, eds.  Clinical Immunology
Roitt I, et al, eds.  Immunology

menus.Name: tobacco-smoke
menus.Text:
TOBACCO SMOKE
Active or passive exposure to tobacco smoke is associated with increased susceptibility to respiratory infectious diseases and several systemic infectious diseases with bacterial and viral pathogens.  Compounds found in tobacco or tobacco smoke interfere with several host defense mechanisms in the respiratory tract and elsewhere in the body.

[References](references)

Rich RR, et al, eds.  Clinical Immunology
Roitt I, et al, eds.  Immunology

menus.Name: leukocytosis
menus.Text:
# LEUKOCYTOSIS

The majority of leukocytosis cases are due to infection, but a sizable minority are associated with physiological stress, inflammation, medications (e.g.
glucocorticoids), and hematological conditions. In a review of 100 cases of extreme leukocytosis (more than 25,000 leukocytes per microliter with more than 50% granulocytes) at the Minneapolis VA, only 48 were from infectious problems.

Infection should be considered as a possible stimulus for leukocytosis in a patient with leukocytosis, especially when total white blood cell count is greater than or equal to 25,000 per micro liter. Antimicrobials should be administered if the patient has a syndrome or disease that calls for antimicrobials. Refer to those recommendations for treatment. Antimicrobials should not be administered solely to treat a patient with leukocytosis and no other sign or symptom of infection.

---

References:

- Wanahita et al., Clinical Infectious Diseases (2002), 34.1585-92
- Reding et al., The American Journal of Medicine (1998), 104.12-16
- Up-to-date article: Approach to the patient with neutrophilia

# MASCC RISK INDEX FOR FEBRILE NEUTROPENIA

SCORING TOOL TO IDENTIFY LOW RISK FEBRILE NEUTROPENIC PATIENTS Patients with minimal risk of severe or rapidly progressive infection can be treated with oral antimicrobials safely.  Many can be treated as outpatients.

Use the scoring index to identify febrile neutropenic patients who at sufficiently low risk for severe infections and can be treated with outpatient oral antimicrobials.

# SCORING INDEX

# CharacteristicScore

Severity of symptoms of illness (choose one only)

No symptoms or mild symptoms5
Moderate symptoms  3
No hypotension  5
No chronic obstructive pulmonary disease4
Solid tumor or no previous fungal infection4
No dehydration  3
Outpatient status at onset of fever3
Age less than 60 years2
Sum total __

# Interpretation

The highest possible score is 26. A risk index score of 21 or greater indicates that the patient is likely to be at LOW RISK for complications and morbidity.

This is a guide.  Always use clinical judgement.

# STAPHYLOCOCCUS AUREUS INFECTIONS IN BONE OR JOINT PROSTHESES

Consult Infectious Diseases for specific management advice.

# Treatment Following 2-stage Exchange or Resection Arthroplasty Without Planned

# Staged Reimplantation of Prosthesis

Treat with intravenous antibiotic for 6 weeks for all joint types.

# Treatment Following 1-Stage Exchange of Prosthesis

Treat with intravenous antibiotic for 2 to 6 weeks followed by 3 months of an oral antibiotic combined with rifampin for all joint types.

# Rifampin Synergy

Rifampin is recommended for treatment with debridement and retention or one stage exchange. When rifampin is combined with a beta-lactam or vancomycin in vitro, bacterial killing is enhanced. Do not use rifampin alone, as bacterial resistance develops rapidly. If patient does not tolerate rifampin it may be omitted from treatment regimen. Contact Infectious Diseases for more information.

# Chronic Suppression

Chronic suppression with oral antimicrobials may follow treatment based on individual patient circumstances.

---

menus.Name: biliary-surgery-prophylaxis
menus.Text:
BILIARY SURGERY
Surgical prophylaxis is indicated for open procedures and high risk laparoscopic procedures.  Additional doses should not be given after incisions are closed. Surgical prophylaxis is not indicated in elective low risk laparoscopic procedures.

The risk of infectious complications after laparoscopic cholecystectomy is increased after emergent procedures, procedures lasting more than 120 minutes, intraoperative gall bladder rupture or bile spillage, conversion from laparoscopic to open cholecystectomy, and insertion of a prosthetic device.

The risk is increased in patients who have had an episode of colic or a biliary procedure within 30 days before the procedure, patients with acute cholecystitis or jaundice, patients with a nonfunctional gallbladder, patients with immunosuppression, pregnancy, diabetes, age greater than 70 years, or American Society of Anesthesiologists classification of 3 or greater.

If one of these risk factors exists, prophylaxis is indicated for laparoscopic cholecystectomy.  If there is a substantial likelihood that one of these risk factors will develop during a procedure, the surgeon may elect to order prophylaxis.

[Click here to go to CIED Surgery Prophylaxis](cied-surgery-pre-op-prophylaxis)

[Click here to go to CV \(open heart\) Surgery Prophylaxis](meds-delayed-pre-op-antibiotics-cv-surgery2)

Antimicrobial prophylaxis is not indicated before cardiac catheterization with or without stent placement or for transesophageal echocardiogram.

For patients undergoing cardiac procedures the recommended regimen is a single pre-incision dose of antibiotic with additional doses while incisions are open for long procedures.

Prophylaxis should not be continued beyond 24 hours even if drains or intravenous catheters remain in place.

Cefazolin is preferred for prophylaxis, as it is more active than vancomycin against methicillin-susceptible staphylococci.  Vancomycin should be used when methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus infection is likely.

Consult Cardiothoracic Surgery or Infectious Diseases for more information.

menus.Name: neurosurgery-prophylaxis
menus.Text:
## NEUROSURGERY

Risk factors for postoperative infections following neurologic procedures include diabetes, procedure duration longer than two to four hours, placement of a foreign body, repeat surgery, emergency surgery, cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) leak, postoperative intracranial pressure monitoring or presence of a ventricular drain for more than five days postoperatively, and concurrent or prior infection of an incision or shunt.

In spinal surgery, the infection rate after conventional lumbar discectomy is low, but due to the severe consequences of postoperative infection at this site antimicrobial prophylaxis is recommended. Infection rates are higher after prolonged spinal surgery or spinal procedures involving fusion or insertion of foreign material, and antimicrobial prophylaxis is also recommended.

Antimicrobial prophylaxis is warranted for patients undergoing clean craniotomy CSF shunt procedures, or intrathecal pump placement.

For all other neurosurgical procedures, antimicrobial prophylaxis is not indicated.

Cefazolin is preferred for most patients as it penetrates into the cerebrospinal fluid and is more active than vancomycin against susceptible staphylococci.

Vancomycin should be used when the patient is colonized or has been recently infected with methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus. Consult Neurosurgery or Infectious Diseases for more information.

- Bratzler DW, et al.  Clinical practice guidelines for antimicrobial prophy in surgery, Am J Health-Syst Pharm. 2013 Vol 70 page 195-283

menus.Name: orthopedic-surgery-prophylaxis
menus.Text:
ORTHOPAEDIC SURGERY
Antimicrobial prophylaxis is not recommended for most clean procedures, including knee, hand or foot procedures, arthroscopy, or other procedures without implantation of foreign materials.

Prophylaxis is indicated for internal fixation of fracture, total joint replacement, and any implanted foreign body. Open fractures should be treated as infected.

Cefazolin is preferred for prophylaxis, as it is more active than vancomycin against susceptible staphylococci, the most common surgical pathogens.

Vancomycin should be used in patients who are colonized or recently infected with methicilin-resistant Staphlococcus aureus (MRSA).

Prophylaxis beyond 24 hours is not supported by current data and guidelines.

Longer durations provide no additional benefit and are associated with side effects, increased costs, and bacterial resistance.

Also, there is no evidence of benefit of antimicrobial administration until all drains or catheters are removed.

menus.Name: surgical-prophylaxis-general-information
menus.Text:
SURGICAL PROPHYLAXIS COMMON PRINCIPLES
Potential pathogens are introduced into normally sterile areas of the body during most surgical procedures.  The purpose of antimicrobial prophylaxis is to reduce the intraoperative microbial burden so that local host defenses can eliminate microorganisms and prevent disease.  Prophylaxis cannot be expected to sterilize tissues.

Antimicrobial agent for surgical prophylaxis should be:

1. active against the pathogens most likely to contaminate the surgical site
2. given in an appropriate dosage and at a time that ensures adequate serum and tissue concentrations during the period of potential contamination
3. safe, and
4. administered for the shortest effective period to minimize adverse effects, the development of resistance, and costs.

# References:

- Bratzler DW, et al.  Clinical practice guidelines for antimicrobial prophylaxis in surgery, Am J Health-Syst Pharm. 2013 Vol 70 page 195-283
- Antimicrobial Prophylaxis for Surgery, Treatment Guidelines from The
- Medical Letter 2012 Vol 10 pages 73-77

menus.Name: surg-timing-dosing-prophyl-abx
menus.Text:
TIMING AND DOSING (INCLUDING RE-DOSING) OF PROPHYLACTIC ANTIMICROBIALS For optimal prevention, antimicrobial concentrations should be above the minimal inhibitory concentration (MIC) of potential pathogens from initial incision until closure.

There is no advantage to giving post-operative doses. Despite a lack of demonstrated benefit, post-operative doses are sometimes given in clinical practice.  If post-operative doses are given, they should be discontinued by 24 hours after closure of the incision.

When prophylaxis consists of a single dose as should be the case in the majority of procedures, adjustment for renal or hepatic dysfunction is not necessary.

The optimal time for administration of preoperative doses is 30 to 60 minutes before surgical incision for most antimicrobials.

Infusions of drugs like fluoroquinolones and vancomycin that require longer infusion times should begin 60 to 120 minutes before first incision.

During procedures that last so long that concentrations might fall below the MICs of potential pathogens, repeated doses of antimicrobials should be given.

Re-dosing may also be warranted if prolonged or excessive bleeding occurs.

[Doses and Redosing Recommendations for Common Antimicrobials](surg-prophylaxis-doses-and-redosing)

[References](references)

Bratzler DW, et al.  Clinical practice guidelines for antimicrobial prophylaxis in surgery, Am J Health-Syst Pharm. 2013 Vol 70 page 195-283 Antimicrobial Prophylaxis for Surgery, Treatment Guidelines from The Medical Letter 2012 Vol 10 pages 73-77

menus.Name: surgical-wound-classification
menus.Text:
SURGICAL WOUND CLASSIFICATION AND ANTIMICROBIAL PROPHYLAXIS RECOMMENDATIONS

# >>  Clean  <<

A wound resulting from a procedure in which no inflammation or infection was encountered and the respiratory, alimentary, genital, or uninfected urinary tract was not entered.  Clean wounds are closed at the end of surgery and if drainage is necessary wounds are closed with drains in place.

Antimicrobial prophylaxis is usually not indicated.  Exceptions are procedures in which prosthetic material will be inserted or for operations in which a surgical site infection would be catastrophic.  These exceptions include most cardiac operations, joint replacement, revascularization procedures in legs, and most neurosurgical operations.

# >>  Clean contaminated  <<

Clean-contaminated wounds are those in which the respiratory, alimentary, genital, or urinary tracts are entered but there is no evidence of infection and there is no major break in technique.  These include operations on the biliary tract, appendix, vagina, and oropharynx.

Antimicrobial prophylaxis is indicated for most of these procedures.

# >>  Contaminated  <<

Contaminated wounds include an open, fresh, accidental wound, or operations with major breaks in sterile technique, gross spillage from the gastrointestinal tract, or incisions in which acute, non-purulent inflammation is encountered.

Antimicrobials are therapeutic and not prophylactic.

# >>  Dirty-Infected  <<

Dirty-infected wounds are old traumatic wounds with devitalized tissue and those that involve existing infection or perforated viscera.  The organisms usually have been present in the operative field since before the operation.

Antimicrobials are therapeutic and not prophylactic.

[References](references)

Bratzler DW, et al.  Clinical practice guidelines for antimicrobial in surgery, Am J Health-Syst Pharm. 2013 Vol 70 page 195-283 Antimicrobial Prophylaxis for Surgery, Treatment Guidelines from The Medical Letter 2012 Vol 10 pages 73-77

menus.Text:
# TOXOPLASMA SPP.

If patient is immunocompetent and not pregnant, treatment is usually not needed as disease is usually self-limited. Patients who are immunocompromised, pregnant or have severe disease should be treated. Consult Infectious Diseases in all cases.

---

# Non-pregnant patients

---

# Duration of antimicrobial therapy

Treat immunocompetent patients for 2-4 weeks. Treat immunocompromised patients for 6 weeks or longer if radiologic disease is extensive or response is incomplete at 6 weeks.

---

# Chronic Maintenance therapy for immunocompromised patients

---

Discontinue maintenance therapy if patient has remained asymptomatic and CD4 >200 cells per microliter.

menus.Name: transplantation
menus.Text:
TRANSPLANTATION
Organ transplantation is associated with many host defense defects.  Early on, surgical wounds may become infected.  Preparation for transplantation and anti-rejection drugs can induce neutropenia.  Later, CMI defects predominate.

Patients become infected with exogenous pathogens and also endogenous pathogens like cytomegalovirus that might have been present in latent or subclinical form.

Cell-mediated immune defects caused by anti-rejection drugs cause patients to be especially susceptible to infections with organisms that infrequently cause disease in healthy people.  They include: Pneumocystis jirovecii (formerly Pneumocystis carinii), mycobacteria, salmonella, candida, aspergillus, Toxoplasma gondii, varicella-zoster virus, cytomegalovirus, Epstein-Barr virus, and cryptosporidia.

The approach to fever or other signs or symptoms suggesting the possibility of an infectious disease depends on the specific defects present in the patient, the nature of the presenting signs and symptoms and a bedside assessment of the severity of illness.  Empirical antimicrobials are usually not indicated for fever alone unless the patient has a host defense defect that predisposes to rapid progression of illness like severe neutropenia or splenectomy.  Contact Infectious Diseases for more information.

[References](references)

Rich RR, et al, eds.  Clinical Immunology
Roitt I, et al, eds.  Immunology

Summary of Adult

internal medicine, 2021,
174(3)374-384.
<!-- COLUMN 2 -->
## Recommended populations
## __________________________
*All adults who want to be
protected from hepatitis A
virus (HAV) infection.
*People who travel or work
anywhere EXCEPT the U.S.,
most, but not all of
Western Europe, New
Zealand, Australia,
Canada, and Japan.
*People with chronic liver
disease, injecting and
non-injecting drug users,
people who have HIV
infection, men who have
sex with men, people who
are homeless or live in
temporary housing (e.g., a
shelter), people who work
with HAV in lab settings.
*People who anticipate
close personal contact
with an international
adoptee from
a country of high or
intermediate endemicity
during the first 60d
following the adoptee's
arrival in the U.S.
*Postexposure: adults with
recent (within 2wks)
exposure to HAV, give
HepA. Vaccine may be used
in conjunction with IG at
the provider's discretion
in adults older than age
40 or immunocompromised
<!-- COLUMN 3 -->
## Administration Schedule
## __________________________
*Give 2 doses, spaced 6-
12 months apart.
*If dose #2 is delayed, do
not repeat dose #1. Just
give dose #2.
<!-- COLUMN 4 -->
## Contraindications/Precautions
## __________________________
## Contraindications:
History of severe allergic
reaction (e.g.,
anaphylaxis) to a previous
dose or a vaccine
component.
## Precautions:
Moderate or severe acute
illness with or
without fever.

menus.Text:
## Vaccine route, orders, names
## __________________________
## Route: IM
## Outpatient MenACWY orders:
2 dose series
Booster Dose
## CPRS name:
MENINGOCOCCAL
OLIGOSACCHARIDE
CONJ. VACC INJ,SUSP
## Stocked brand name:
Menveo
## Other names:
Meningococcal conjugate
(MenACWY)
References:
Immunization Action
Coalition,
Summary of Adult
Immunizations, 2021, P2011
Freedman et al., Annals of
internal medicine, 2021,
174(3)374-384.
<!-- COLUMN 2 -->
## Recommended populations
## __________________________
*People with anatomic or
functional asplenia, HIV
infection, or persistent
complement component
deficiency, or complement
inhibitor use.
*People who travel to or
reside in countries in
which meningococcal
disease is hyperendemic or
epidemic (e.g., the
meningitis belt of Sub-
Saharan Africa).
*Microbiologists routinely
exposed to isolates of N.
meningitidis.
*For first year college
students living in a
residence hall, regardless
of age,
>> if unvaccinated, give 1
dose.
>> if history of 1 dose
given when younger than
age 16, give dose #2.
>> if most recent dose
given after 16th birthday
and more than 5 years
have elapsed, give 1 dose.
<!-- COLUMN 3 -->
## Administration Schedule
## __________________________
*Give 2 initial doses of
MenACWY separated by 2m to
adults with risk factors
listed in 1st bullet in
column to left.
*Give 1 initial dose of
MenACWY to all other
adults with risk factors
(see 2nd-4th bullets in
column to left).
*Give booster doses of
MenACWY every 5yrs to
adults with continuing
risk (see the 1st-3rd
bullets in column to
left).
<!-- COLUMN 4 -->
## Contraindications/Precautions
## __________________________
## Contraindications:
History of severe allergic
reaction (e.g.,
anaphylaxis) to a previous
dose or a vaccine
component.
## Precautions:
Moderate or severe acute
illness with or
without fever.

menus.Text:
## Vaccine route, orders, names
## __________________________
## Route: Subcutaneous
## Outpatient MMR orders:
2 dose series
One dose
## CPRS name:
MEASLES/MUMPS/RUBELLA
VIRUS VACCINE INJ
## Stocked brand name:
M-M-R II
## Other names:
Measles, mumps, rubella
(MMR)
References:
Immunization Action
Coalition,
Summary of Adult
Immunizations, 2021, P2011
Freedman et al., Annals of
internal medicine, 2021,
174(3)374-384.
<!-- COLUMN 2 -->
## Recommended populations
## __________________________
*People born in 1957 or
later (especially those
born outside the U.S.)
should receive at least 1
dose of MMR if they have
no laboratory evidence of
immunity to each of the 3
diseases or documentation
of a dose given on or
after the first birthday.
*People in high-risk
groups, such as healthcare
personnel (paid, unpaid,
or volunteer), students
entering college and other
post-high school
educational institutions,
and international
travelers, should receive
a total of 2 doses.
*HIV infection with CD4
count >/=200 cells/mm3 for
at least 6 months and no
evidence of immunity to
measles, mumps, or rubella
should receive a total of
2 doses. MMR
contraindicated for HIV
infection with CD4 count
<200 cells/mm3
*People born before 1957
are usually considered
immune, but evidence of
immunity (serology or
documented history of 2
doses of MMR) should be
considered for healthcare
personnel.
*Women of childbearing age
who do not have acceptable
evidence of rubella
immunity or vaccination.
<!-- COLUMN 3 -->
## Administration Schedule
## __________________________
*Give 1 or 2 doses (see
criteria in 1st and 2nd
bullets in box to left).
*If dose #2 is
recommended, give it no
sooner than 4wks after
dose #1.
*If woman of childbearing-
age is found to be rubella
susceptible and is not
pregnant, give 1 dose of
MMR. If she is pregnant,
the dose should be given
postpartum. This includes
women who have already
received 1 or 2 doses of
rubella-containing
vaccine.
*If 2 or more of the
following live virus
vaccines are to be given -
MMR, LAIV, Var, ZVL,
and/or yellow fever - they
should be given on the
same day. If they are not
given on the same day,
space them by at least 28d
(30d for yellow fever).
May use as post-exposure
prophylaxis if given
within 3d of exposure.
<!-- COLUMN 4 -->
## Contraindications/Precautions
## __________________________
## Contraindications:
*History of severe allergic
reaction (e.g.,
anaphylaxis) to a previous
dose or a vaccine
component.
*Pregnancy or possibility
of pregnancy within 4wks.
*Severe immunodeficiency
(e.g., hematologic and
solid tumors, receiving
chemotherapy, congenital
immunodeficiency, long-
term immunosuppressive
therapy, people with human
immunodeficiency virus
(HIV) infection who are
severely
immunocompromised (CD4
count <200 cells/mm3).)
## Precautions
*Moderate or severe acute
illness with or without
fever.
*If blood, plasma, and/or
immune globulin were given
in past 11m, see ACIP's
Best Practices Guidance
regarding time to wait
before vaccinating.
*History of
thrombocytopenia or
thrombocytopenic purpura.
*Need for tuberculin skin
testing (TST) or
interferon-gamma release
assay (IGRA) testing.
note: If TST or IGRA and
MMR are both needed but
not given on same day,
delay TST or IGRA for at
least 4wks after MMR.

menus.Text:
# Non-occupational:

Post-Exposure Prophylaxis (nPEP) for Exposure to Blood or Body Fluids for HIV (sexual, injection drug use, or other substantial non-occupational HIV exposure)

# Eligibility for nPEP requires ALL:

1. Less than 72 hours since exposure < AND >
2. High-risk anatomic site of exposure < AND >

(vagina, rectum, eye, mouth or other mucous membrane, nonintact skin, percutaneous inoculation)

3. High-risk type of fluid < AND >

(blood, semen, vaginal secretions, rectal secretions, breast milk, any body fluid visibly contaminated with blood)

4.  Known (or strongly suspected) HIV-positive source

When source HIV status is unknown, recommend erring on the side of providing antivirals for nPEP given the safety and tolerability of these medications, while including the patient in shared decision making.

# **ID on-call is available if there are any questions.**

# Estimated per-act risk for acquiring HIV from infected source, by exposure act:

[< SELECT HERE > FOR TABLE](pep-non-occupational-hiv-risk-table)

# \*\*\*\*\*\* Complete/assess all four items below for nPEP: \*\*\*\*\*\*

# For initial laboratory orders for assessment:

[< SELECT HERE > INITIAL LABORATORY ORDERS](pep-non-occupational-baseline-labs)

# For Follow-up Laboratory Orders and Schedule Return to Clinic Appointment(s):

[< SELECT HERE > 4 Week Follow-up Labs and RTC orders](pep-non-occupational-labs-and-rtc)

# IF risk factors for HIV persist place HIV Clinic (MRTC) consult:

If risk factors for HIV persist, place a consult to HIV Clinic (MRTC) for consideration of PrEP prior to the 28 days of nPEP ending.

<<ORDER>> HIV Clinic Outpatient Consult

References:

- CDC Guidelines 2025

menus.Text:
# Post-Exposure Prophylaxis (PEP) for Exposure to Blood or Body Fluids

# A.  Please review and follow the Post-Exposure Prophylaxis Protocol:

Post-Exposure Prophylaxis Protocol

# B.  Order the following laboratory tests for the source patient and employee:

Blood Borne Pathogen Labs

# C.  Evaluate employee for post-exposure prophylaxis antiviral medications:

If the source patient is known or suspected of having HIV infection, you are strongly encouraged to call the infectious diseases staff physician on call for advice any time, day or night.

If there has been a significant known or potential exposure to blood or body fluids from a patient with HIV infection, the employee must be seen in Occupational Health by the end of the next business day.  Post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) medications should be recommended to the employee.  If acceptable to the employee, medications should be started within two hours of of exposure and should be taken for up to 28 days.  To get the medications started, order a 5-day supply of antiviral medications here (see link below).

Additional medications can only be ordered by Occupational Health personnel after the employee is seen.

# If the employee accepts PEP, employee baseline labs CBC, LFTs,

# Basic Metabolic(SMA-7) should be drawn:

Select to place order for labs CBC, LFTs, Basic Metabolic(SMA-7)

menus.Text:
# RABIES PRE-EXPOSURE PROPHYLAXIS

For patients exposed to a rabid animal, refer to the Rabies Post-Exposure Prophylaxis recommendations in the emergency department CDSS.
[Rabies Post-Exposure Prophylaxis](rabies-post-exposure-prophylaxis)

# Rabies Vaccination

People in Risk Category Groups 1-4 (see below for full descriptions) should be vaccinated against rabies.
Rabies vaccine, 2-dose series (0, 7 days)

# Rabies Booster

A booster vaccination is given for groups 1 through 3 (not 4 or 5). For groups 1 and 2, this is dictated by rabies serum titer levels. For group 3, a one-time booster is recommended at a specific time interval.  For those in risk category 1, check titer every 6 months. For those in risk category 2, check titer every 2 years). See below for information regarding timing of the one-time booster for risk category 3.

Rabies virus rapid fluorescent focus inhibition test
Rabies booster vaccine

# CDC guidelines categorize patients into five categories based on exposure risk

Risk Category 1 (Highest risk): People who work with live or concentrated rabies virus in laboratories Recommendation: Give rabies vaccination. Check titer every 6 months and give booster dose if titer is low Risk Category 2: People who frequently do at least one of the following: handle bats, have contact with bats, enter high-density bat environments like caves, or perform animal necropsies Recommendation: Give rabies vaccination. Check titer every 2 years and give booster dose if titer is low Risk Category 3: People who interact with, or are at higher risk to interact, with mammals other than bats that could be rabid, for a period longer than three years after they receive PrEP. This group includes: Most veterinarians, veterinary technicians, animal control officers, wildlife biologists, rehabilitators, trappers, and spelunkers (cave explorers). Certain travelers to regions outside of the United States where rabies in dogs is commonly found.
Recommendation: Give rabies vaccination. Either a one-time titer check after 1 and up to 3 years following the first 2-dose vaccination < OR > 1-dose booster between 3 weeks and 3 years following the first vaccine in the 2-dose vaccination Risk Category 4: Same population as risk category 3, but at a higher risk for ?
three years after they receive PrEP.
Recommendation: Give rabies vaccination. Routine boosters not recommended.
Risk Category 5: People who do not have special occupational risks.
Recommendation: Rabies vaccination and boosters not recommended.

---

References:

- Rao et. Al., MMWR. Morbidity and mortality weekly report 71 (2022) https://www.cdc.gov/rabies/hcp/clinical-care/pre-exposure-prophylaxis.html

menus.Term2: Risk factors for antimicrobials in pregnancy
menus.Text:
# RISK FACTORS FOR ANTIMICROBIALS DURING PREGNANCY

# The FDA amended its rules in 2015 concerning the Pregnancy, Labor and delivery, and Nursing mothers subsections of the Use in Specific Populations section of product labeling. Pregnancy categories A, B, C, D, and X have been removed.

# Drugs approved after June 30 will use the new format immediately, while drugs approved after June 30, 2001 will be phased in gradually.

See Sanford Guide for comprehensive antimicrobial pregnancy risk and lactation safety information

Sanford Guide Pregnancy Risk & Lactation Safety Table

Risk Factors (A,B,C,D,X) were assigned to all drugs, based on the level of risk the drug poses to the fetus. Risk Factors were designed to help the clinician quickly classify a drug for use during pregnancy. They do not refer to breastfeeding risk. The definitions of the Risk Factors are those used by the FDA.

# Category Description

# A Controlled studies show no risk

Adequate, well-controlled studies in pregnant women have failed to demonstrate risk to the fetus.

# B No evidence of risk in humans

Either animal findings show risk (but human findings do not) or, if no adequate human studies have been done, animal findings are negative.

# C Risk cannot be ruled out

Human studies are lacking and animal studies are either positive for fetal risk or lacking as well. However, potential benefits may justify the potential risk.

# D Positive evidence of risk

Investigational or postmarketing data show risk to fetus. Nevertheless, potential benefits may outweigh the risk.

# X Contraindicated in pregnancy

Studies in animals or humans, or investigational or postmarketing reports have shown fetal risk which clearly outweighs any possible benefit to the patient.

References

- Up-to-Date website
- Sanford website

menus.Name: warfarin-interactions-with-antimicrobials
menus.Term1: Drug-drug interactions between antimicrobials and warfarin (Navigation)
menus.Text:
# DRUG-DRUG INTERACTIONS BETWEEN ANTIMICROBIALS AND WARFARIN

Several antimicrobials will affect metabolism or the effect of warfarin on a patient's clotting function. If possible, avoid using an antimicrobial with a significant interaction with warfarin. If you decide that an antimicrobial that interacts with warfarin is needed or you stop an antimicrobial that could interact with warfarin, you should determine the INR more frequently than usual and adjust dosage accordingly. Instruct patients to inform their primary warfarin provider whenever an antimicrobial is prescribed for them.

Antimicrobials can alter warfarin's anticoagulant effect by decreasing intestinal synthesis or absorption of vitamin K or by affecting distribution or metabolism of the vitamin. Some antimicrobials increase synthesis of coagulation factors.

Antimicrobials can decrease the rate of warfarin absorption, compete with warfarin at sites of warfarin metabolism, induce warfarin metabolic enzymes, or inhibit the function or synthesis warfarin metabolic enzymes. Some antimicrobials displace warfarin from protein binding sites.

Check for warfarin-antimicrobial interactions on Lexicomp:

Lexicomp Drug Interactions

References

- Holbrook, Anne M., et al. Archives of internal medicine 165.10 (2005): 1095-
- 1106

menus.Name: more-about-parotitis
menus.Text:
# MORE ABOUT PAROTITIS

Suppurative Parotitis. Acute bacterial parotitis affects primarily elderly, malnourished, dehydrated or post-operative patients. Symptoms include fever, toxicity, and tender swelling along the mandible with purulent drainage from the parotid duct. Suppurative parotitis is usually unilateral whereas viral parotitis is usually bilateral. Pain is intense and aggressive, analgesic therapy is required. Progression of infection may lead to massive swelling of the neck, respiratory obstruction, septicemia and osteomyelitis of adjacent facial bones. Empiric antibiotics are required for coverage of Staphylococcus aureus if bacterial, and surgical drainage is usually necessary.

Chronic Parotitis. Parotitis is recurrent with intermittent acute exacerbations.

Chronic, low-grade bacterial infection results in functional destruction of the salivary gland. It may be confused with Sjogren's syndrome, a noninfectious illness. Therapy includes systemic antibiotics. Parotidectomy may eventually be required for patients with long-standing infection.

Viral Parotitis. Mumps parotitis is characterized by the rapid, painful swelling of one or both parotid glands within 2 to 3 weeks after exposure to the mumps virus. Mumps usually involves both parotid glands whereas bacterial parotitis is unilateral. Other viral causes of parotitis include influenza and enteroviruses.

Mumps parotitis usually resolves spontaneously in 5 to 10 days. Provide symptomatic relief of pain and fever and maintain hydration to prevent secondary bacterial infection.

---

References:

- Wilson et al., Am Fam Physician. 2014, 89(11)882-888
- Mandell chapter:  Principles and Practice of Infectious Diseases
- Sanford keyword: Parotitis

# VIRAL GASTROENTERITIS

Infectious diarrhea caused by viral pathogens such as Adenovirus, Astrovirus, Norovirus, Rotavirus, and Sapovirus is usually self-limited. Treatment includes supportive measures such as oral rehydration and unrestricted nutrition.

Antiviral therapy is not recommended and for most viruses is unavailable.

Antimotility agents may be used for one or two days in patients with mild to moderate volume depletion. Antiemetic agents may be used for one or two days in patients with vomiting.

# COLONIZED WOUNDS

Open wounds are usually colonized with bacteria and often fungi. This is true of ulcers (see below), post-operative wounds, traumatic wounds, and others. Then bacteria can be of relatively low virulence (eg, coagulase negative staphylococci, diphtheroids) or of potentially greater virulence (Staphylococcus aureus, enterobacteriaceae, pseudomonas). Candida is commonly present on wounds that are moist or covered. There is no need to treat patients with systemic antimicrobials simply because a wound culture is positive for a potential pathogen. Topical antimicrobials are not effective in nearly all circumstances and can select for resistant organisms or lead to other adverse effects.

Systemic antimicrobial therapy may be indicated if there are signs of infection.

menus.Name: not-benefitted-bacteriuria
menus.Text:
# BACTERIURIA, CANDIDURIA, AND PYURIA

Asymptomatic bacteriuria (>= 100,000 bacteria per ml of urine) is common in middle aged and older people, especially those who have chronic medical conditions. Pyuria is common in persons with bacteriuria and individuals with indwelling catheters in place. By itself, the presence of pyuria is not sufficient to diagnose bacteriuria, and the presence or absence of pyuria does not differentiate symptomatic from asymptomatic urinary infection. Candiduria is less common than bacteriuria, but the implications of candiduria are similar to those of bacteriuria.

Many studies, including randomized clinical trials have shown that treatment of asymptomatic bacteriuria and candiduria, with or without pyuria is of no benefit, except in certain well-defined circumstances. Antimicrobial therapy is always accompanied by risk of harms, including drug reactions, Clostridium difficile colitis, anaphylaxis and death. Except in circumstances specified below, it is best to not order urinalysis or urine culture in asymptomatic persons. If bacteriuria, candiduria or pyuria is discovered in an asymptomatic person for some reason, antimicrobial therapy should not be given except as specified below.

# Pregnant women or patients undergoing urological procedures with bacteriuria

[Treatment of Asymptomatic Bacteriuria](asymp-bacteriuria)

# Patients undergoing urological procedures or neutropenic patients with candiduria

[Treatment of Candida Urinary Tract Infections](candida-uti)

References

- Pappas et al, Clin Infect Dis, 2016, 62.409
- Nicolle et al, Clin Infect Dis, 2005, 40:643

menus.Name: stasis-dermatitis
menus.Text:
# STASIS DERMATITIS

Stasis dermatitis is a common condition that is often confused with bacterial cellulitis. Stasis dermatitis does not benefit from antimicrobial therapy. It is important to distinguish between the two. The provider should be mindful of the fact that bacterial cellulitis can occur on skin with underlying stasis dermatitis. (See link below for bacterial cellulitis)

Common risk factors for venous stasis include advancing age, family history of venous disease, increased body mass index, smoking, a history of trauma, prior venous thrombosis and pregnancy. Chronic venous disease and arterial vascular disease have some common risk factors (eg, smoking, obesity) and pathophysiological processes. The most common symptoms reported by patients with chronic venous disease are limb discomfort (tired, heavy legs), pain, and limb swelling. Swelling is often worse with prolonged standing and improves with leg elevation and walking. The skin of the anterior surfaces of the lower legs often has brown or blue-grey hyperpigmentation.

People with venous stasis are prone to develop stasis dermatitis which is one of the most common and earliest dermatologic signs of chronic venous insufficiency. Stasis dermatitis is an inflammatory process that presents as an eczematous rash characterized by itching, erythema, scaling, weeping, erosions, and crusting. Longstanding cases may develop lipodermatosclerosis a fibrosing panniculitis of the subcutaneous tissue. Lipodermatosclerosis typically starts with a firm area of induration at the medial ankle. As the process progresses, the entire leg lower leg can become involved with extension up to the mid leg in more advanced cases. The skin overlying the panniculitis is typically heavily pigmented and bound down to the subcutaneous tissues. Brawny edema above the fibrotic area and on the foot below is seen in advanced cases. Leukocytosis and fever are common in people with stasis dermatitis.

Chronic venous disease is the most common cause of leg ulcers. They are usually found low on the medial ankle over a perforating vein, or along the course of the great or small saphenous veins. They occur more proximally if precipitated by trauma. Venous ulcers are not found on the forefoot or above the level of the knee. Venous ulcers can be multiple or single, and can be exquisitely tender, shallow, exudative and have a granulation base.

The ulcer borders are usually irregular but not undermined. They can extend circumferentially around the leg if left untreated.

Arterial ulcers are typically painful, and punched out or stellate. The surrounding skin is red and taut. Some arterial ulcers are pale - others have a black or yellow eschar. They are often associated with trauma and commonly occur on the foot over pressure points. There may be other signs of arterial insufficiency on the lower limb including thin atrophic or hairless skin, poor pedal pulses, diminished capillary refill, or hypertrophic deformed nails.

Patients with stasis or lipodermatosclerosis are prone to bouts of bacterial cellulitis, usually caused by Staphylococcus aureus or encapsulated streptococci. Typically, stasis dermatitis develops slowly, over a week or more. It is often bilateral. The onset of bacterial cellulitis is usually abrupt, typically developing over 1 or 2 days. Bacterial cellulitis often starts in one area and spreads to adjacent areas. Bacterial cellulitis is unilateral. Both can present with fever and leukocytosis.

In a patient with stasis and cellulitis and the physician is uncertain about whether bacterial cellulitis is present, the physician should consider a trial of bed rest, leg elevation, and if there is fluid overload, diuresis If the cellulitis improves in 24-48 hours, antibacterial therapy and the attendant adverse reactions can be avoided. If it is clear that bacterial cellulitis has occurred, antimicrobial therapy should be given.

[Bacterial Cellulitis](cellulitis)

References

- Stevens et al, Clin Infect Dis, 2014, 59(2): e10-52
- Up-to-Date article: Stasis dermatitis

Upper respiratory infections include several common syndromes including the common cold, bronchitis (see below), pharyngitis (see below) and sinusitis (see below). Most are caused by viruses and there is no benefit from antimicrobial therapy. If a patient presents with a URI, consider specific infections that do respond to antimicrobial therapy like herpes simplex stomatitis, pertussis or thrush. If no condition that benefits from antimicrobial therapy is present, antimicrobials will almost certainly not help but will likely select for antimicrobial resistance and may lead to other adverse effects.

menus.Text:
# FEVER OF UNKNOWN ORIGIN

Fever of unknown origin (FUO) is the occurrence of several episodes of fever greater than 101 degrees Fahrenheit over a period of at least 3 weeks despite 1 week of hospital evaluation. Cases with FUO are often classified in four categories: (1) classical, (2) neutropenic, (3) nosocomial, and (4) fever in persons with HIV/AIDS. Empirical antimicrobial therapy is rarely indicated in patients with FUO.

Note that FUO in neutropenic patients refers to persistent fever that has remained undiagnosed after extensive diagnostic work and empirical antimicrobial therapy. New fever in patients with profound neutropenia is a different syndrome and does require empirical antimicrobial therapy. Infectious Diseases should be involved in any case where empirical treatment for fever of unknown origin is being considered. For more information refer to the neutropenic fever recommendations.

[Neutropenic fever](immunocom-neut-fever)

# MYCOBACTERIUM AVIUM INTRACELLULARE (MAI OR MAC)

MAI colonization in patients with chronic lung disease is common. These patients should not be treated with antimicrobials.

Occasionally, MAI causes pulmonary disease in patients who are not immunosuppressed. Diagnosis and management are complex. Consult Infectious Diseases and/or Pulmonary.

MAI causes systemic disease commonly in patients with HIV/AIDS. Most of these cases do not involve the lungs. After treatment, long-term prophylaxis is usually given. Consult Infectious Diseases in all cases.

[Treatment for pneumonia](m-avium-pneumonia)

[Treatment for disseminated disease](disseminated-m-avium)

[Prophylaxis](prophylaxis-m-avium)

menus.Name: osteomyelitis
menus.Text:
# OSTEOMYELITIS

Obtain material for gram-stain and culture before initiating antimicrobials.
Blood and bone cultures are ideal.

Antibiotics should be held if patient does not have adjacent skin/soft tissue infection.
Duration of treatment and route will vary with differences in location of infection, infecting organism, and host comorbidities.

For patients with infections associated with prosthetic materials see [Infections in bone or joint prostheses](pros-joint-bone-infect)

## Recommend Infectious Disease consultation.

Bone culture is essential and diagnostic. If patient is not clinically ill and a diagnostic procedure is planned, antibiotics can be held until after the procedure.

Therapy should be modified when culture results and patient response to therapy are known.

Duration of treatment is 4 to 6 weeks.

---

menus.Name: copd-exacerbation
menus.Text:
# EXACERBATION OF CHRONIC OBSTRUCTIVE PULMONARY DISEASE (COPD)

Exacerbation of COPD (ECOPD): dyspnea and/or cough and sputum worsening over < 14 days. An acute change in one or more of the following:

- Increased cough frequency and severity
- Increased sputum volume and/or changes in character
- Increased dyspnea

Dyspnea differential: acute coronary syndrome, worsening heart failure, pulmonary embolism, pneumonia, medication non-adherence. Test for influenza and COVID.

---

References:

- Global Initiative for Chronic Obstructive Lung Disease (GOLD) 2025. Access: http://www.goldcopd.org
- Vollenweider DJ Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2018 Oct 29:10(10):CD010257
- Quon BS Chest 2008:133(3):756
- Mathioudakis AG. Eur Respir Rev 2017:26(143):160073
- Lee RA Ann Intern Med 2021:174(6):822
- UpToDate COPD exacerbations: management (March 2025)
- Sanford keyword: Bronchitis, Chronic with Acute Exacerbation
- Mandell Chapter (2020): acute exacerbations of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease
menus.Therapy:
## Inpatient

Available evidence is limited but suggests antibiotics are beneficial for COPD exacerbations in hospitalized patients. Antibiotics are strongly recommended for all patients admitted to the ICU for COPD exacerbation and those with sputum purulence (new or increased from baseline).

Antibiotics are not routinely recommended for non-critically ill patients with clear non-infectious causes for exacerbations (e.g. medication non-adherence, environmental exposures) or known viral infections.

### NOTE: Fluoroquinolones are not listed as a choice because of the risk of serious side effects outweigh the benefits.

Fluoroquinolones FDA Serious Adverse Reactions

### General Ward patients

Preferred:

Amoxicillin-clavulanate 875-125 mg PO q12h R for 5 days

< OR >

Doxycycline 100 mg PO q12h DI for 5 days

< OR >

Azithromycin 500mg PO once, then 250mg q24h days 2-5 O

Unable to tolerate oral antibiotics:

Ampicillin-sulbactam 3 gm IV q6h R for 5 days

History of Pseudomonas in a respiratory isolate in the past year:

Cefepime 2 gm IV q8h R for 5 days

### ICU patients

Preferred:

Ceftriaxone 2 gm IV q24h R for 5 days

History of Pseudomonas in a respiratory isolate in the past year or immunosuppression:

Cefepime 2 gm IV q8h R for 5 days

< OR >

Piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 gm IV q6h R for 5 days

## Outpatient

Patients at risk for poor outcomes are most likely to benefit from early, appropriate antibiotics and close follow-up. Risk factors: age > 65, FEV1 < 50% predicted, 2 or more exacerbations in the past year, hospitalization for exacerbation in the past year, continuous supplemental oxygen, ischemic heart disease or heart failure.

A home action plan with on demand oral corticosteroids and antibiotic is recommended if a patient with moderate or severe COPD had an exacerbation requiring treatment (outpatient, ER, or inpatient) in the previous 12 months.

### COPD Management & Respiratory Symptom Treatment

[Acute Respiratory Infection (ARI) Symptomatic Therapy](ari-symptomatic-therapy)

### Antibiotics:

Antibiotics recommended for patients with moderate or severe chronic COPD
plus an exacerbation with 2 or more of the following:

- Increase or change in sputum purulence
- Increased sputum volume
- Increased dyspnea

Doxycycline 100 mg PO BID for COPD exacerbation 5 days ($) DI
Non-VA order for above
< OR >
Trimethoprim 1 DS tablet BID for COPD exacerbation 5 days ($) R,DI
Non-VA order for above

### Antibiotics if risk factors for poor outcomes:

FEV1 < 50% predicted, 2 or more exacerbations in the past year, hospitalization for exacerbation in the past year, continuous supplemental oxygen, ischemic heart disease or heart failure
Azithromycin 500 mg PO x1 on day 1 then 250 mg PO qday for 4days ($) M
Non-VA order for above

< OR >
Amoxicillin/clav 875/125 mg po bid COPD exacerbation 5 days ($) R
Non-VA order for above

### Pseudomonas in respiratory isolate in past year:

Levofloxacin 750mg PO qday for COPD Exacerbation for 5 days ($) R,DI
Non-VA order for above

menus.Name: influenza-chemoprophylaxis
menus.Text:
# EARLY TREATMENT OF INFLUENZA AS AN ALTERNATIVE TO CHEMOPROPHYLAXIS

In most cases, if a person is suspected of having been exposed to influenza, early treatment, should signs or symptoms develop, is preferred rather than chemoprophylaxis.

The provider should explain the early signs and symptoms of influenza to the patient and advise the patient to immediately contact a health care provider for evaluation and possible early treatment if these symptoms or signs develop.

Influenza-like symptoms or signs include fever, cough, sore throat, runny or stuffy nose, body aches, headache, chills, fatigue, vomiting, and diarrhea.

Influenza can present without fever.

Health care providers should use clinical judgment regarding situations where early recognition of illness and treatment might be an appropriate alternative to chemoprophylaxis.

---

References:

- Centers for Disease Control (CDC) (Accessed 9/8/23) https://www.cdc.gov/flu/hcp/antivirals/summary-clinicians.html
- UpToDate Seasonal influenza in adults: Role of antiviral prophylaxis for prevention
menus.Therapy:
## Early treatment alternative or chemoprophylaxis may be considered:

\*Persons who are part of a high-risk group and are household or close contacts of someone with influenza-like illness Chemoprophylaxis duration: 7 days after last known exposure

# Chemoprophylaxis recommended:

\*For control of outbreaks in institutional settings (long-term care facilities and hospitals)

Chemoprophylaxis duration: minimum of 2 weeks and continuing up to 1 week after the last known case is identified.

Note: Antiviral chemoprophylaxis is recommended for all residents, including those who have received influenza vaccination.

# Chemoprophylaxis considered:

\*Atypical situations (such as case clusters). Contact the state health department for consultation.

# Antiviral Prophylaxis Recommendations

Preferred:
Oseltamivir 75 mg po q24h R
Non-VA order for above

(See information above for length of prophylaxis)

# \*\*Below is for information only, quick orders are not available

Alternative treatment:
Zanamivir is not recommended for patients with chronic respiratory diseases such as asthma or chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. These patients may have bronchospasm with zanamivir. If zanamivir must be used, and patients are using an inhaled bronchodilator, zanamivir should be taken just after the bronchodilator.

Requires Infectious Disease Approval
Zanamivir 2 inhalations (2 x 5 mg)daily [O] (see above for duration of prophylaxis)

# EMPIRIC TREATMENT: HOSPITAL ACQUIRED PNEUMONIA (HAP)

Development of pneumonia 48 hours or more after hospital admission.

## Empiric Treatment (see below for MRSA history or clinically unstable patients)

Obtain MRSA nasal PCR and sputum culture before antibiotics, whenever possible.

Narrow therapy based on results of culture and susceptibility tests. Discontinue MRSA and/or Pseudomonas coverage if not isolated from respiratory cultures.

Discontinue MRSA coverage if MRSA nasal PCR negative.

menus.Name: c-difficile-2-step-testing
menus.Text:
# Clostridioides difficile 2-step Testing

Minneapolis Clinical On-Call Schedule (Infectious Disease)

The Minneapolis VA Health Care System (MVAHCS) is using 2-step testing for C. difficile infection (CDI), updating our current testing method which is a single Polymerase Chain Reaction (PCR) test.

Benefits of 2-step testing are that it can be useful in differentiating patients with true infection vs. those that may simply be colonized.

# What will change:

- All positive PCR tests for CDI (whether stand-alone CDI tests or the enteric pathogen panel testing for CDI and other pathogens) will reflex to a toxin test (a test that detects C. difficile toxin responsible for disease).
- Patients with BOTH a positive PCR and toxin will be reported as "Toxigenic C. difficile detected. Repeat testing should not be performed."
- Patients with a positive PCR but a NEGATIVE toxin test will be reported as "C. difficile detected by PCR, toxin negative by EIA. Possible disease or colonization. Interpretation requires clinical judgement."

# What will not change:

- C. difficile testing should be performed on patients with high suspicion of of CDI, WITHOUT other potential causes of diarrhea (e.g., laxatives, tube feedings, other medications)
- Negative PCR tests will be reported as negative
- Repeat testing within 7 days is strongly discouraged, unless there is a significant change in stool pattern/disease severity
- Patients with ongoing diarrhea (regardless of cause) should be placed in contact plus precautions
- Formed stool will not be tested

# Infectious Disease Service is always available to discuss CDI testing/results.

# Test Interpretation:

Negative PCR: "Negative"

Positive PCR, Positive Toxin: "Toxin producing C. difficile detected"

Positive PCR, negative toxin: "C. difficile present, no toxin detected.

This may represent colonization or disease. Interpretation requires clinical judgement. Consider treatment for severe illness otherwise consistent with CDI. Discussion with Infectious Disease may be helpful."

**From 11pm to 7am, PCR test results will be reported WITHOUT the confirmatory toxin test, which will be run the next morning. Postive PCR results will be reported as:

"C. difficile detected by PCR, confirmatory toxin testing pending. Recommend deferring antibiotic treatment in clinically stable patients where the diagnosis of C. difficile is not certain."

Isolation for patients who are suspected of having CDI and who are receiving treatment.
menus.Inpt: ORZID2 GMENU ABX C DIFFICILE 2 STEP TESTING

# NON-CHOLERA VIBRIO

Non-cholera vibrio is associated with gastroenteritis, septicemia, and wound infections. Vibrio vulnificans infections are acquired from contact with seawater or seafood, especially raw oysters. V. vulnificans cases are more severe than cases with other species. V. parahaemolyticus causes gastroenteritis and milder wound infections.

Antimicrobials do not shorten the course of disease in immunocompetent patients with mild gastroenteritis.

Respiratory papillomas are usually associated with human papillomavirus infection. The papillomas are found in the pharynx, usually in the larynx.  They can be surgically removed, but they often recur.

Cidofovir is injected into the respiratory mucosa after papillomas are removed to prevent recurrences.

menus.Name: rabies-post-exposure-prophylaxis
menus.Text:
# RABIES POST-EXPOSURE PROPHYLAXIS

Patients are given post-exposure prophylaxis based upon their risk including type of exposure, epidemiology of rabies in the area where contact occurred, circumstances of the exposure incident, species and the availability of animal involved. The Minnesota Department of Health has staff available 24/7 to consult health care providers on risk-status of individuals. They can be contacted by phone at 651-201-5414. Refer to link below for more information.

Minnesota Department of Health Guide on Animal Bites and Rabies Risk

Discussion with Infectious Diseases inpatient attending by phone is highly recommended. Use the link below to obtain the pager number for on-call staff.

Infectious Diseases On-Call Schedule

# Wound cleansing

All post-exposure prophylaxis should begin with immediate thorough cleansing of all wounds with soap and water. After cleansing, use povidine-iodine solution to irrigate the wounds.

Povidine-iodine irrigation solution

# Patients without history of rabies vaccination

After wound cleansing, administer rabies immune globulin and first dose of rabies vaccine series immediately.

Rabies immune globulin STAT < AND > rabies vaccine STAT

Administer second, third and fourth doses of rabies vaccine series on days 3, 7, and 14. An additional dose is given on day 28 for immunocompromised patients.

# Patients with history of rabies vaccination

Patients with a history of complete pre-exposure vaccination regimen and a documented antibody response to the rabies virus, do not require rabies immune globulin administration. If the patient does not meet these criteria, treat as a patient without history of rabies vaccination above. If patient does meet these criteria, after wound cleansing, administer first dose of rabies vaccine series.

Rabies vaccine STAT

Administer second dose of rabies vaccine series on day 3.

# Tetanus Prophylaxis

In bite wounds that break the skin, tetanus vaccine is indicated if patient has received <3 doses of tetanus vaccine or immunization history is unknown. Tetanus immune globulin is also indicated in these patients if they have a tetanus prone wound. For patients with 3 or more documented tetanus vaccine doses, tetanus vaccine is indicated if >5 years since last booster in tetanus prone wounds and indicated if >10 years since last booster in non-tetanus-prone wounds.

Tetanus and Diphtheria (Td) vaccine booster dose STAT

# Treatment of infection

[Bite wounds recommendations \(outpatient\)](bite-wnds-s-aureus)

---

References:

- Manning SE, Rupprecht CE, Fishbein D, et al. Human rabies prevention-United States, 2008: recommendations of the Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices. MMWR Recomm Rep 2008, 57:1.
- Rupprecht, Charles E., et al. Use of a reduced (4-dose) vaccine schedule for postexposure prophylaxis to prevent human rabies: recommendations of the advisory committee on immunization practices. MMWR Recomm Rep 59.RR-2 (2010): 1-9

# 10 months

Polio - 3 of 3

Pneumococcal 20 valent (only if GVHD negative)
< OR >

Administer seasonal influenza and COVID-19 via standing orders per CDC recs
Hib (if titers negative - check yearly until positive)

Hepatitis B (if titers negative - check yearly until positive)

# IMMUNIZATION OF PREGNANT PATIENTS

Pregnant women should receive the tetanus, diphtheria, and acellular pertussis vaccine (Tdap) during pregnancy and the influenza vaccine during or before pregnancy. Live vaccines are contraindicated (e.g. MMR and Varicella). See immunization information pages located at the bottom of this page for other indications, contraindications, and one-time dose orders to listed vaccines.

Patient vaccine history
