menus.Name: approach-to-bacteremia
menus.Text:
# APPROACH TO BACTEREMIA

Bacteremia usually results from a focal infection somewhere in the body. If a focal infection is not obvious, a careful search should be made beginning with a detailed history and physical examination.

If a focal infection seems to be the source of the bacteremia, select antimicrobials active against pathogens likely to be present in the focal infection. Return to the main menu and select the relevant diagnosis or syndrome.

# For infections with signs and/or symptoms of severe sepsis, like hypotension or end organ dysfunction

[Sepsis, severe sepsis, and septic shock](sepsis-and-shock)

# Sequence of evaluation

Obtain blood cultures before starting antibiotics when signs or symptoms suggest bacteremia. Obtain 2 or 3 blood culture sets from different venipuncture sites within a 24 hour period. When suspicion is strong and the patient's signs and symptoms have not responded, obtain 2 blood culture sets the next day. For more information about blood cultures, see recommendations on the Q-drive Q:\MICROBIOL INFO FOR CLINICIANS\BLOOD CULTURE Recommendations.doc

# Empirical treatment of suspected bacteremia if local infection is not apparent and blood cultures are not yet positive

[Suspected bacteremia, blood cultures not yet positive](suspected-bacteremia-cultures-not-yet-positive)

Cultures usually become positive after 1 or more days. Usually interim results are reported first, followed by final identification and sensitivities after another day or two. Adjust antimicrobials as appropriate as this sequence unfolds.

# Preliminary results of a positive culture are available

When a focal infection is not apparent, the type of bacteria growing in blood culture might suggest a focal infection and direct the search for a diagnosis.

When a focal infection is apparent, it may suggest the identity of the bacteria growing in blood cultures before the laboratory completes its identification.

Preliminary positive results should lead to changes in antimicrobial therapy to target suspected pathogens, narrow the spectrum, reduce toxicity, and reduce costs.

[Interim report of Gram-positive cocci in pairs](interim-gram-positive-cocci-pairs)

[Interim report of Gram-positive cocci in pairs and clusters](interim-gram-positive-cocci-clusters)

[Interim report of Gram-positive cocci in pairs and chains](interim-gram-positive-cocci-chains)

[Interim report of Gram-negative bacilli](interim-gram-negative-bacilli)

[Interim report of Gram-negative cocci](interim-gram-negative-cocci)

[Interim report of Gram-positive bacilli](interim-gram-positive-bacilli)

[Interim report of yeast](interim-yeast)

References

- Mandell Chapter Sepsis, Severe Sepsis and Septic Shock

menus.Text:
# INTERIM REPORT OF GRAM-NEGATIVE BACILLI

Most Gram-negative bacilli grow in aerobic or anaerobic bottles. Pseudomonas nearly always grows in aerobic bottles. One drug is sufficient to treat Gram-negative bacillus bacteremia, unless the patient is critically ill.

References

- Medical Letter Choice of Antimicrobials 2010, 8.94
- Sanford keyword: Pseudomonas aeruginosa
- Up-to-Date article: Gram-negative bacillary bacteremia in adults

Ceftriaxone 2 gm IV q24h ($) M

## Empirical treatment if pseudomonas is suspected

Piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 gm IV q6h (Cost $$) R

For patients with non-severe penicillin allergy
Cefepime 2 gm IV q8h (Cost $$) R

For patients with severe penicillin allergy
Aztreonam 2 gm IV q8h (Cost $$$$) R

## Empirical treatment for critically ill patients or resistant organism likely

Gentamicin 5 mg/kg IV q24h (Cost $) R,O <AND> piperacillin-tazobactam
4.5 gm q6h (Cost $$) [R]

menus.Name: interim-gram-positive-bacilli
menus.Text:
# INTERIM REPORT OF GRAM-POSITIVE BACILLI
There are three typical morphologies (1)large and regular, (2)medium sized and variable, and (3)small and pleomorphic.  The large, uniformly rod-shaped Gram-positive bacilli are usually Bacillus spp. (aerobic) or Clostridium species (anaerobic).  Bacillus spp. include Bacillus subtilis (usually a contaminant), Bacillus cereus, and Bacillus anthracis.  Medium-sized Gram-positive bacilli are usually Lactobacilli (anaerobic).  Small and pleomorphic bacilli are usually Listeria (aerobic), diphtheroids (aerobic), Propionibacteria (anaerobic), and Corynebacteria (aerobic).

[LARGE UNIFORM BACILLI in an AEROBIC bottle](interim-large-bacilli-aerobic-bottle)

[LARGE UNIFORM BACILLI in an ANAEROBIC bottle](interim-large-bacilli-anaerobic-bottle)

[SMALL PLEOMORPHIC BACILLI in AEROBIC bottle](interim-small-bacilli-aerobic-bottle)

[SMALL PLEOMORPHIC BACILLI in ANAEROBIC bottle](interim-small-bacilli-anaerobic-bottle)

menus.Name: interim-gram-positive-cocci-chains
menus.Term1: Gram-positive cocci in pairs and chains bacteremia
menus.Term2: Interim blood culture: Gram-positive cocci in chains
menus.Text:
# INTERIM REPORT OF GRAM-POSITIVE COCCI IN PAIRS AND CHAINS

If chains are reported, streptococci are likely. If short chains are reported, enterococci are likely. Beta-lactam antimicrobials are more effective than vancomycin in killing susceptible streptococci and enterococci, so penicillin or ampicillin should be used if resistance is unlikely.

If the patient is severely ill or is likely to be colonized with resistant organisms, treat with vancomycin until susceptibility results are known.

References

- Medical Letter Choice of Antimicrobials 2010, 8.94
- Sanford keyword: Enterococci
- Sanford keyword: Streptococci

# INTERIM REPORT OF GRAM-POSITIVE COCCI IN PAIRS AND CLUSTERS

This suggests staphylococci. Empirical therapy should cover methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus. If a susceptible isolate is identified, beta-lactam antimicrobials should be used as they are most effective at killing staphylococci. When a final pathogen is identified, treatment depends on which specific bacterium is identified.

References

- Medical Letter Choice of Antimicrobials 2010, 8.94
- Sanford keyword: Staphylococci

menus.Text:
# INTERIM REPORT OF GRAM-POSITIVE COCCI IN PAIRS

A preliminary report of gram-positive cocci in pairs suggests staphylococci, streptococci, or enterococci. If the patient is severely ill, is likely colonized with resistant organisms, or if staphylococci or enterococci are likely, treat with vancomycin until susceptibility results are known.

Cephalosporins are not active against enterococci or methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus.

References

- Medical Letter Choice of Antimicrobials 2010, 8.94
- Sanford keyword: Enterococci
- Sanford keyword: Staphylococci
- Sanford keyword: Streptococci

menus.Name: interim-large-bacilli-aerobic-bottle
menus.Text:
# LARGE UNIFORM BACILLI IN AN AEROBIC BOTTLE

Large uniform bacilli in an aerobic bottle usually suggest Bacillus species.

Bacillus subtilis is usually a contaminant, Bacillus cereus is uncommon but usually pathogenic. If Bacillus anthracis is suspected or isolated contact Infectious Diseases immediately.

References

- Hendricks et al., Emerg Infect Dis 2014, 20.2
- Medical Letter Choice of Antimicrobials 2010, 8.94
- Up-to-Date article: Bacillus cereus and other non-anthracis Bacillus species

# LARGE UNIFORM BACILLI IN AN ANAEROBIC BOTTLE

Large uniform bacilli in an anaerobic bottle usually suggest clostridium, a potentially severe pathogen. Combination therapy is recommended for necrotizing infections as clindamycin has the theoretical benefit of inhibiting toxin production.

References

- Medical Letter Choice of Antimicrobials 2010, 8.94
- Sanford keyword: Clostridium perfingens
- Stevens et al., Clinical Infectious Diseases 2014 59.2

menus.Name: interim-small-bacilli-aerobic-bottle
menus.Text:
# SMALL PLEOMORPHIC BACILLI IN AEROBIC BOTTLE

Small pleomorphic bacilli in aerobic bottle are usually diphtheroids. These are usually contaminants. Uncommonly such organisms prove to be Listeria monocytogenes, which when present in a blood culture is likely a pathogen.

Listeria is more likely in patients with impaired cell-mediated immunity, pregnant women, elderly and patients on immunosuppressive therapy for transplantation.

References

- Mandell chapter: Listeria Monocytogenes
- Mandell chapter: Other Coryneform Bacteria and Rhodococci
- Medical Letter Choice of Antimicrobials 2010, 8.94
- Sanford keyword: Listeria monocytogenes
- Sanford keyword: Propionibacterium acnes
- Sanford keyword: Corynebacterium

menus.Name: interim-yeast
menus.Text:
# INTERIM REPORT OF YEAST

Consult Infectious Diseases in all cases. If the yeast appear to be or are known to be Candida species treat as follows. If other yeasts (e.g.

Cryptococcus, Histoplasma) are suspected, contact Infectious Diseases for treatment advice.

Refer to specific organism for yeasts other than candida
[Fungi](fungi)

Most Candida can be treated with fluconazole. If the patient is critically ill or neutropenic or has recently taken an azole antifungal, or if Candida krusei or C. glabrata are suspected, micafungin should be used initially. Removal of central venous catheter is associated with decreased mortality. Call Infectious Diseases for advice.

References

- Andes et al, Clinical Infectious Diseases 2012, 54.8
- Mandell chapter: Candida Species
- Pappas et al, Clinical Infectious Diseases 2016, 62.4e1-50
- Sanford keyword: Candidiasis
menus.Therapy:
## Empirical treatment for patients with mild to moderate illness who have no prior azole antifungal therapy

Fluconazole 800 mg PO once then 400 mg PO q24h ($) R,DI

For patients who cannot take oral medication
Fluconazole 800 mg IV once then 400 mg IV q24h ($) R,DI

## Empirical treatment for critically ill patients, neutropenic patients, patients who have recently taken azole antifungals, or if C. glabrata or C. krusei are suspected

Micafungin 100 mg IV q24h ($$$) DI
